0.body: This book specifies the language that interrexx implements: the Rexx language as ooRexx extends it. It describes what a program means, and what the interpreter must do when it runs one.
0.title: Introduction

1.body: The book is written for three readers: an engineer changing the interpreter, who needs the exact behavior before touching code; an LLM agent doing the same work, which may read one page at a time with no history behind it; and a reviewer judging whether a change is correct. It assumes you can read Rexx, and it does not teach the language.
1.title: Who it is for

40.12 [conv.whole.digits] On a 64-bit host, which is what interrexx targets, the value of a whole-number argument is its number rounded to 18 significant digits; when the first digit dropped is 5 or more, the magnitude rounds up, otherwise down. The caller's NUMERIC DIGITS setting plays no part. If the rounded value has a fractional part other than zero, or its magnitude is 10**18 or more, the argument raises SYNTAX 40.12; otherwise its value is that integer. (The reference manual gives 9 digits for 32-bit hosts; this book does not specify those.) say substr('abcdef', '2.000', 1) substr('abcdef', '1.0000000000000000001', 1)

[util.sysfilecopy.answer] When source is a file that may be read, and target is a name that a file may be written under, the call writes the bytes of source to target and answers 0. target is made when no entry has the name; when a file has it, its bytes are replaced and none of the old ones are left. A target that names a symbolic link is written through the link: the link stays a link and the file it points to gets the bytes, and a link that points to nothing has that file made. A source that is a symbolic link is read through the link, so the copy is a file of its own. The bytes are copied as they are, so a file with no bytes copies to a file with none, and source is not changed. The names are not patterns. call charout 'c1zqcpa', 'a' || '00ff0d0a'x || 'bc'

First, when source names an entry and target names the same file, under the same name, under another spelling of its name, such as ./ before it, through a symbolic link or through a hard link, the call answers 17 and changes nothing. Two names are the same file when they are on the same device and have the same inode number ( Deviation 155 ). 1005.body: SysTempFileName(template [, filler]) rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysTempFileName SysTempFileName invents the name of a file that does not exist, from a template in which some characters stand for digits. It makes nothing: it only finds a name. The template is read as the chapter page says for every name, except that the filler characters are counted in it as it is written.

[util.systempfilename.answer] Every filler character of template is replaced by a digit, chosen at random, and the answer is the full name of the result: when the template is relative, the name is taken from the current directory, and it is cleaned up as for every name . A filler in the directory part of the template is replaced as well, and the directory need not exist. Which digits are chosen is not specified, and two calls with one template can answer different names. The call makes no file, so a name that it answers is free until a program takes it. here = directory()
p = here || '/c1zqtf'
n = SysTempFileName('c1zqtf???')
parse var n (p) d
say digits(d, 3) SysFileExists(n) SysIsFile(n)

[util.syssearchpath.found] The answer is the full name of the first file that the search finds, in the form that every name is cleaned up to: it starts with a slash and has no . or .. component and no run of slashes. A file is a regular file, or a symbolic link to one, and a link in the name is not replaced by what it points to. The current directory, when option is C, and then each directory of the list are tried by joining it and name with a slash. The first of them in which that is the name of an entry, with symbolic links followed, decides. When the entry is a file, the answer is its name. When it is anything else, such as a directory or a fifo, the answer is the null string, even when a later directory holds a file of the name. A symbolic link that points to nothing, and a name in a directory that the program may not search, are no entry, and the search goes on. A name that is not found, or is the null string or ., has no answer: the call answers the null string. Blanks, * and ? are characters of the name, so g is not g and no pattern is expanded. Times, the sizes of directories, the permission bits a new file gets and the order in which matches are stored belong to the host or to the file system. [util.sysfiletree.spec] filespec is a path whose last component is the pattern. * matches any run of characters, including none and including a leading period, ? matches one character, [ ] matches one of the characters listed in it or in one of its ranges such as a-o, and [! ] or [^ ] one that is not. The entries . and .. that every directory holds are never matches. In a class, a ] that comes first and a - that comes first or last stand for themselves, a range whose ends are in the wrong order matches nothing, and a name such as [:upper:] or [:digit:] stands for the characters of that kind. A [ with no ] after it is an ordinary character, and so is \: nothing in a pattern is escaped. Only the last component is a pattern. In an earlier component *, ? and [ are ordinary characters of a directory's name, so s*/x looks in a directory whose name is s*. The match is case-sensitive, and the option letter I makes it ignore case for the last component only: the directory part of a path always has to be spelled as the directory is. A pattern with no wildcards matches the entry of that name. d = 'c2zqft05'

A filespec whose last component is . or .. names a directory and not a pattern: it matches the entries of that directory, as the same path with a slash at its end does, so dir/sub/.. and dir/. both match the entries of dir. A path that has a component that is a file, a component that does not exist, a directory on the way that the program may not search, or a directory that the program may not read whose entries are needed (the one the last component is matched in, or the one a filespec ending in a slash names), matches nothing and is not an error; the unreadable directory itself is still matched by its own name. A relative path is read as every name is . A filespec that starts with ~ is read as the home rule says, with these exceptions. A filespec that is ~name alone, where no user has that name, is a pattern for the entries of the current directory, so it matches a directory ~name there. A filespec that starts with ~name/, where no user has that name, starts at / when only one component follows the slash, and matches nothing when more follow. A HOME that does not start with a slash is taken from the current directory, as any relative name is. Each name stored is the full name of the match, formed as QUALIFY forms a name: made absolute, with the repeated slashes, the periods and the .. components of the path taken out ( Deviation 34 says where ooRexx takes out a different component). [util.sysfiletree.none] A path that matches nothing gives .0 equal to 0 and the answer 0, whatever the reason: a pattern that no entry fits, a directory or file that is not there, a path through a file, a directory whose entries the program may not read. Where a directory is unreadable, a search with S stores what it finds elsewhere and does not report it. The entries of a directory that the program may read but not search are not found either ( Deviation 154 ). d = 'c2zqft14'

unreadable, S: 0 1 [util.sysfiletree.deviation.154] An entry that cannot be examined is treated in one of two ways. An entry of a directory that the program may read but not search has a name that can be read and data that cannot, so it is left out of every listing, whatever options are given. A symbolic link that points to nothing is a file, listed with the data of the link itself: its size is the length of the name it holds, its permissions are those of a link, and its kind is l. It is not a directory, so the D option leaves it out. ooRexx lists both entries with the date, size and permissions that belong to another entry. The example is not run against it. d = 'c2zqft18'

102.body: ANSI: 6.3.2.10, 8.3.5; rexxref: General Concepts > Clauses and Instructions > Commands; General Concepts > Commands to External Environments > Commands Deviations: D40 A command hands work to something outside the program. The clause is a bare expression, and the interpreter works out its value as a string and sends that string to an environment, which runs it and answers with a return code. This page specifies what is sent, where the return code goes and what else a command leaves behind. Which clauses are commands is decided by the lexical rules . Which environment is current, how the ADDRESS instruction changes it and what the environments are belong to the ADDRESS instruction and to the environment chapter, so the examples here use the environment named system, which runs its commands in the host's shell, and the name that the ADDRESS function reports is the one the ADDRESS instruction set. What a command does is the business of the environment, and the examples need of it only that exit n for a small n answers the return code n and that echo writes its arguments.
102.title: Commands

1020.body: SysFileSearch(target, file, stem, [options]) rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysFileSearch SysFileSearch reads a text file and stores the lines that contain a string in a stem or an array, in the order of the file, with their line numbers when asked. It answers 0, or 3 when the file cannot be read. Note. The examples write the files they search themselves and remove them.
1020.title: SysFileSearch

The call follows the argument rule : a missing required argument raises SYNTAX 88.901, a fifth argument raises SYNTAX 88.922, and an argument that is an object other than a string is read by its string value, or raises SYNTAX 88.909 when it has none. stem is the exception to the last point: an array object or a stem object is the stem itself, and any other object that has no string value raises SYNTAX 40.925, as a name that is not a stem name does. It answers 0, or -1 when it did not set the time. Note. The examples set times in the middle of a day and a month, far from the changes between summer and winter time, because the time is a local time of the host. 1031.body: SysDumpVariables([filename]) rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysDumpVariables SysDumpVariables writes the variables of the code that calls it, one line for each, to the standard output or to the end of a file. It answers 0 when it has done so. Note. The order in which the lines of a dump come is not specified, so the examples of this page read the lines back and print them in the order of their bytes, with a routine called show. 1035.body: SysStemCopy(fromstem, tostem, [from], [to], [count], [option]) rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysStemCopy SysStemCopy copies items of one stem array to another stem array, either over the items that are there or between them. It answers 0 when it has done so. A call that cannot be done raises a SYNTAX condition and never answers another number. The stem arrays are the ones that the chapter page describes: the tail 0 holds the number of items and the tails 1 and up hold the items. Note. Most examples of this page run in a routine that sets the source to the four items a b c d and the target to the two items x y before every call, and that prints the answer or the error code, and then the target as its count, a colon and its items.
1035.title: SysStemCopy

1036.body:
[util.sysstemcopy.args] fromstem and tostem are required. They name stems as the stem name rule says, and may name the same stem. from, to, count and option are optional, and an omitted one takes its default: from and to are 1, count is the number of items of the source from from to its end, and option is O. The call follows the argument rule : a missing required argument raises SYNTAX 88.901 and an argument past the sixth raises SYNTAX 88.922 ( Deviation 101 is about which of the two comes first). from and to are read as whole numbers that are at least 1, and an argument that is 0, negative, fractional, text, the null string or too large raises SYNTAX 88.905. count is read as a whole number that is at least 0, and an argument that is negative, fractional, text, the null string or too large raises SYNTAX 88.904. A number is read with its blanks, a leading plus sign, a decimal point and an exponent, so that ' 2 ' and 1e0 are numbers. The value is read as the whole-number rule says, so that 1.0000000000000000001 is fractional, and it must be less than 10**18. An object that is not a string is read by its request('STRING'), and when that answers no string, by its STRING method, so that .nil is read as The NIL object and raises SYNTAX 88.905, or SYNTAX 88.904 for count. option is read by its first character, in either case: I inserts the items, O overwrites the items, and the rest of the argument is not read, so Insert is I. Anything else raises SYNTAX 40.920: the null string, a blank before the letter, another letter. An option that is an object whose request answers no string, .nil among them, raises SYNTAX 88.909, and it has no STRING fallback either: an object that has only a STRING method that answers I raises SYNTAX 88.909. The items of the target below to, above the last tail written, and past its count are not touched. An item is copied as it is, so that an object that is an item of the source is then the item of the target too. [util.sysstemcopy.insert] With I, the call first moves the items of the target from to to its count up by count places, and then copies as O does. So the copied items stand at the tails to to to + count - 1, the items that were there follow them, and the count of the target is its old count plus count, written as a plain whole number. to may be one past the count of the target, which appends the items. 1041.body: SysStemDelete(stem, start, [count]) rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysStemDelete SysStemDelete removes one or more items from a stem array and closes the gap: the items after them move down, and the count of the stem gets smaller. It answers 0 when it has done so. A call that cannot be done raises a SYNTAX condition and never answers another number. The stem array is the one that the chapter page describes. Note. Most examples of this page run in a routine that sets the stem to the four items a b c d before every call, and that prints the answer or the error code, and then the stem as its count, a colon and its items.
1041.title: SysStemDelete

1042.body:
[util.sysstemdelete.args] stem and start are required, and count is optional and is 1 when it is left out. stem names a stem as the stem name rule says. The call follows the argument rule : a missing required argument raises SYNTAX 88.901 and a fourth argument raises SYNTAX 88.922 ( Deviation 101 is about which of the two comes first). start and count are read as whole numbers that are at least 1, with their blanks, a leading plus sign, a decimal point and an exponent, so that ' 2 ' and 1e0 are numbers. The value is read as the whole-number rule says, so that 1.0000000000000000001 is fractional, and it must be less than 10**18. An argument that is 0, negative, fractional, text, the null string, blank or too large raises SYNTAX 88.905, and a count of 0 is such an argument too: the call cannot be used to delete nothing. An object that is not a string is read by its request('STRING'), and when that answers no string, by its STRING method, so that .nil is read as The NIL object and raises SYNTAX 88.905. call try "SysStemDelete()"

[util.syssteminsert.insert] The call moves the items position to the count of the stem up by one place, one at a time from the last, and stores value in the tail position. The count of the stem is then its old count plus one, written as a plain whole number. position may be one past the count, and the value is then appended; the stem may be empty, and position is then 1. A tail above the old count is overwritten when an item moves into it. The value is stored as it is, so that an object is the item itself and not its string, and .nil is stored as .nil. 1049.body: SysStemSort(stem, [order], [type], [start], [end], [firstcol], [lastcol]) rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysStemSort SysStemSort puts the items of a stem array, or of a part of it, in order. The order is that of the items as strings of bytes, read from a column of each item if the call says so, and the call can ignore the case of letters and reverse the order. It answers 0 when it has done so. A call that cannot be done raises a SYNTAX condition and never answers another number. The stem array is the one that the chapter page describes. Note. Most examples of this page put the items of a stem s. in a routine called fill, whose arguments are the items, and print them with a routine called dump, which writes each item in square brackets. Both are shown in the first example that uses them.

1050.body:
[util.sysstemsort.args] stem is required, and the six other arguments are optional. An omitted argument takes its default: order is A, type is C, start is 1, end is the count of the stem, firstcol is 1 and lastcol is the end of each item. stem names a stem as the stem name rule says, with the addition of the next rule . The call follows the argument rule : a missing stem raises SYNTAX 88.901 and an eighth argument raises SYNTAX 88.922 ( Deviation 101 is about which of the two comes first). start, end, firstcol and lastcol are read as whole numbers that are at least 1, with their blanks, a leading plus sign, a decimal point and an exponent. The value is read as the whole-number rule says, so that 1.0000000000000000001 is fractional, and it must be less than 10**18. An argument that is 0, negative, fractional, text, the null string or too large raises SYNTAX 88.905. An object that is not a string is read by its request('STRING'), and when that answers no string, by its STRING method, so that .nil is read as The NIL object and raises SYNTAX 88.905. order is read by its first character, in either case: A is ascending and D is descending, and the rest of the argument is not read, so Descending is D. type is read the same way: C respects the case of letters and I ignores it, and Ignore is I. Anything else in order or type raises SYNTAX 40.920: the null string, a blank before the letter, another letter. An order or type that is an object whose request answers no string, .nil among them, raises SYNTAX 88.909, and it has no STRING fallback either: an object that has only a STRING method that answers I raises SYNTAX 88.909 as type. A MutableBuffer that holds D is D. call try "SysStemSort()"

88.905 [util.sysstemsort.name] A name that has characters after its first period names the array whose tails start with those characters. The letters a to z among them are put in upper case and every other character stays as it is, and a period is added after them unless they already end in one. The part up to the first period is a name as the stem name rule says. The other three functions that take a stem name raise SYNTAX 40.919 for such a name. 1051.body:
[util.sysstemsort.compare] The items are compared as strings of bytes, from the first byte of each, so that the order is that of the byte values. With A an item that compares less comes first, and with D an item that compares more comes first. An item that is the start of a longer one is less than it, and blanks count as any other byte, so that a is less than a and the null string is less than a blank. The byte 00 is an ordinary byte too. The items are not read as numbers: 10 is less than 9, and 01 is less than 1. Items that compare as equal keep the order they had before the call, with A and with D alike. call fill 'b', 'a ', 'a', '', 'ab', '10', '9', 'B', '_', ' '
call SysStemSort 's.'
say dump()

say dump()

[util.sysstemsort.cols] firstcol and lastcol choose the bytes of each item that are compared: the bytes from the column firstcol to the column lastcol of the item, the first byte being column 1. An item that has fewer bytes than the column firstcol compares as the null string, so that it is less than any item that has a byte there; lastcol may be past the end of an item, and then the comparison reaches the end of the item. The columns change only what is compared: the whole items are what the call puts in order. call fill 'b2', 'a9', 'c1'

1053.body:
[util.sysstemsort.range] start and end choose the items that are put in order, the items from start to end; the items outside them keep their places and their values, and are not read, so they may have no value. An item that is alone in the range, as with start equal to end, is still read. The call raises SYNTAX 40.923, and changes nothing, when start or end is more than the count of the stem. An end of 999999999999999999, the largest that is allowed, is taken as an end that is left out, the count of the stem. A stem with the count 0 has no item, and then no range is checked: the call answers 0 and does nothing, for every start and end that pass the checks before the tail 0 ( the order rule ), so that a start above a given end still raises SYNTAX 40.921. The tail 0 is never changed, and the tails above the count are not touched. A count below 0 raises SYNTAX 40.922. call fill 'f', 'e', 'd', 'c', 'b', 'a'

1055.body: rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysAddRexxMacro; Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysDropRexxMacro; Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysQueryRexxMacro; Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysReorderRexxMacro The macrospace is a table of named routines that the interpreter's service keeps for every program that uses it. A program puts a routine into it with SysAddRexxMacro , and a program calls the routine by its name, as it calls any other routine that it does not define itself. A routine of the table is a macro. This page says what a macro is and how it runs; the pages of the functions that work on the table say how each one is called and what it answers: SysAddRexxMacro , SysDropRexxMacro , SysQueryRexxMacro and SysReorderRexxMacro : putting a macro in, taking it out, asking whether it is there, and moving it before or after the files. SysClearRexxMacroSpace , SysSaveRexxMacroSpace and SysLoadRexxMacroSpace : emptying the table, and keeping it in a file or bringing it back. Note. The examples add only macros of their own, whose names start with C4ZQ (and, to show a point, LEFT and the null string), and drop each one again, so that a macro that an example leaves does not change what a later one finds.
1055.title: The macrospace

1056.body:
[util.macrospace.shared] A macro belongs to the service and not to the program that added it. It is found by every program that uses the service, whether that program started before the macro was added or starts later. It stays until it is dropped, until the macrospace is cleared, or until the service ends; how long the service lives is not specified. In the example a program starts another with a command: the child finds the macro of its parent, adds a macro and drops the macro of the parent, and the parent, after the child has ended, finds the one and not the other. call lineout 'c4zqshared.rex', 'return "from the parent" arg(1)'

0 [] [util.macrospace.run] A call of the name of a macro, whether as a function or by CALL, runs the program that the macro was made from, as a routine of the code that makes the call. The call passes its arguments the way a call of any routine does: arg() holds their number and an omitted argument is empty. Each call starts a fresh run, so the variables of the caller are not there and the variables of an earlier run are gone. A RETURN with a value ends the macro with that value as the answer; a RETURN without one, or the end of the program, leaves the call without an answer, so that a function call raises SYNTAX 44.1 and a CALL sets no RESULT. An EXIT ends only the macro, and the caller goes on: the value of the EXIT is the answer, and an EXIT without a value leaves the call without one. A SYNTAX condition that the macro raises is raised in the caller, with the same code. For PARSE SOURCE, the second word is FUNCTION or SUBROUTINE as for any routine, and the third is the name as the call wrote it, whatever case the macro was added in: in capitals for a name written as a symbol, and as written for a name written as a string. 1057.body: SysAddRexxMacro(name, file [, order]) rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysAddRexxMacro SysAddRexxMacro reads a Rexx program from a file and puts it into the macrospace under a name, as a macro that a call of that name runs. It answers 0 when the macro is in, and a number that is not zero when it is not.
1057.title: SysAddRexxMacro

1058.body:
[util.sysaddrexxmacro.args] name and file are required strings, and order is optional. The count and the omission of an argument, and an object in the place of one, follow the argument rule : a call with no name or no file, or with either one omitted, raises SYNTAX 88.901, a fourth argument raises SYNTAX 88.922, and .nil raises SYNTAX 88.909. An object that is not a string but has a string value is read by that value. The rules for what a name is are on the page of the macrospace . A file that is the null string names no file that can be read, so the call answers 7. When more than one check fails, the count and the omission come first, then the order (the next rule), and only then is the file read, so that a bad order is reported for a file that is not there. call lineout 'c4zqargs.rex', 'return "x"'

1069.body: SysClearRexxMacroSpace() rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysClearRexxMacroSpace SysClearRexxMacroSpace removes every macro from the macrospace , and answers 0.
1069.title: SysClearRexxMacroSpace

107.body: DO [LABEL name] [COUNTER name] [repetitor] [conditional]; instructions; END [name] ANSI: 6.3.2.12, 8.3.6; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > DO Deviations: D1, D25, D26, D38, D47, D118 DO opens a block of instructions that ends at a matching END. Without anything after the keyword it groups the clauses so that they stand where the language expects one instruction. With a repetitor, a condition, or both, it runs the block again and again: a number of times, for ever, with a variable that steps through a range, or once for each item of a collection. This page specifies each form, the order in which the parts of the clause are evaluated, the tests that end a loop, the value that the control variable has afterwards, and the errors. LOOP is the same instruction under another keyword, and LEAVE and ITERATE steer a loop from inside. The clause has one of these shapes, where each part in brackets is optional. The LABEL and COUNTER phrases come first, in either order. Then comes at most one repetitor, which is a count, FOREVER, name = expression with TO, BY and FOR phrases, name OVER expression, or WITH with an INDEX and an ITEM phrase and OVER expression. Then comes at most one WHILE or UNTIL phrase. The block follows, and END closes it.

[instr.do.group] A DO with nothing after the keyword, or with only a LABEL phrase, is a simple group. The interpreter runs the clauses between the DO and its END once, in order, and no variable changes because of the DO. A group lets several clauses stand in the place of one, as the branch of an IF does. It is not a loop, so a LEAVE or an ITERATE with no name does not see it, as the LEAVE rule says, while a LEAVE that names its label does leave it. x = 1

[util.syscreatepipe.answer] The answer is two whole numbers, a blank between them: the first names the end of the pipe that is read, the second the end that is written. They are numbers of open files of the program, which stay open for the rest of its run: a command that ADDRESS starts has them too, and can write to the second number and read from the first, as a shell does with >& and <& and a number (the example runs its commands through bash, because some shells, dash among them, refuse a number of 10 or more). What is written is read in the order in which it was written. Two calls make two pipes, whose four numbers are all different, and what is written to one is not read from the other. 1089.body:
[util.syssetpriority.args] delta is a required whole number. class is a whole number too, and may be omitted; its value, and a place that is left empty, make no difference to the call ( the next rule ). A number is read as the whole-number rule says, and is a whole number when it then has no fraction or only zeros, as 1.0, 1e0 and 2.00000000000000000001 have, in the range -2147483648 to 2147483647. A value that is not a whole number or is out of that range raises SYNTAX 88.907: a fraction such as 1.5 or .5, the null string, a word, and the words IDLE, NORMAL, LOWEST and the like, with which some descriptions of the function name classes and deltas, are not numbers here. A value that is given is checked before the omission of delta is reported, so that SysSetPriority('x') raises 88.907 and SysSetPriority(1) raises SYNTAX 88.901; three arguments raise SYNTAX 88.922. When an argument past the last one comes with an omitted or wrong argument, Deviation 101 says which error is raised. [instr.do.count] DO expression runs the block a fixed number of times. The expression is evaluated once, when the DO is reached, and its value is the number of passes, so a later assignment to a variable of the expression changes nothing. 1099.body: SysCreateEventSem([name], [reserved]); SysOpenEventSem(name); SysPostEventSem(handle); SysResetEventSem(handle); SysWaitEventSem(handle, [timeout]); SysCloseEventSem(handle); SysPulseEventSem(handle) rexxref: Deprecated Rexx features > RexxUtil Semaphore functions Deviations: D20, D43, D158 The functions SysCreateEventSem, SysOpenEventSem, SysPostEventSem, SysResetEventSem, SysWaitEventSem and SysCloseEventSem make and use an event semaphore, a counter of posts that an activity can wait on. They are deprecated; the EventSemaphore class takes their place, and differs from them: one post of an object of the class ends the wait of every activity that waits and stays until it is reset, and one post of these functions ends one wait. The mutex semaphore functions work the same way for a lock. A semaphore is named by its handle, a string of digits that the function that made it answers. Every function that takes a handle takes it as its first argument, and answers 0 when it did what it was asked; the other numbers that a function answers are listed with it.

1106.body: SysCreateMutexSem(name); SysOpenMutexSem(name); SysRequestMutexSem(handle, [timeout]); SysReleaseMutexSem(handle); SysCloseMutexSem(handle) rexxref: Deprecated Rexx features > RexxUtil Semaphore functions Deviations: D20, D43, D158 The functions SysCreateMutexSem, SysOpenMutexSem, SysRequestMutexSem, SysReleaseMutexSem and SysCloseMutexSem make and use a mutex semaphore, a lock that one activity at a time can hold. They are deprecated; the MutexSemaphore class takes their place, and differs from them in two ways that the rules below show: a lock of the class has an owner, the activity that took it, and the owner can take it again, where a lock of these functions is not owned and is taken once. The event semaphore functions own the rules for the handle, for the timeout and for closing, which these functions share.

[instr.do.over] DO name OVER expression runs the block once for each item that a collection yields, and assigns the item to name before the pass. The expression is evaluated once, before name is assigned, and the loop sends it the message MAKEARRAY , whatever the class of the object is: an instance of a subclass of List is sent it as any other collection is ( Deviation 118 ). The items are those of the Array that comes back, in its order, and they are taken when the loop starts, so a change to the collection during the loop does not add, remove or alter an item that the loop visits. An Array yields its items in index order and skips an index that holds none, and a List and a Queue yield theirs from first to last. A String yields its lines, so a null string yields none. A Stem , a Directory and a Table yield their indexes, which for a Stem are the tails of the existing compound variables, and a Set yields its members. The order of those four is not specified, as Deviation 1 says for a Stem and Deviation 33 for the others. 1112.body: SysCls() rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysCls SysCls clears the screen of a terminal. It does so by running the program clear of the system, and it answers what the system reports about that run. What clear writes, and whether it writes anything, depends on the terminal that the environment names; so the examples of this page put a clear of their own in front of the system's, in a directory that they make and remove, and print what that one does.

[util.syscls.run] SysCls hands the command clear, with no argument, to the shell of the system. The shell looks for clear along the environment variable PATH as it is at the moment of the call, so a program that sets PATH with VALUE changes which clear runs. [util.sysformatmessage.substitutions] substitutions gives the strings that fill the places &1 to &9. It is sent MAKEARRAY, and the items of the array that it answers, in order, are the inserts: the first item is for &1, the second for &2, and so on. A string is split at its line ends, as its makeArray splits it. So a string with no line end is one insert, the one for &1, and 'a' || '0a'x || 'b' gives two. 1126.body: SysGetMessage(num [, filename [, str]...]) rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > SysGetMessage (Unix-like systems only) SysGetMessage answers a message from a message catalog, with the places in it for inserts filled with the strings that the call gives. The catalog is either the interpreter's own, which holds the messages of the interpreter, or a Unix message catalog that the program names. The call takes its message from the first message set of the catalog; SysGetMessageX takes a set as an argument. Which numbers the interpreter's own catalog has a message for, and what the messages say, is not part of the book (see the rule on error messages ), so the examples of this page that use it look only at the inserts and at the answers for numbers that have no message, and the examples that print a message make a catalog of their own.
1126.title: SysGetMessage

1127.body:
[util.sysgetmessage.args] num is a required argument. filename is an optional string, and the arguments after it are optional strings, the inserts. A call with no num, or an omitted num, raises SYNTAX 88.901. num is read as a number, and a string that is not a number, a number that is not whole, a whole number that is not above zero and a whole number of more than 18 digits raise SYNTAX 88.905. A sign, leading zeros, blanks around the number and an exponent are allowed when the value is a whole number above zero. The value is read as the whole-number rule says. The number of the message is the remainder of num divided by 4294967296. So 4294967297 names message 1, and a multiple of 4294967296 names no message, which the answer rule covers. A filename of .nil raises SYNTAX 88.909. A call with more than nine inserts raises SYNTAX 40.1. The checks go from left to right, each argument in full before the next: num, then filename, then the count of inserts. So a bad num is reported before a .nil filename, and either one before too many inserts. An omitted place at the end of the call adds nothing to the count. filename is read from an object that is not a string as the argument rule says, so an object whose request answers no string raises SYNTAX 88.909. num and the inserts have a fallback. An object that is not a string is replaced by the string that its request with the argument STRING answers. When that answer is not a string, the object is replaced by the answer of its STRING method. So .object~new, whose STRING answers an Object, raises SYNTAX 88.905 as num and is put in as an Object as an insert, and an object whose only method is a STRING that answers 2 names message 2. call try "SysGetMessage()"

[instr.do.counter] A COUNTER phrase names a variable that holds the number of the current pass. The variable is set to zero before the expressions of the repetitor are evaluated, so they can read it, and then to 1, 2, and so on at the start of each pass, once the tests have decided that the pass runs. A test of WHILE therefore sees the number of the previous pass. An assignment to the variable in the block does not disturb the count, which the loop keeps itself, so the next pass sets the variable again. After the loop the variable holds the value that the last pass left in it: the number of that pass unless the block assigned the variable. The phrase belongs to a loop and not to a simple group, and a COUNTER on a DO with nothing else raises SYNTAX 27.905. The name may be a compound symbol, and it comes before any repetitor. do counter c i = 5 to 7 say c i
end

1130.body:
[util.sysgetmessage.inserts] In the text of a message, a place for an insert is an & and a digit from 1 to 9: the place &n is replaced by the nth string after filename. A place whose string the call does not give, or leaves empty, becomes the null string, and a string that no place names has no effect. An insert is put in as it is: a & in it is not read as a place. Every other character of the text stays as it is: a % and a letter, an & with a 0 after it, an & at the end, and an & that is followed by another &. A digit after a place is a character of the text, so that &10 is the first insert and a 0. The example makes a catalog with gencat in the current directory and shows these cases. call lineout 'c6zqcat.msg', '$set 1'

[instr.do.label] A LABEL phrase gives the block a name that LEAVE, ITERATE and END can use. The name is the label when the block has a LABEL phrase, and otherwise the control variable of a controlled loop or of an OVER loop. A block with neither has no name. The interpreter compares a name to the names in those clauses without regard to case, and a compound symbol matches by its text, without working out the tail. Once a block has a LABEL, the name of its control variable no longer names it, so LEAVE, ITERATE and END have to use the label. When two active blocks have the same name, the name means the innermost. The phrase works on every form, a simple group included. It comes before any repetitor, and in either order with COUNTER. A LABEL phrase does not create a label for CALL or SIGNAL. rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil); Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > List of Rexx Utility Functions The Rexx Utilities of Windows include functions that make no sense on a Unix-like system: they work with drives, volumes, printers, the console screen, code pages and the attributes of files on Windows file systems. interrexx does not provide them on a Unix-like system, and this page lists them and says what a call of one of them does there. Support for them on Windows is tracked in issue #215. The Windows-only functions are these: RxMessageBox, RxWinExec, SysBootDrive, SysDriveInfo, SysDriveMap, SysFileSystemType, SysVolumeLabel, SysSystemDirectory, SysWinVer: message boxes, programs, drives, volumes and the system; SysCurPos, SysCurState, SysTextScreenRead, SysTextScreenSize: the cursor and the text of the console screen; SysFromUnicode, SysToUnicode, SysGetLongPathName, SysGetShortPathName: code pages and Windows file names; SysIni, SysShutdownSystem, SysSwitchSession, SysWaitNamedPipe: the registry files, the session and named pipes; SysIsFileCompressed, SysIsFileEncrypted, SysIsFileNotContentIndexed, SysIsFileOffline, SysIsFileSparse, SysIsFileTemporary, SysWinDecryptFile, SysWinEncryptFile: the attributes of a file on a Windows file system; SysWinGetPrinters, SysWinGetDefaultPrinter, SysWinSetDefaultPrinter: printers. [instr.do.syntax] Errors in the shape of the clause are found when the program is read, so a program with one runs no clause at all, as the read-first rule says. The text of an INTERPRET is read in the same way, as the INTERPRET rule says. A TO, BY, FOR, INDEX or ITEM phrase given twice raises SYNTAX 27.902, an unwanted word after FOREVER 27.901, a WHILE and an UNTIL together 27.1, an INDEX or ITEM phrase with no OVER 27.904, and a COUNTER on a simple group 27.905. A missing expression raises SYNTAX 35.904 after the =, 35.905 after BY, 35.906 after TO and 35.907 after FOR, 35.911 after OVER, and 35.929 after WHILE or UNTIL. A LABEL with no symbol, or with a string there, raises SYNTAX 20.918, a COUNTER with no symbol or with a string 20.934, and an INDEX or ITEM with no symbol 20.929. A control, COUNTER, INDEX or ITEM name that starts with a digit raises 31.2, and one that starts with a period 31.3. Anything that follows a COUNTER or LABEL phrase out of its place is part of the expression before it, so that the errors of that expression are raised instead. The errors of a value, 26.2, 26.3 and 41.1, are raised when the clause runs. say 'before'

Note. The input and output builtins read and write streams. A stream is a source of characters, a destination for them, or both: a file, or one of the three standard streams. The rules here hold for every stream builtin; the pages link to them instead of restating them. The examples keep their files in the current directory under names of their own, and delete them. [bif.index.stream.name] A stream builtin names its stream with a string, its name argument. For a file the name is the file's name, taken from the current directory when it is not absolute (see Deviation 34 ). While the stream is open, a name denotes the same stream, whichever stream builtin it is given to, so what one builtin writes another reads. This holds in the main program and in one call of a method, and in the routines that either of them calls. Each call of a method has streams of its own, which a routine called from it shares, so a name that the method uses is not the stream that the main program, a routine called from the main program or another call of the method uses under that name. f = 'spec-streams-name.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'first'
call charout f, 'second'
say linein(f) '/' charin(f, , 3)
call sysfiledelete f first / sec f = 'spec-streams-name2.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'one'
call lineout f, 'two'
call lineout f, 'three'
call stream f, 'C', 'CLOSE'
say 'main' linein(f)
o = .o~new
say 'call 1' o~two(f)
say 'call 2' o~two(f)
say 'main' linein(f)
call stream f, 'C', 'CLOSE'
call sysfiledelete f
::class o
::method two use arg f return linein(f) linein(f) main one
call 1 one two
call 2 one two
main two [bif.index.stream.std] The names STDIN, STDOUT and STDERR denote the standard input, output and error streams, each with a colon after it or without one and with its letters in any case. A null string or an omitted name denotes the default stream of the builtin: the standard input for a builtin that reads, the standard output for a builtin that writes. call charout 'stdout', 'one '
call charout 'Stdout:', 'two '
call charout , 'three '

ANSI: 6.3.2.59, 8.3.7; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > DROP Deviations: D70 DROP returns variables to the state they had before any assignment: they have no value, and a reference to one yields the name of the variable in upper case. Its operands are variable symbols, written as the names themselves or, in parentheses, as a variable whose value is a list of names. This page specifies what each kind of name drops, the order in which the names are processed, the list form, how DROP treats a variable that a routine or a method has exposed, and the errors. How a variable gets a value is the business of the assignment page .

1203.body:
[bif.changestr.result] CHANGESTR scans haystack from its first character to its last. At each position where needle occurs, it appends newneedle to the result and continues with the character after the occurrence; where needle does not occur, it appends the character at that position and continues with the next one. Every occurrence found this way is replaced, up to count of them when count is given: after the countth replacement the rest of haystack is appended unchanged. The match is exact, so case matters, and every character of the strings, whitespace and '00'x included, is an ordinary character. say changestr('o', 'foolish', '') changestr('o', 'foolish', '0') changestr('o', 'foolish', '0', 1)

banana a_b__c
61000062 [bif.changestr.overlap] Occurrences that overlap are not all replaced: an occurrence is replaced only when it begins after the end of the one replaced before it, as COUNTSTR counts them. The text that newneedle brings in is never searched again, so a newneedle that holds needle does not make the call replace more. say changestr('aa', 'aaaaa', 'b') changestr('aba', 'ababababa', 'X'), changestr('a', 'aaaa', 'aa') changestr('a', 'aaaa', 'aa', 2) bba XbXba aaaaaaaa aaaaaa [bif.changestr.count.zero] When count is 0, nothing is replaced and the result is haystack unchanged. count is still checked, as it always is. say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', 0) changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', '0.0')

say changestr('a', 'banana', 'x', 'zero')
a: say condition('o')~code banana banana
40.12 [bif.changestr.empty-needle] When needle is the null string, it is taken to occur nowhere, so nothing is replaced and the result is haystack unchanged, for every newneedle and every count that passes its check. say '['changestr('', 'abc', 'x')']' '['changestr('', 'abc', 'x', 2)']'
say '['changestr('', '', 'x')']' [abc] [abc]
[] [bif.changestr.empty-haystack] When haystack is the null string, needle occurs in it nowhere, and the result is the null string, for every count that passes its check. say '['changestr('a', '', 'x')']' '['changestr('a', '', 'x', 3)']'
signal on syntax name a
say changestr('a', '', 'x', -1)
a: say condition('o')~code [] []
93.906 [bif.changestr.empty-newneedle] When newneedle is the null string, the occurrences replaced are deleted: the result is haystack without them. This is not the same as omitting newneedle, which is an error . say changestr('a', 'banana', '') '['changestr('banana', 'banana', '')']'

124.body: EXIT [expression [, expression]...] ANSI: 6.3.2.61, 8.3.8; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > EXIT EXIT ends the program at once, however many routines, loops and INTERPRET texts it is in, and the value of its expression is the program's value. In a method or in a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive it ends only that unit, as RETURN would. This page specifies where EXIT stops, the end of the program as an implied EXIT, what the expression is, and how the value of the main program becomes the exit code of the process.

1244.body: DATATYPE(string [, type]) ANSI: 9.3.8; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > DATATYPE DATATYPE examines the characters of a string. Called with the string alone, it names the string NUM when it is a number and CHAR when it is not; called with a type, it answers 1 when the string is of that type and 0 when it is not. The types are about the form of the string, never about its meaning: they ask whether it is a number, a whole number, a string of hexadecimal or of binary digits, a string of letters or of letters and digits, a symbol, or a logical value.

[bif.datatype.number] Type N answers 1 when the string is a number: a string of the whole-number form whose value is within the exponent range of the language. The strings that a number argument rejects with SYNTAX 93.943 are exactly the strings for which N answers 0: the null string, a string of only whitespace, a string with a character that the form does not allow, and a number whose exponent is out of range. The digits of the string are not rounded and NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part. say datatype(' + 2.50E1 ', 'N') datatype('.5', 'N') datatype('5.', 'N'), datatype('- 7', 'N')

[bif.datatype.hex] Type X answers 1 when the string is a string of hexadecimal digits, as the digit rule defines the digits, and where a conversion function would raise an error for the string, X answers 0: whitespace in the string only where the group rule allows a gap, so that every group after the first has an even count of digits; no whitespace at the start or the end; and a character that is neither a digit nor whitespace. The null string is a string of hexadecimal digits, while a string of only whitespace is not. A string with an odd number of digits is hexadecimal when it has no gap. say datatype('4a4B', 'X') datatype('4a 4B', 'X') datatype('4 4a4b', 'X'), datatype('abcdef 12', 'X') datatype('abc', 'X') datatype('', 'X')

The null string is a string of binary digits, a string of only whitespace is not. A string with a count of digits that is not a multiple of four is binary when it has no gap. say datatype('0101', 'B') datatype('1 0101', 'B') datatype('11111 1111', 'B'), datatype('010', 'B') datatype('', 'B')

Type A answers 1 when the string has at least one character and only letters and digits. Type M answers 1 when it has at least one character and only letters. Type L answers 1 when it has at least one character and only lowercase letters, and type U when it has at least one and only uppercase letters. The null string is therefore none of these. say datatype('aB3', 'A') datatype('aB', 'M') datatype('abc', 'L') datatype('ABC', 'U')

The other characters are not symbol characters, among them $, @, #, whitespace and the null character. Case does not matter, and the string is not translated or looked up as a variable. say datatype('abc', 'S') datatype('A.b', 'S') datatype('5', 'S') datatype('.', 'S'), datatype('a!?_', 'S') datatype('1e3', 'S')

[instr.exit.program] EXIT in the main program, or in an internal routine of it that a CALL or a function call started, ends the program. No clause after the EXIT runs, the routines that were being called are abandoned without returning, and a function call that is still waiting for its value does not raise SYNTAX 44.1. An EXIT in the text of an INTERPRET that such code runs ends the program too, and in a method or a ::ROUTINE it ends that unit, as the rule on leaving the text says. say 'start'
call outer
say 'not reached'
exit 1
outer: procedure do i = 1 to 3 say 'outer' i if i = 2 then call inner end return
inner: say 'inner' exit 9 start
outer 1
outer 2
inner say 'start'
x = quit()
say 'not reached'
quit: exit start [instr.exit.unit] EXIT in a method or in a routine that a ::ROUTINE directive defines ends that unit, including the internal routines it called, and hands the value to the sender of the message or to the caller of the routine in the way that RETURN does. The program goes on, so the main program is not ended by it. say 'start'
r = .box~new~go
say 'main goes on' r
call early
say 'and on' result
exit 3
::class box
::method go call helper say 'not reached'
helper: exit 'from method'
::routine early exit 'from routine' start
main goes on from method
and on from routine [instr.exit.end] When the program runs past its last clause, it ends as if there were an EXIT without an expression, so the program has no value and the exit code is 0. This holds when the last clause is in the body of a routine that a CALL started, because the routine does not return from the end of the program; the caller does not continue. say 'a'
call f
say 'not reached'
f: say 'in f' a
in f [instr.exit.end.unit] A method or a routine of a ::ROUTINE directive that runs past its last clause is different: it returns to its sender without a value, as a RETURN without an expression does, and the program goes on. signal on syntax name e
.box~new~m
say 'a' symbol('result')
call r
say 'b' symbol('result')
say 'c' .box~new~m
e: say condition('o')~code
exit

::method m nop

b LIT

1250.body: DATE([option [, [string] [, [informat] [, [osep] [, isep]]]]]) ANSI: 9.8.1; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > DATE DATE answers a calendar date. With no string it answers the current local date; with a string it reads a date written in one format and writes it in another. The dates are those of the Gregorian calendar, extended back to year 1 and forward to year 9999, and a date has no time zone. The current date changes from day to day, so the examples of this page convert fixed dates, or check only the form of the current one and how its formats agree with each other.
1250.title: DATE

1251.body:
[bif.date.args] DATE takes up to five arguments and requires none: option, string, informat, osep and isep. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules : a call with more than five arguments raises SYNTAX 40.4, and a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. DATE does not run as a String method : sending the message DATE to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. option and informat name formats by their first letter , and osep and isep are separators . say date('S', '1 Jan 2000') date(, '1 Jan 2000') date('S', '20000101', 'S', , )
signal on syntax name a
say date('S', '1 Jan 2000', 'N', '', '', 1)
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say 'S'~date
b: say condition('o')~code 20000101 1 Jan 2000 20000101
40.4
97.1 [bif.date.default] An omitted option is N, and so is an omitted informat. A call with no string answers the current date, in the format option names; a call with a string is a conversion . say date(, '29 Feb 2024') date('N', '29 Feb 2024') date(, '20240229', 'S')
say (date() == date('N')) (date(, , , '-') == date('N', , , '-')) 29 Feb 2024 29 Feb 2024 29 Feb 2024
1 1

1252.body:
[bif.date.out.text] Six options write a date as its day, month and year in one string. N writes the day without a leading zero, the month as the first three letters of its English name with a capital (Jan, Feb, Mar, Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug, Sep, Oct, Nov, Dec) and the year in four digits, separated by blanks. E writes dd/mm/yy, O writes yy/mm/dd and U writes mm/dd/yy; S writes yyyymmdd and I writes yyyy-mm-dd. A year is in four digits with leading zeros, or in the last two digits of the year (E, O and U), and a month or a day other than N's is in two digits with a leading zero. d = '5 Mar 2024'

M writes the full English name of the month, W the full English name of the day of the week, and L writes the day without a leading zero, the full name of the month and the year in four digits, separated by blanks. Both names begin with a capital letter. list = ''

[bif.date.current] A call with no string answers the current date in the local time zone, written in the format option names, as of the moment the clause reads the clock. Every format of the current date is the same date: converting the current date in S form to any format other than F and T gives the answer that format gives. F and T include the time of day: each is the figure that the conversion of the same date gives, which is for the start of the day, plus the time since then, a number of microseconds (F) or seconds (T) that is not negative and is less than a day. numeric digits 20

40.19 [bif.date.in.number] The informats B, F and T read a count: the number of days, of microseconds or of seconds that B, F and T write . The string may have any form of a number, such as 5, 5, +5, 5.0 and 5e0, and NUMERIC DIGITS does not apply. A string whose value is not a whole number raises SYNTAX 40.19 when it has at most nine significant digits for B, or at most 18 for F and T, its significant digits being those from the first digit that is not 0 to the last digit that is not 0. 1268.body: DIRECTORY([newdirectory]) rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > DIRECTORY DIRECTORY answers the name of the current directory, and with an argument first makes another directory the current one. The current directory is where a relative file name starts: the stream builtins , QUALIFY and the commands the program starts all read it. The rules here are those of a Unix-like system, where the components of a name are separated by slashes. The names of other platforms are not specified. Note. The current directory at the start of a program belongs to whoever started it, so the examples name no directory of their own. They build their expected values from the answer of a call without an argument, or use the root directory, /, which every Unix-like system has.

127.body:
[instr.exit.code] The value of the main program, which is that of its EXIT or of a RETURN that ends it, becomes the exit code of the process in this way. A value that is not a string is first replaced by a string as the conversion rule says; where that rule refuses the conversion, as for an object whose REQUEST is private, or whose MAKESTRING or STRING method is private and would be sent, the exit code is 0 and no error is raised. A string that has the form of a whole-number argument , and that is a whole number from -2147483648 to 2147483647, is handed to the host as that integer. Blanks around the number, an exponent, and a decimal part of zeros do not matter. An integer from 0 to 255 is the exit status itself. What a host makes of an integer outside 0 to 255 is not specified. Any other value gives the exit code 0 and raises no error: no value, a fraction, a string that is no number, a whole number outside the 32-bit range, and an object whose string is none of these. A string of more than 18 digits, zeros included, is not specified. Note. Unix-like hosts keep the low eight bits of the integer, so that 257 and -1 give 1 and 255; another host may report the integer as it is. An expression such as -2147483647 is not a string but a negation, whose result is rounded at the NUMERIC DIGITS setting, so exit -2147483647 gives 0 and exit -1073741823 gives 4, while the strings '-2147483647' and '-1073741823' give 1. exit .apm~new

1272.body: ENDLOCAL() rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > ENDLOCAL (Linux only) ENDLOCAL takes back the most recent save that SETLOCAL made: it makes the directory the current one again, and gives the environment variables the values they had when the save was made. It answers 1 when there was a save to take back and 0 when there was none. Note. The examples use names that start with SPEC_ENDLOCAL for the environment variables they change. Each example takes at most one save back, counting the one that the reference implementation puts back at the end of a ::routine , a method or the program, because that implementation can fail in a program that takes a save back a second time. The rule on nested saves therefore has no example; a test of interrexx backs it.

1337.title: Arguments

1338.body:
[bif.overlay.result] OVERLAY returns the concatenation of three strings, in this order. The first is the first n - 1 characters of target, followed by as many copies of pad as it takes to make n - 1 characters when target has fewer. The second is new adjusted to exactly length characters: cut at the right when it has more, and followed by copies of pad when it has fewer. The third is the characters of target from position n + length on, which is the null string when target has fewer than that many characters. So the result keeps every character of target outside the run of length characters from position n, and the result is longer than target when the run reaches past its end. say '['overlay(' ', 'uvwxyz', 4)']' '['overlay('#', 'uvwxyz', 2, 3)']' '['overlay('zz', 'wxyz', 4)']'

When n is exactly one more than the length of target, new is appended with no padding between. This holds when length is 0, so the result is then target padded to n - 1 characters. say overlay('xyz', 'abc', 5, 2, '-') overlay('xyz', 'abc', 4, 2, '-') overlay('xyz', 'abc', 5, , '-')
say overlay('X', 'ab', 5, 3, '.') overlay('xyz', 'ab', 5, 5, '.')

[bif.pos.result] Let n be the length of haystack and m the length of needle. The characters that the search covers are those at the positions from start through start + length - 1 (through n when length is omitted), and at no position beyond n; this is the window, and it holds no characters when start is greater than n or length is 0. 1343.body: QUALIFY(name) ANSI: 9.7.7; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > QUALIFY Deviations: D34 QUALIFY answers the full name of a file: the name made absolute, with the current directory put in front of a relative one and the parts of the path that go nowhere taken out. It looks at no file, so the file need not exist. The rules here are those of a Unix-like system, where a name is separated into its components by slashes; the names of other platforms are not specified. Note. The result of a relative name depends on the current directory. The examples build their expected value from the current directory, which the DIRECTORY builtin answers when it has no argument, and name no directory.
1343.title: QUALIFY

1344.body:
[bif.qualify.args] name is a string , the name of a file or directory. QUALIFY is not a String method . It takes one argument, by the call rules : a call with none raises SYNTAX 40.3, and a call with a second one raises SYNTAX 40.4. A name that is not a string is used by its string value. signal on syntax name a
say qualify()
a: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name b
say qualify('x', 'y')
b: say condition('o')~code

say 'x'~qualify
c: say condition('o')~code

A name with a blank in it, or one that is a number, is a name like any other, and so is one that has a ~ anywhere but first. 1347.body: QUEUED() ANSI: 9.8.2; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > QUEUED QUEUED answers how many lines the current external data queue holds. It takes no line out of the queue and puts none in. The external data queue is a list of lines kept outside the program, where the QUEUE and PUSH instructions put lines and the PULL and PARSE PULL instructions take them out. A program has one current queue at a time, which RXQUEUE names and changes. The queue called SESSION is the current queue when a program starts. Note. The examples create a queue of their own, make it the current queue, and delete it when they are done, so they leave nothing behind and do not depend on what the SESSION queue holds when they start. A queue can be reached by other programs, and the lines such a program puts into or takes out of it are not specified.
1347.title: QUEUED

A trailing omitted place adds nothing to the count, so QUEUED(,) is a call without an argument. QUEUED does not run as a String method : sending the message QUEUED to a string raises SYNTAX 97.1. signal on syntax name a

b: say condition('o')~code

1350.body: RANDOM([min] [, [max] [, seed]]) ANSI: 9.8.3; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > RANDOM RANDOM answers a quasi-random whole number from a range. A call can start a new sequence of numbers from a seed, and a sequence started with a seed is the same on every run of a program. A sequence started without a seed is not: the numbers of such a sequence are not specified, so the examples of this page check what they can say about them, their range and their form, and show values only for seeded sequences.
1350.title: RANDOM

1351.body:
[bif.random.args] RANDOM takes up to three arguments and requires none: min, max and seed, each a whole-number argument , and each also accepted when written as a number of the form but not as an integer (3.0, 3e0, 3), as long as its value is a whole number. The argument count is checked by the builtin call rules : a call with more than three arguments raises SYNTAX 40.4, and a call with only omitted places counts as a call with no arguments. A min, max or seed that is not a whole number, the null string included, raises SYNTAX 40.12. 1362.body: RXFUNCADD(name, module [, procedure]) rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > RXFUNCADD RXFUNCADD asks for a function of a library to be made callable by name like any other function. It answers 0 if the function is callable afterwards and 1 if it is not. RXFUNCQUERY asks whether a name is available, and RXFUNCDROP removes a registration again. A library is named by module. The library the examples use is rxmath, which ships with both interpreters on a Unix-like system and provides the mathematical functions RxCalcSqrt, RxCalcExp, RxCalcLog and their relatives. The names of libraries and the way a name is turned into a file are those of a Unix-like system; those of other platforms are not specified. Which libraries a program can name beyond rxmath is not specified. Note. A registration can outlive the program that made it, and a registration that a program makes can be removed only by that program. The examples that leave one behind drop it before they end, so they leave nothing behind and do not depend on registrations of other names. Making a function of a library such as rxmath available is not a registration: it lasts until the program ends and nothing removes it, so each example picks a function of that library that no other example on this page uses. A registration is shared with programs that are not part of the examples, and what they register or drop is not specified.

It answers 0 if it removed a registration and 1 if it did not. RXFUNCQUERY asks whether a name is available afterwards. Note. The examples drop every registration they make, so they leave nothing behind and do not depend on registrations of other names. A registration can be removed only by the program that made it. 1368.body: RXFUNCQUERY(name) rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > RXFUNCQUERY RXFUNCQUERY asks whether a function of the given name is available to the program without a library having to be asked for it first. It answers 0 for an available function and 1 otherwise, and it changes nothing. RXFUNCADD makes functions of a library available, and RXFUNCDROP removes a registration. Note. The examples register nothing that they do not drop, so they do not depend on registrations of other names. Making a function of the library rxmath available is not a registration that can be dropped, as RXFUNCADD explains: it lasts until the program ends, and the example that does it picks a function that no other example on this page uses.

1371.body: RXQUEUE(option [, queuename]) rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > RXQUEUE RXQUEUE creates, deletes and asks after the external data queues, and names or changes the current one. A queue is a list of lines kept outside the program, in a service that every program of a session can reach, where the QUEUE and PUSH instructions put lines and the PULL and PARSE PULL instructions take them out. A program has one current queue, the one those instructions use and QUEUED counts. The queue called SESSION is the current queue when a program starts, it always exists, and it cannot be deleted. Note. The examples create a queue of their own under a name no other example uses, and delete it when they are done, so they leave nothing behind and do not depend on what the SESSION queue holds when they start. A queue that a program creates and does not delete stays until something deletes it, even after the program ends.

1374.body: SETLOCAL() rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > SETLOCAL (Linux only) SETLOCAL records where the program is and what every environment variable holds, so that ENDLOCAL can put both back later. It answers 1. The save itself changes nothing the program can see; what the program does afterwards to the current directory and to the environment variables, for instance with DIRECTORY and VALUE , is what ENDLOCAL undoes. The environment variables are those of the process, which the ENVIRONMENT selector of VALUE reads and writes and which the commands the program starts inherit. Variables of the program itself are not among them. Note. The examples change only variables whose names start with SPEC_SETLOCAL, and compare the current directory with the one the program started in, so they do not depend on what the program starts with. A program that calls SETLOCAL and no ENDLOCAL leaves nothing for the other examples to see. Each example takes at most one save back, counting the one that the reference implementation puts back at the end of a ::routine , a method or the program, because that implementation can fail in a program that takes a save back a second time.
1374.title: SETLOCAL

1375.body:

1387.body: STREAM(name [, operation [, command]]) ANSI: 9.7.8; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > STREAM Deviations: D34, D35, D49, D55, D57, D59, D62, D74, D79, D98, D100, D145 STREAM asks a stream for its state, describes the state, or carries out a command on the stream: opening and closing it, moving its positions, and asking about the file behind it. 1393.body:
[bif.stream.seek] SEEK sets a position of the stream and answers the new one. POSITION is the same command. After the word there is an offset, and then options in any order. The offset is a whole number, which may have a prefix: = or no prefix for a position counted from the start of the data, 1 being its first character; < for a position counted back from the end, <0 being the one past the last character; + and - for a position counted forward or back from the read position with READ, and from the write position with WRITE (see Deviation 49 ). READ sets the read position, WRITE the write position, and when neither is given a stream open for reading and writing has both set to the answer, and a + or - then counts from the read position (see Deviation 49 ). CHAR counts characters and is the default; for LINE see the next rule . A position past the end of the data is allowed: a read there finds nothing, and a write there fills the gap , except on a stream opened APPEND, where a write goes after the last character wherever the write position is. A stream that is not open is opened by SEEK; when it cannot be, SEEK answers 0, raises NOTREADY , leaves the state ERROR, and creates nothing. An offset that is not a whole number or an option that is not one of these raises SYNTAX 93.0, and a missing offset SYNTAX 93.903. f = 'spec-stream-seek.tmp'

1413.body: TIME([option [, [string] [, informat]]]) ANSI: 9.8.5; rexxref: Functions > Built-in Functions > TIME TIME answers a time of day. With no string it answers the current local time, or the reading of an elapsed-time clock that the program can start and reset; with a string it reads a time written in one format and writes it in another. The current time changes from moment to moment, so the examples of this page convert fixed times, or check only the form of the current time and how its formats agree with each other, and the elapsed-time clock is checked against pauses and not against figures.

F and T are local like the rest: the UTC reading of F is F - O. 142.body: GUARD ON | OFF [WHEN expression [, expression]...] rexxref: Keyword Instructions > GUARD A method of an object can run on several activities at once, for instance when it was started with ~start . GUARD controls whether a running method has exclusive use of its object's variables, and it can make the method wait until an object variable has a given value. This page specifies the exclusion, the WHEN form and its conditions, the places where GUARD may stand, and the errors. 1428.body:
[bif.translate.upper] When tableo, tablei and pad are all omitted, TRANSLATE returns string with each character of the run from pos for length characters uppercased as UPPER does , and every other character unchanged. The result is then UPPER(string, pos, length), with the same defaults for pos and length. say translate('hello, world') translate('hello, world', , , , 8, 3) HELLO, WORLD hello, WORld [bif.translate.result] When at least one of tableo, tablei and pad is given, TRANSLATE returns a string of LENGTH(string) characters. Each character c of string at a position from pos to pos + length - 1 is looked up in tablei. When c occurs in it, let k be the position of its first occurrence: the result has, in place of c, the character of tableo at position k when LENGTH(tableo) is at least k, and pad otherwise. When c does not occur in tablei, it is copied unchanged, and so is every character of string outside the run. say translate('a1b2c3', 'xyz', 'abc') translate('a1b2c3', 'xyz', '123', , 3) x1y2z3 a1bycz [bif.translate.first] When a character occurs more than once in tablei, its first occurrence alone decides what it becomes; the characters of tableo at the positions of the later occurrences are never used. say translate('mom', 'abc', 'mmo') translate('mom', '123', 'omo') aca 212 [bif.translate.tableo.length] tableo need not be as long as tablei. When it is shorter, a character found in tablei at a position past the end of tableo is replaced by pad; when it is longer, its characters past the length of tablei are never used. say translate('wxyz', 'WX', 'wxyz', '+') translate('wxyz', 'WXYZ123', 'wx') WX++ WXyz [bif.translate.pad-only] When both tables are omitted and pad is given, every character of the run is replaced by pad, since every character is found in the default tablei and the default tableo has no characters. say translate('secret', , , '*') translate('secret', , , '*', 3, 2) ****** se**et Note. The ANSI draft (9.3.23) uppercases whenever both tables are omitted and ignores pad then. This page follows ooRexx, where the reference manual says a given pad replaces the whole string. [bif.translate.tablei.empty] When tablei is given as the null string, no character is found in it, and the result is string unchanged, for every tableo, pad, pos and length that pass their checks. say translate('abc', 'xyz', '') translate('abc', , '', '*') translate('abc', '', '') abc abc abc Note. This holds however the null string was produced, which ooRexx does not do: see Deviation 94 . [bif.translate.past-end] When pos is greater than LENGTH(string), no character is translated and the result is string, for every pos past the end that passes its check. When the run reaches past the end of string, it stops there, and nothing is added. say translate('abc', , , '*', 4) translate('abc', , , , 999999999999999999), translate('abc', , , '*', 2, 50) abc abc a** [bif.translate.length.zero] When length is 0, no character is translated and the result is string, for every pos that passes its check. pad is still checked, as a pad always is. say translate('abc', , , '*', 2, 0) translate('abc', , , , 1, 0)

[instr.guard.exclusion] While an activity runs a method of an object with the guard of the method's scope held, no other activity runs a method of the same scope of that object that also holds it ( the lock of a scope ). A method that is guarded starts with the guard held and keeps it until it ends or gives it up, and a method that is unguarded starts without it. GUARD ON takes the guard for the rest of the method, waiting until the activity that holds it has released it. GUARD OFF gives it up for the rest of the method, or until the next GUARD ON. An unguarded method can read and write the object variables without it, so it can be called while another activity holds the guard. Repeated GUARD ON or GUARD OFF instructions do not count: the counting rule says how often a lock is held. log = .array~new
say 'keeping the guard'
o = .vault~new(log, .true)
h = o~start('holder')
do until o~inside; end
p = o~start('probe')
o~release
h~result; p~result
say log~makeString('l', ' ') log = .array~new
say 'giving up the guard'
o = .vault~new(log, .false)
h = o~start('holder')
do until o~inside; end
p = o~start('probe')
p~result
o~release
h~result
say log~makeString('l', ' ')
exit

holder-end probe
giving up the guard
probe holder-end Note. The example starts a method that holds the guard and a second guarded method while the first still runs. The first waits for a flag that only the main program sets, so the log shows whether the second could run before the first ended. In the second run the first method gives up the guard, and the second runs at once. [instr.guard.end] A guard that a method holds when it ends is released with it, whether the method held it from its start, took it with GUARD ON or kept it after GUARD ON WHEN. A method that is waiting for the guard is not kept waiting by a method that has ended. o = .box~new

[instr.if.run] IF evaluates its expression once. When the value is 1, the instruction after THEN runs, and when it is 0, the instruction after ELSE runs, if there is one. Control then continues with the clause after the whole IF, which is after the ELSE instruction when there is an ELSE. The branch is one instruction: a second instruction on the same line or the next line is not part of it, so it runs whatever the test said. A DO group, a SELECT or another IF is a single instruction, so a branch that holds one of them can hold many clauses. THEN need not stand in the clause of the expression: the rule for THEN says where it may begin. n = 3
if n > 2 then say 'big'; else say 'small'
if n > 5 then say 'huge'
else say 'not huge'
if n = 3 then say 'a'; say 'b'
if n = 4 then say 'c'; say 'd'
if n = 3 then do say 'e1' say 'e2'
end
else say 'no'
say 'end' big
not huge
a
b
d
e1
e2
end [instr.if.then] THEN may begin a later clause than the expression. Any number of null clauses may stand between the expression and THEN, so a line end, a semicolon, blank lines and comments there do not end the IF, and a THEN on the next line belongs to the IF above it. The same holds for the WHEN of a SELECT . The null clauses after THEN are the subject of the rule for branches . if 1
then say 'a'
if 1; then say 'b'
if 1;; then say 'c'
if 1 /* c */ /* c2 */
then say 'd' a
b
c
d

[bif.xrange.method] XRANGE takes any number of arguments, none included, and every argument may be omitted. It does not run as a String method : a string has no message named XRANGE, and sending it raises SYNTAX 97.1. Each argument is one character, an omitted place or the name of a class, as the rules below read them; an argument that is not a string is first converted as any string argument is . say length(xrange()) length(xrange('a')) length(xrange('a', 'c', 'digit', 'x'))

97.1 [bif.xrange.groups] XRANGE reads its arguments from left to right as a series of groups, and the answer is what the groups select, joined in that order. A group starts at an argument that is omitted or one character long: that argument is the group's start and the argument after it is its end, so the group takes two arguments and selects a range . A group starts at any other argument, the null string among them, and takes that argument alone: the argument names a class . The argument after a group starts the next group. The arguments read are the first count of them, where count is the argument count of the call: the omitted places after the last argument that is not omitted are not read and start no group. say xrange('a', 'c', 'x', 'z') xrange('a', 'b', 'digit', 'c', 'd')

1487.body: A Deviation is a declared difference between interrexx and ooRexx. Every example on which the two answer differently belongs to one; any other difference is a defect. Each entry says what interrexx does and how ooRexx differs. A number is never reused: a withdrawn Deviation keeps its number and says what replaced it. This chapter is informative; where a Deviation touches a page of this book, that page states it as a rule whose identifier ends deviation.N.

1488.body: interrexx indents trace lines, and the indentation a program reads back through ~traceLine or a condition's traceback, by block structure alone. ooRexx keeps the indent in a counter that drops a level too far when a loop ends on a failing control test, so its later lines sit one level short until an enclosing construct restores it.
