[instr.if.value] The value of the expression must be a string that is exactly 0 or exactly 1, with the rules that the logical operators give for their operands: 01, 1.0, a blank around the digit, the null string and every other text are refused. An IF that gets another value raises SYNTAX 34.1, and no branch runs. A value that is an object and not a string counts as the string it converts to, which the conversion rule gives. An object that converts to 1 takes the THEN branch, and one that converts to any other string, such as .nil, raises 34.1. The test does not look at the number form: 1 + 0 and 5 - 5 are logical because they come out as 1 and 0, and 01 is not logical because it is the text 01. call try '1 + 0'

1586.body: A close of the standard input, output or error is a logical close, as for a file, whether it is a CLOSE command of STREAM or a call of CHAROUT or LINEOUT that gives no string. The state is then UNKNOWN, and the next stream builtin that reads from it, writes to it, counts what is left in it (CHARS or LINES) or opens it opens it again on the same input or output, so that later reads and writes carry on. In ooRexx, output written to the standard output or error after the close does not appear at once: it appears when the program next closes, flushes or opens the stream, and what is written after the last of these is lost. Output written before the close can be lost too, as when the stream is a file and the later output replaces it. On the standard input, a CLOSE has the same outcome on both until the program first reads from it; after a read, ooRexx can lose the input not yet read. A CHAROUT or LINEOUT that gives no string on the standard input leaves it in the ERROR state in ooRexx and raises NOTREADY there, and LINEOUT answers 1.

It also reports these before the count: the stem name of SysStemCopy, SysStemDelete and SysStemInsert when it fails its check, and a whole-number argument of SysStemCopy, SysStemDelete, SysStemInsert or SysStemSort that fails its check, a number out of range among them. It reports the count before an argument's value: an option it does not allow, or any other number out of range, except a negative semaphore handle, which it reports before the count. SysOpenEventSem and SysOpenMutexSem are the exception: in both engines they report an omitted name and an object that has no string value before the count.

1595.body: A string that names a number is the same string to every message, however it was written or computed. A number literal such as 12 used as the message name of send, sendWith, start, startWith or Message~new names the message 12, and request('ARRAY') sent to it answers the array that makeArray answers. ooRexx raises SYNTAX 93.946 for the first and answers .nil for the second when the number is stored as a whole number, as a whole-number literal or the result of arithmetic is. Equal literals of a program share one stored value, so a quoted '12' behaves the same way when the literal 12 was used before it. The same storage shows where a string is read as text: an item of an Array whose objectName answers such a number is written by makeString and toString as the digits; ooRexx writes bytes of its stored form.

1596.body: When subclass, mixinclass, defineMethods or enhanced takes the methods of an object through its supplier method, the object that supplier answers is used through the messages available, index, item and next when it is not a Supplier; an object that does not answer one of them raises SYNTAX 97.1 as for any message. A Supplier, an instance of a subclass included, is read directly, as a String subclass instance is read by its characters ( Deviation 109 ). ooRexx reads the answer as a Supplier without checking it and crashes when it is not one.
1596.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 108. A supplier that is not a Supplier

1597.body: An instance of a subclass of String is read by its own characters wherever a string, a number, a logical value or a whole number is needed, as receiver and as argument, and as the operand of SAY; REQUEST, MAKESTRING and STRING are not sent to it for that. ooRexx sends such an instance request with STRING or MAKESTRING in many of these places, as an argument of a method, an operator or a builtin function, as the receiver of the numeric and logical methods and operators, dataType and ?, as the operand of SAY, and in new, so an override of either method can change what is read; elsewhere it reads the instance's own characters, so one instance can answer differently to = and to ==. As the message name of send, sendWith, start, startWith or Message~new, ooRexx sends it request('ARRAY') instead and raises SYNTAX 93.946.
1597.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 109. String subclass instances are their characters
1597.title: 109. String subclass instances are their characters

1598.body: Provisional. An object sees every change made, at any time, to the methods of its class, of that class's superclasses and of their mixin classes, by define, defineMethods, delete, inherit and uninherit, also when the object has methods of its own from setMethod or enhanced and when the class has been changed before. ooRexx copies the method table into existing instances. A define, defineMethods or delete sent to a class, even one that changes nothing, does not reach the instances that exist already, and no later change reaches them after it: not to the class, not to its superclasses or their mixin classes, and not inherit or uninherit. An object given a method by setMethod sees no later change to its class or to the classes behind it. A class object sees no change to its metaclass or to the classes behind it that is made after the class itself.

1598.title: 110. Instances follow every change to their class

1599.body: A security manager is sent requires for a ::REQUIRES name or a loadPackage name first with the name as it was written, and then, when nothing was replaced, with the full name of the file found for it. A NAME replaced in the information of the first message chooses the file: that file is loaded, and the manager is not sent a second requires message for it, so it is never asked to approve its own replacement. A NAME replaced in the second message chooses the file as well. ooRexx uses a replacement made at the first message only to look for a package that is already loaded under that name; otherwise it sends the second message with the full name of the file the program asked for, and loads that file.

1606.body: An instance of a subclass of List is read as any other collection is wherever an array is wanted: DO OVER and the collection methods that read a collection through makeArray send it makeArray, and the methods and instructions that read an argument array or a source through request with ARRAY (sendWith, startWith, Message~new with the option A, Message~replyWith, FORWARD with ARGUMENTS, Method~new, Routine~new, Routine~callWith, Package~new, loadPackage, Supplier~new and init, the unknown of a Stem, a VariableReference, a Directory, a StringTable or a Monitor, File~writeLines and File~searchPath with a path that is no string) send it request, so an override is used. ooRexx sends such an instance neither message and uses the items it holds, unlike the subclasses of the other collection classes.

1606.title: 118. A List subclass is sent makeArray and request

1607.body: A notification target of an Alarm or a Ticker is sent cancel once, when the alarm or ticker is cancelled while it is waiting; a second cancel of the same alarm or ticker sends it nothing. ooRexx sends the target cancel once or twice for a second cancel, depending on timing.

1607.title: 119. A second cancel of an Alarm or a Ticker sends nothing

1608.body: previous of an index with a component beyond its dimension, one or all of the components, answers the index of the last item in the order of allItems whichever index is given, and next answers .nil. ooRexx answers an index that depends on the position the beyond index names: in a 2 by 2 array holding items at 1,1 and 2,2, previous(4, 4) answers 1,1 and previous(5, 5) answers 2,2.

1608.title: 120. previous of an index beyond the array answers the last item

1609.title: 121. Queue put beyond the last item

161.body: ITERATE [name] ANSI: 6.3.2.63, 8.3.11; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > ITERATE ITERATE ends the current pass of a loop and starts the next one. The rest of the block does not run for that pass. The loop then does the work that ends a pass: the step, the tests, and the next pass. Without a name it acts on the innermost loop that is running, and with a name on the loop that has that name, which can be one further out. This page specifies what the next pass begins with, which loops a name can select, and the errors. It describes loops by the terms of DO , and LEAVE is the instruction that ends the loop itself.

1610.body: A comparison operator, and the method of the same name, converts a right operand that is not a string once. ooRexx converts the right operand twice for the normal comparisons =, \=, <>, ><, <, >, <=, >=, \< and \> when the two operands are not both numbers.
1610.breadcrumbs: Deviations » 122. A right operand that is not a string is read once
1610.title: 122. A right operand that is not a string is read once

1611.body: isEmpty of a Directory agrees with items: it answers 0 for a directory that holds a method of a name other than UNKNOWN, also when that is all it holds, and 1 when items answers 0. ooRexx answers 1 for a directory that holds only methods.

1611.title: 123. isEmpty of a directory that holds only methods

1612.body: An answer of request with ARRAY that is used as an array of arguments (sendWith, startWith and run with the option A of Object, new, sendWith, startWith and replyWith of Message, callWith of Routine, unknown of Stem, VariableReference, Directory, StringTable and Monitor, and the value of ARGUMENTS of FORWARD) or as an array of items or indexes (new and init of Supplier) is accepted only when it is an Array or an instance of a subclass of Array of one dimension; any other object, a Queue included, raises the error that the reading method gives for an answer that is no array. ooRexx uses the items of a Queue or a CircularQueue as the arguments, or as the items or indexes of a Supplier, except that Message passes as many arguments as the queue has storage, the items followed by omitted ones, and for the arguments it crashes for a List, a Bag, a Table or a Directory.

1612.title: 124. An argument array answered by request is an Array

1613.title: 125. A List operand is read in its own order

The error follows the isA that is sent to the argument and precedes every other message. ooRexx answers 1 or -1 for an argument of another class, whatever the receiver is.

1615.body: DateTime + TimeSpan, DateTime - TimeSpan and TimeSpan + DateTime answer an instance that has the offset of the DateTime operand. ooRexx gives the answer of - with a span, and of a span plus a DateTime, the offset of the host's zone, so that the same arithmetic on one instant answers another instant on a host in another zone.

1615.title: 127. Adding a span to a DateTime keeps the offset of the DateTime

1616.body: hashCode of a DateTime is computed from the instant, so two instances that = finds equal have equal hash codes whatever their offsets, and an instance equal to another is found in a Set or Table that holds the other. ooRexx computes it from the fields, so equal instants at different offsets have different hash codes.

1616.title: 128. A DateTime hash code follows the instant

1617.body: elapsed of a DateTime answers the span from the instant the receiver stands for to the current instant, so the offset of the receiver does not change it: two instances of one instant answer the same span, within the time between the two calls. ooRexx subtracts the fields of the receiver from the host's current local time, so the answer moves by the difference between the offset of the receiver and the host's.

1617.title: 129. elapsed lies between two instants

1618.body: A method of DateTime or TimeSpan that reads a whole number (the fields and the offset of new, the offset of today, of the from methods and of toTimezone, the years of addYears, the days of fromBaseDate, the seconds of fromTicks, and the count and the parts of TimeSpan new) reads it as a whole-number argument of a builtin is read ( the form rule , the digits rule ), with the method's own error for a value those rules refuse: 2017.0, 2.017E3 and '2017 ' are 2017, 2017.0000000001 is refused, and 2017.00000000000000000001 is 2017. ooRexx reads some of these forms as an error, 2017.0 for a year among them, reads 2017.0000000001 as year 1, accepts 1.0000000001 for an hour, and rounds the days of fromBaseDate to nine digits.

A controlled loop steps its variable and runs its end tests, a WHILE phrase is tested before the next pass, and an UNTIL phrase is tested at once, so an ITERATE can end the loop when the UNTIL holds. A COUNTER variable counts the next pass as usual. If the selected loop is not the innermost, every block open inside it is closed first, and the control variables of those blocks keep their values. The clauses after the ITERATE do not run in the pass that it ends. do i = 1 to 3 if i = 2 then iterate say 'pass' i

A condition that the routine raises is not answered at that point again: its routine is called after the next clause that ends, as the rule for CALL traps puts it for any clause. In the example the routine h1 is called after the RAISE returns, at the line of the call, h2 is called at the ITERATE after the test, and h3, which h2 raised, is called after the first clause of the next pass. A blank anywhere, an offset whose minutes are above 59 or whose hour or minutes have one digit, a fraction of seven digits, a point with no digits after it, and a Z or an offset followed by anything are refused; so are, for a span, an hour, minute or second that is out of range or written with one digit, days with a leading zero or the days 0., a plus sign, and a minus sign before a span of 0. ooRexx accepts most of these spellings and reads them in its own way, +02:60 as +03:00 and 24:00:00.000000 as one day.

169.body: LOOP [LABEL name] [COUNTER name] [repetitor] [conditional]; instructions; END [name] ANSI: 6.3.2.12, 8.3.6; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > LOOP LOOP is the repetitive form of DO under a second keyword. Every clause that follows the keyword has the same meaning that it has after DO, and the block ends at the same END. The one difference is the clause that has nothing after the keyword: a DO with nothing is a group that runs once, and a LOOP with nothing is a loop that never ends by itself. This page states that difference and the places where the keyword matters. The standard defines DO only, so LOOP is an addition of ooRexx, and the ansi citation of this page names the sections of DO.
169.title: LOOP

17.body:
ANSI: 6.2; rexxref: General Concepts > Structure and General Syntax This chapter specifies how the text of a program becomes tokens. A program is a sequence of clauses, and a clause is a sequence of tokens. The chapter covers the level below the clause: which characters a program may hold, how comments and strings are written, and where one token ends and the next begins. The meaning of a clause, and of the expressions inside it, is the business of the chapters that follow. Every token is a string in quotes, a symbol or number, an operator of one to three characters, or a special character, and strings carry an optional radix suffix that makes them hexadecimal or binary. Blanks and comments sit between tokens and are not tokens themselves. The chapter has these pages: Characters : the characters a program may use, case, blanks and line ends. Comments : block comments, nesting and line comments. Literals : strings, hexadecimal strings and binary strings. Symbols : the characters of a symbol, constant, simple, stem and compound symbols, and environment symbols. Operators : special characters and how operator tokens form. Clauses : where a clause ends, null clauses, labels and continuation. [lex.index.read-first] A program is read in full before any clause of it runs, so a fault anywhere in the text, even after an exit or inside a routine that is never called, is raised before the first clause runs. A fault in the lexical form of the text is an unmatched quote or comment delimiter (SYNTAX 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3), a character outside the character set (SYNTAX 13.1) or a malformed hexadecimal or binary string (SYNTAX 15.1 to 15.6). The program then produces no output, and the interpreter exits with the negated error number, so that the exit status is 256 minus the error number: 243 for 13.1. The text given to INTERPRET is read when the INTERPRET instruction runs, so the same fault there is an ordinary SYNTAX condition that a trap can handle, and the instructions before it in the string never run. say 'before'; exit

13.1 [lex.index.token-end] A token ends at the first character that cannot be part of it. A string ends at its closing quote, a symbol at the first character that is not a symbol character, and an operator character is a token of its own or joins a following operator character where the two form one operator, also across blanks and comments, as the gap rule says. Blanks are needed only where two tokens would otherwise read as one, so 1+2 and 1 + 2 are the same three tokens. A string may also touch the symbol after it . say 1+2 1 + 2

171.body: rexxref: General Concepts > Clauses and Instructions > Message Instructions; General Concepts > Message Instructions Deviations: D36 A message instruction is a clause that sends a message to an object for what the object does, where a message term in an expression is evaluated for what it answers. The clause is a message term with nothing after it, or a message term followed by = and an expression, which sets a value on the receiver. This page specifies how the interpreter treats the answer of a message instruction, how a message assignment is turned into a message, the order in which its parts are evaluated, and the errors. The syntax of a message term and the messages that strings and operators understand are in the expressions chapter , and the classes specify what their methods do.
171.title: Message instructions

The kinds rule says which other clauses are commands , among them one with an operator after the message. A message instruction does not set RC, and a command does not set RESULT. address system

[instr.message.assign] The clause term~name = expression sends the message name=, which is the name with an equal sign added, to the value of the term. The value of the expression is the first argument. A name written as a string gets the equal sign in the same way, and the case of the name does not matter. The clause term[i, j] = expression sends the message []= the same way, with the value of the expression first and the values of the index expressions after it, and the brackets may hold no expression at all. When the message has its own arguments, as in term~name(a) = expression, the value comes first and the arguments follow. The answer of the message is treated as for any message instruction, so it is assigned to RESULT, or RESULT is dropped. Rexx has two kinds: a block comment, written between /* and */, which may span lines and nest, and a line comment, which starts with -- and runs to the end of the line. A comment is not a token, but it ends the token before it, so it separates a symbol, a number or a string from what follows. 191.body: PROCEDURE [EXPOSE [name | (name)]...] ANSI: 6.3.2.76, 8.3.18; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > PROCEDURE Deviations: D70 PROCEDURE gives an internal routine variables of its own. Without it a routine works on the variables of its caller. With it the routine starts with none, the variables it sets are dropped when it returns, and only the names that EXPOSE lists stay shared with the caller. This page specifies the routine's own variables, the one place where PROCEDURE may stand, the forms of the names, the list form (name), and the errors. [instr.procedure.list] A name in parentheses is exposed as a name outside them is, and its value in the routine after that is a list of further names. The name may be a simple, a stem or a compound symbol. The value is converted to a string as the DROP list rule describes, split at whitespace , and each word is exposed as if it had been written in the clause, as a simple, stem or compound symbol. A list that is empty or all whitespace exposes nothing. The routine sees the variable that holds the list, and an assignment to it reaches the caller. When the caller's i is unset too, the exposed variable is A.I itself and its value is the list, as the third example shows. 2.body: This book is normative in its own right: its rules define the language interrexx implements, and no other document or implementation does. When the interpreter and a rule disagree, one of them has a defect, and the disagreement is settled here before it is settled in code. Behavior the book does not state is not promised, and where a reader might expect a promise the book says explicitly that a behavior is not specified. Rules and examples are normative. Everything else is informative: the overview at the top of a page, and every note, which is set as a block quote that begins Note. A note explains where a rule comes from or how another definition of Rexx differs; it never adds to or changes a rule.
2.title: Authority

20.body: ANSI: 6.2.2, 6.2.1.1; rexxref: General Concepts > Structure and General Syntax > Tokens A literal is a token whose value is written in the program: a string in quotes, or a hexadecimal or binary string, which spells a string by the codes of its characters. All three have a string as their value, and none is a number or a name. A string never changes when the program runs, whatever characters it holds. This page gives the forms, the faults that the reader of a program finds in them, and how a literal sits next to the tokens around it.
20.title: Literals

200.body: RAISE condition [DESCRIPTION expr] [ADDITIONAL expr | ARRAY (expr, ...)] [RETURN [expr] | EXIT [expr]] rexxref: Keyword Instructions > RAISE Deviations: D65 RAISE raises a condition on purpose, and it also ends the code that runs it. The condition is raised in the code that called the code that ended, so the instruction is how a routine or a method reports an event to its caller, whose traps answer it as they answer any condition. SYNTAX and the main program are the exceptions, and so is the text of an INTERPRET with RETURN; this page specifies them. The instruction names the condition, carries the values that the condition object holds, and chooses whether the code ends as RETURN or as EXIT does, which also decides who is the caller. This page specifies the form of the clause, what each option sets, where the condition is raised for each kind of code, what happens when no trap answers, and the PROPAGATE form that raises a trapped condition again. What a trap does, and what a program reads from a condition, belong to the conditions chapter , and the rules here link the ones they use.
200.title: RAISE

201.body:
[instr.raise.form] RAISE is followed by a condition word: ERROR, FAILURE, HALT, LOSTDIGITS, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE, PROPAGATE, SYNTAX or USER, in any case. ERROR and FAILURE then take a code, SYNTAX takes a number and USER takes a name, and the other words take nothing. The options come after that, in any order, each at most once: DESCRIPTION and an expression, ADDITIONAL and an expression or ARRAY and a parenthesized list of expressions (the two are one option, so a clause has at most one of them), and RETURN or EXIT with an optional expression (again one option). The code, the number and the expression of an option are each one term: a literal string, a constant symbol, an environment symbol or an expression in parentheses. A variable symbol is not a term here, so its value is written in parentheses. A RETURN or EXIT that has no expression ends the clause: any option after it is read as its expression. ANY is not a condition word, because the names rule says that nothing raises it. call on user alpha name h

exit

ERROR and FAILURE take a code, which is any string: the text of the literal, of the constant symbol in upper case, or of the value of the parenthesized expression, with no check that it is a number. The user conditions take a name, which the name rule specifies. 208.body: REPLY [expression] rexxref: Keyword Instructions > REPLY REPLY ends a method call early. The caller gets the answer at once and goes on, and the method goes on with the clauses after the REPLY, on an activity of its own. It is how a method hands out a result and then does the slow part of its work while the caller carries on. This page specifies what the caller and the continuation each see, what the continuation may and may not do, the places where REPLY may stand, and the errors. The order in which the caller's later clauses and the continuation's clauses run is not specified, unless a wait, a guard or the instruction itself puts them in order. Every example below puts them in order, so that its output does not depend on it.
208.title: REPLY

209.body:
[instr.reply.early] REPLY evaluates its expression and hands the value to whoever sent the message, as RETURN does, and the caller continues with it. A REPLY with no expression hands over no value, and the caller sees what it sees after a RETURN with none, as the message rule says. The method does not end. The clause after the REPLY runs next, on a new activity, with the variables of the method as they were, its arguments, and its object variables. For a message sent with ~start , the value of the REPLY is the ~result of the message object. The method call that sent the message is over for the caller, so the method's later RETURN or EXIT has no value to hand over. log = .array~new

213.body: RETURN [expression [, expression]...] ANSI: 6.3.2.80, 8.3.22; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > RETURN RETURN ends the routine, method or program that is running and hands an optional value back to whoever started it. What the starter does with the value depends on how the code was started: a CALL stores it in RESULT, a function call uses it as the value of the call, a message answers it, and for the main program it becomes the program's exit code. This page specifies RETURN in each of these places, the list form with several expressions, and the errors of the clause. EXIT is the instruction that ends the whole program from any depth, and the page of the exit code is that one.
213.title: RETURN

214.body:

A RETURN with an expression hands its value to the caller, and a CALL stores it in RESULT as the CALL rule says. A RETURN without an expression hands over no value, so a CALL drops RESULT, and a function call that has no value raises SYNTAX 44.1, as the rule for a call in an expression says. The caller's settings come back as the CALL rule says. call find 6

[instr.return.program] A RETURN in the code of the main program, outside any internal routine, method or routine directive, ends the program, as EXIT does, and its value is the program's value, whose use as the exit code is specified with EXIT . This holds for a RETURN inside a DO, IF or SELECT, and for a RETURN after a label that the program reached by running into it, since no CALL started that code. A RETURN without an expression gives no value and the exit code 0. say 'main'

A CALL of the routine stores the value as for an internal routine. o = .box~new

218.body: SAY [expression] ANSI: 6.3.2.81, 8.3.23; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > SAY Deviations: D40, D98 SAY writes one line of text to the standard output. It evaluates its expression, converts the result to a string and writes that string followed by a line end. Without an expression it writes an empty line. The instruction does nothing else: it sets no variable, and it leaves the special variables RC and RESULT as they were. The output goes to the same stream that the builtins with no stream name write to, so SAY mixes with them in the order the program ran them.

[instr.say.write] The expression is everything after the keyword. SAY evaluates it, takes the string value of the result and writes the string, then a line end. The expression is an ordinary expression , so the operators join, add and compare as they do anywhere else, and a number is written in the form that the operation that made it gave it. numeric digits 4

It does not change control characters or other unprintable ones, it adds no padding and it does not stop at a character that other contexts treat as an end of text, such as '00'x or '1A'x. A line feed in the string is written as it is, so it breaks the line where it stands, and the line end that SAY adds follows the string. Which bytes make up the line end that SAY adds is not specified. say 'a' || '00'x || 'b' || '0D'x || '1A'x || '7F'x

[instr.say.deviation.40] SAY and the builtins that write to the standard output share one stream, and the text of all of them appears in the order the program wrote it. A standard output that is a pipe or a file is buffered, and it is handed over at the points that Deviation 40 names. ooRexx writes each line at once, so text still buffered when the process is killed or crashes is lost here and is not lost there. say 'one'

In ooRexx the line does not appear at once, and what is written after the last close, flush or open is lost. SAY raises no NOTREADY condition in either, whatever the state of the standard output, so the trap in the example does not run. say 'one'

223.body: SELECT [LABEL name] [CASE expression]; WHEN expression [, expression]... [;] THEN [;] instruction ... [OTHERWISE [instructions]] END [name] ANSI: 6.3.2.17, 8.3.24; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > SELECT Deviations: D39 SELECT chooses one of several alternatives. The block holds a sequence of WHEN clauses, each with a test and one instruction, and an optional OTHERWISE part. The tests run in order and the instruction of the first true one runs, after which control leaves the block at its END. In the second form, SELECT CASE, the tests compare a value that SELECT computes once. This page specifies the order of evaluation, what a test must be, the CASE comparison, the label of the block and the errors. The two-way choice is IF .
223.title: SELECT

224.body:
[instr.select.run] SELECT evaluates the expressions of its WHEN clauses from the first to the last, and it stops at the first one that is true. The instruction after the THEN of that clause runs, and control then passes to the clause after the END of the SELECT, so the WHEN clauses after it are not evaluated and the OTHERWISE part does not run. THEN may begin a later clause than the expression of its WHEN, as the rule for THEN says, and the instruction after each THEN follows the rules of IF for null clauses and for the implied semicolons after THEN. n = 7
select when n < 5 then say 'small' when n < 10 then say 'medium' when f(n) then say 'never evaluated' otherwise say 'large'
end
say 'after'
exit

The first SELECT below has a THEN on a later line than its WHEN, and a semicolon and a comment before it. The second has a null clause after the THEN. select when 0 then say 'no' when 1; /* c */ then say 'yes' when 1;; then say 'not reached' otherwise say 'other'
end
select when 1 then ; say 'branch'
end yes

225.body:
[instr.select.when] In a SELECT without CASE, the expression of a WHEN must have the value 0 or 1, as the value of an IF must, and any other value raises SYNTAX 34.2. A WHEN can hold a list of expressions separated by commas, and the list is true and is evaluated as the list of an IF is. An expression of the list that is evaluated and is not 0 or 1 raises SYNTAX 34.6. The error is raised when the WHEN is reached, so a WHEN that comes after a true one is never evaluated and cannot raise it. call try 'select; when 2 then nop; end'

227.body:
[instr.select.case] SELECT CASE evaluates its expression once, before the first WHEN, and each WHEN then holds one expression or a comma-separated list of them. The WHEN is true when the strict comparison == of the case value with one of its expressions is true, where the case value is the receiver and the expression the argument, and the list is evaluated from left to right and stops at the first true comparison. The comparison is the strict one, so 1 does not equal 1.0, a blank counts, and the case of letters counts. The expressions need not be 0 or 1, and no value of a WHEN raises SYNTAX 34.2, so a case that matches no WHEN raises SYNTAX 7.3 as above. When the case value is an object, the == message goes to it, and its answer must be 0 or 1: any other answer, such as the text banana or the number 2, raises SYNTAX 34.905. x = 'b'

232.body: SIGNAL {label | [VALUE] expression | ON condition [NAME label] | OFF condition} ANSI: 6.3.2.82, 8.3.25; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > SIGNAL SIGNAL moves control to a label, and it also switches the trap of a condition on or off. The jump goes to a label by name, anywhere in the program, and it abandons the blocks that are open in the routine, so it is the instruction for leaving a deeply nested construct and for a handler that does not come back. The other form, with ON or OFF, does not move control. This page specifies how the label is found, what the jump ends, what it sets, and the shape of the ON and OFF forms. What a trap does when its condition occurs belongs to the chapter on conditions , which also specifies SIGNAL's role there.
232.title: SIGNAL

233.body:
[instr.signal.label] SIGNAL name continues at the first label that has the text of the name, among the labels of the code that holds the SIGNAL: the main program, or the body of the one routine or method that the SIGNAL is in. A name written as a symbol is read in upper case, and a name written as a string is used as it is written. The label rule says which labels these find and which of several of one name is the first. A symbol is a constant here: its value as a variable plays no part. When no label has the name, the instruction raises SYNTAX 16.1. The error is raised when the SIGNAL runs, so the clauses before it have run. A label of the main program is therefore not one that a method or a routine can reach, and the labels of a method are not those of the main program. signal Go

[instr.signal.ends] A jump ends every DO, LOOP, SELECT and IF that is open in the routine that holds the SIGNAL, without running their tests and without stepping a control variable, which keeps its value. The blocks of the callers of the routine are not ended: a routine that jumps inside itself returns to a caller that is still in its loop. SIGL is an ordinary variable that the interpreter sets, so an assignment to it is replaced by the next SIGNAL or CALL, and before the first of them it is unset. 236.body:
[instr.signal.on] SIGNAL ON condition enables the trap of a condition, and SIGNAL OFF condition disables it. The condition is ERROR, FAILURE, HALT, LOSTDIGITS, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE, SYNTAX or ANY, or USER followed by the name of a user condition, which is a symbol read as a constant in upper case, so user foo names the condition USER FOO, and not a string. The label is not looked for when the trap is enabled, so an ON for a label that does not exist is not an error then. What a trap does when its condition occurs, and the role of the label, are the subject of the conditions chapter . OFF takes no NAME. do c over .array~of('error', 'failure', 'halt', 'lostdigits',, 'nomethod', 'nostring', 'notready', 'novalue', 'syntax', 'any') interpret 'signal on' c interpret 'signal off' c say c 'on and off'

237.body: TRACE [setting | VALUE expression | (expression)] ANSI: 6.3.2.85, 8.3.26; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > TRACE; Keyword Instructions > TRACE > The Format of Trace Output Deviations: D0, D7, D50 TRACE chooses how much of a running program the interpreter reports, and the report is a stream of lines in a fixed format. This page specifies the forms of the instruction, when a new setting takes effect, where the lines go and what each kind of line looks like. The nine settings, what the TRACE function answers and how a setting is scoped across calls belong to the TRACE function , and this page links them instead of repeating them. The examples that show trace lines first send them to standard output with .traceoutput~destination(.output), because the lines go to the error stream otherwise, and the examples are checked on standard output only.

[instr.trace.indent] The text of a clause is indented by two blanks for each level of nesting. A level is added inside a DO group or loop, after THEN or ELSE, after WHEN or OTHERWISE, and for each active internal call. THEN, ELSE, WHEN and OTHERWISE are shown on a line of their own, one level in from the IF or SELECT, and the clause after them one level further. DO, SELECT and the IF clause stand at the level of their surroundings, and the END that closes a DO or a SELECT stands there too. The lines of values are indented by the level of their clause and two blanks more. The label of an internal routine and the clauses of its body are shown one level deeper than the CALL that started it. .traceoutput~destination(.output)

247.body: USE [STRICT] ARG [target [= default]] [, ...] | USE LOCAL [name]... rexxref: Keyword Instructions > USE Deviations: D71 USE has two unrelated forms. USE ARG takes the arguments of the running program, routine or method and stores the argument objects themselves in variables, where ARG and PARSE ARG make strings of them and cut them up with a template. USE STRICT ARG is the same with a check of the number of arguments. USE LOCAL is for methods only and decides which of the method's variables are its own. This page specifies the targets and defaults of USE ARG, the strict form and the errors of both forms. How the arguments are counted and read is the matter of the ARG builtin .
247.title: USE

248.body:
[instr.use.arg] The targets of USE ARG are filled from left to right. The target in position n receives argument n, as an object, without any change: it is not converted to a string, its case stays, and a collection is the same collection that the caller passed. A target for which no argument was passed, because the caller passed fewer arguments or left that position empty, is dropped, so a variable it had before is unset. An argument beyond the last target is ignored. The clause may run again, and it reads the arguments the call was made with, not the current values of the variables. A target can be a simple symbol, a compound symbol or a stem symbol, or it can be left empty, which skips its argument and sets nothing. call show 1, 2, 3

call show
call show , 'b'
call show 1, , 3, 4
call take .array~of('x', 'y'), 'Mixed Case', 12
exit

[instr.use.strict] USE STRICT ARG fills the targets as USE ARG does, after it has checked the number of arguments. A target with no default is required, and a target with a default is optional, so the number of arguments passed must not be smaller than the number of required targets, and must not be greater than the number of targets. A position that is left empty counts, but trailing positions left empty do not, in the sense of the ARG builtin . A required position that is left empty is a third fault. In a program, an internal routine or an external routine the three faults raise SYNTAX 40.3, 40.4 and 40.5; in a method they raise SYNTAX 93.901, 93.902 and 93.903. A required target may follow an optional one: the count must still reach it. Without a target the clause demands no argument at all. call s

ANSI: 6.2.2, 6.2.1.1, 6.2.1.2, 7.2; rexxref: General Concepts > Structure and General Syntax > Tokens A symbol is a token written without quotes from letters, digits and a few marks. It plays one of three roles: a name for a variable, a constant whose value is its own text, or a name that the environment of the program resolves. Which role a symbol plays follows from its first character and from where its periods are, not from anything around it. This page gives the characters of a symbol, the three roles, and the limit on its length. What a variable holds, and how a compound symbol is turned into a name when the program runs, belongs to the variables page . [lex.symbols.chars] A symbol is a run of symbol characters: the letters A to Z and a to z, the digits, and the four marks . ! ? _. The run ends at the first character that is not one of these, so a blank, an operator character, a quote mark, a comma or a parenthesis ends a symbol, and so does a comment. A symbol is read in upper case, as the case rule says. The SYMBOL function tests a string against the same characters and the same length limit. a = 5; b = 2; a_b = 'joined'

[instr.use.local] USE LOCAL reverses the division of a method's variables. With it every variable of the method is an object variable, as if it were exposed, except the names the clause lists, which are the method's own. A listed name can be a simple or a stem symbol; a stem lists every compound variable of it. 253.body: ANSI: 6.3.2.71, 8.3.17; rexxref: Parsing Parsing takes a string, the source, and a template, and assigns parts of the source to variables. The template says where to cut the source and which variable receives each part. It is the one mechanism behind PARSE, ARG and PULL: those instructions differ only in where the source comes from and in whether they change its case, and the instructions chapter specifies them. This chapter specifies what a template does with a source once there is one. A template is a list of targets and triggers. A target is a place that receives a value, usually a variable. A trigger is a pattern that finds a place in the source, or a position that names one. The pages of this chapter are: Templates : templates made of targets alone, which cut the source into words, and the period that takes a word and discards it. Patterns : the triggers: strings, positions, relative positions and patterns that come from a variable or an expression. Several strings : the comma that moves on to the next template and the next source string, and the options that change the case of the source or of the comparison. PARSE VALUE and PARSE VAR are the sources the examples use, because each takes a single string. The ARG source is the only one that provides several strings, and its template list is on the last page.
253.title: Parsing

254.body:
[parse.index.elements] A template holds these elements, in any order and number. A target is a variable symbol of any of the three forms, a message term that can stand on the left of an assignment, or a period. A trigger is a string literal , a hex or binary literal included, an expression in parentheses, or a position: a whole number, or one of the characters +, -, =, > and < followed by a whole number or by an expression in parentheses. A comma ends the template and begins the next one. Any other token is a syntax error, and the pattern page describes it. data = 'tag:12:east'
parse var data kind ':' count ':' side
say kind count side
parse var data . 4 text 7 .
say text tag 12 east
:12 [parse.index.pieces] The triggers of a template divide the source into pieces. Each piece lies between two triggers, or between the start or end of the source and a trigger, and the targets that stand between those two triggers share it. A template with no trigger has one piece, the whole source. The targets of a piece take its words as the templates page says, and a piece with no target is skipped. Where each trigger lies, and so where a piece begins and ends, is the subject of the patterns page . parse value 'alpha beta;gamma delta' with u v ';' w y
say u'|'v'|'w'|'y
parse value 'alpha beta;gamma delta' with u v w y
say u'|'v'|'w'|'y alpha|beta|gamma|delta
alpha|beta;gamma|delta|

254.title: What a template is made of

255.body:
[parse.index.order] The interpreter evaluates the source before it assigns anything, so a target that is also the variable of the source does not change what is parsed. It then works through the template one piece at a time, from left to right. For each piece it first finds the trigger that ends it, evaluating the expression of that trigger if it is a parenthesized one, and only then assigns the targets of the piece, left to right. An expression in a trigger therefore sees the values that the targets of the earlier pieces have received, but the old values of the targets of the piece that the trigger itself ends. The tail of a compound symbol that is a target is evaluated when that target is assigned, so it sees the targets before it in its own piece too. When the same variable appears as a target twice, the later assignment is the one that remains. u = 'ef'
parse value 'ab,cd,ab,ef' with u ',' v ',' (u) w
say u v w
n = 2
parse value '5 abcdef' with n =(n) v
say n'|'v
n = 2
parse value '5 abcdef' with n ' ' =(n) v
say n'|'v
text = 'one two three'
parse var text first text
say first'|'text
i = 1
parse value 'p,2,r' with a.i ',' i ',' a.i
say a.1 i a.2
parse value '3 x' with i b.i
say b.3
parse value 'm n' with k k
say '['k']' ab cd ,ef
5| abcdef
5|cdef
one|two three
p 2 r
x
[n] [parse.index.nothing] A parse changes only its targets. No other variable changes, the special variables RC and RESULT are not set, and a template with no target changes nothing at all, even when it contains triggers that find nothing. The source expression of PARSE VALUE is still evaluated. rc = 'keep'; result = 'also'
parse value 'abc' with
parse value 'abc' with 'b' "z"
say rc result
parse value tell() with
say 'done'
exit

256.body: ANSI: 8.3.17; rexxref: Parsing > Simple Templates for Parsing into Words, Parsing > The Period as a Placeholder, Parsing > Message Term Assignments A template with no trigger cuts the source into words. This page specifies that case, and every other template reduces to it: the pieces rule hands each piece of a source to the targets that stand next to it, and what those targets do with a piece is what this page says. The examples use parse var and parse value … with.
256.title: Templates

257.body:
[parse.templates.words] Each target of a piece, except the last, receives one word of it. To find the word, the parse skips the whitespace at the start of what remains of the piece, takes the characters up to the next whitespace character or the end, and then removes one whitespace character after the word, if there is one. A word is what the builtins call one, and whitespace is as the conventions define it, so a line feed can be part of a word. s = ' alpha beta'||'09'x||'gamma delta '
parse var s u v w
say u'|'v'|'w'|'
parse value 'ab'||'0a'x||'cd ef' with u v
say c2x(u) v alpha|beta|gamma delta |
61620A6364 ef [parse.templates.last] The last target of a piece receives all that remains of the piece after the words of the targets before it, and nothing is removed from it: its leading whitespace beyond the one character that ended the previous word, its interior whitespace and its trailing whitespace all stay. A piece with a single target therefore gives that target the whole piece, with the whitespace at both ends. Words beyond the number of targets are therefore in the last target, unless that is a period , which discards them. s = ' alpha beta gamma delta '
parse var s u
say '['u']'
parse var s u v
say '['u']['v']'
parse var s . v
say '['v']'
parse value 'one ' with u v
say '['u']['v']' [ alpha beta gamma delta ]
[alpha][ beta gamma delta ]
[ beta gamma delta ]
[one][ ] [parse.templates.fewer] When the words of a piece run out, each target that remains receives the null string, except that the last target of the piece receives what is left, as the previous rule says, and that is the null string only when nothing is left. So a null source, and a source of whitespace only, give two targets the null string, while a single target receives the whitespace itself. Every target is assigned: a variable that held a value before the parse does not keep it. u = 'old'; v = 'old'; w = 'old'
parse value 'one' with u v w
say '['u']['v']['w']'
u = 'old'; v = 'old'

say '['u']['v']'
u = 'old'; v = 'old'
parse value ' ' with u v
say '['u']['v']'

257.title: Words

258.body:
[parse.templates.period] A period stands where a variable could and discards what that variable would receive. It takes its place in the sequence of targets as a variable would, so it consumes the next word, or the rest of the piece when it is the last, and assigns nothing. A period at the end of a template is the usual way to ignore the surplus of the source. parse value 'red green blue amber' with . second . fourth
say second fourth
parse value 'red green blue amber' with first .
say first
parse value 'red green blue amber' with . . third
say third green amber
red
blue amber
258.title: The period

259.body:
[parse.templates.targets] A target that is a simple symbol or a compound symbol is assigned like the left side of an assignment , and the tail of a compound symbol is evaluated when the assignment is made, as the order rule says. A stem symbol is a target too, and assigning to it gives the stem that value as its default , so that every compound variable of the stem has the value at once. A message term, such as slots[2] or obj~attr, receives its value as a message assignment does, by sending the assignment message with the value as its argument. The answer of that message is discarded, and unlike the instruction a parse does not set RESULT. The receiver and the arguments of the message are evaluated when the target is assigned, and so see the targets assigned before it. parse value 'p q r' with s. t
say s.1 s.any t

k = 1
parse value '2 red blue' with k slots[k * 2] slots[k - 1]
say k slots[4] slots[1]

ANSI: 6.2.2; rexxref: General Concepts > Structure and General Syntax > Tokens An operator character is one that can be part of an operator, and a special character is one that stands alone as a token, such as a parenthesis. Both kinds end the token before them, so no blank is needed beside them. Several operators are written with two or three characters, and the characters of one operator may be spread over blanks and comments. This page gives the operators as tokens, the way characters are joined into them, and the way blanks next to these characters are treated. What an operator computes is the business of the numbers and the expressions chapters. [lex.operators.set] The operators are these tokens. The arithmetic operators are + - * / % // and **. The concatenation operator is ||. The comparison operators are = \= > < >= <= <> >< \> and \<, and the strict comparison operators == \== >> << >>= <<= \>> and \<<. The logical operators are & | and &&. The characters + - and \ are also prefix operators. The blank and the abuttal of two terms are operators too, but they are not tokens, as the blank rule explains. say 7 + 2 7 - 2 7 * 2 7 / 2 7 % 2 7 // 2 7 ** 2

260.body: ANSI: 8.3.17; rexxref: Parsing > Templates Containing String Patterns, Parsing > Templates Containing Positional (Numeric) Patterns, Parsing > Parsing with Variable Patterns, Parsing > Advanced Topics in Parsing > Combining String and Positional Patterns A pattern is a trigger: it makes a break in the source, and the targets on either side of it share the pieces that the break separates. This page says where each kind of trigger puts its break and which characters the pieces hold. What a target does with its piece is the business of the templates page . A break has a start and an end. For a string it is the span of the match, and for a position it is a single point, so its start and its end are the same. Unless a rule below says otherwise, a piece begins where the previous break ends, or at the first character of the source before any break, and it ends where the next break begins, or at the end of the source after the last break. Positions count as the convention says, from 1, and the point at a position lies just before the character there.
260.title: Patterns

261.body:
[parse.patterns.string] A string literal , or a hex or binary literal, finds the first place, at or after the point where the piece begins, where its characters occur in the source, comparing each character exactly as it is, so case matters. The break is the span of that occurrence: the piece ends just before it and the next piece begins just after it, and the matched characters belong to no piece. An occurrence at the very beginning of the piece leaves an empty piece before it, and an empty piece gives its targets the null string. parse value 'id=42;tag=blue' with key '=' val
say key'|'val
parse value 'id=42;tag=blue' with key '=' val ';' rest
say key'|'val'|'rest
parse value 'id=42;tag=blue' with 'id=' num
say num
parse value 'id=42;tag=blue' with before 'id' after
say '['before']['after']'
parse value 'id=42;Tag=blue' with before 'tag' after
say '['before']['after']' id|42;tag=blue
id|42|tag=blue
42;tag=blue
[][=42;tag=blue]
[id=42;Tag=blue][] [parse.patterns.string.missing] When the string does not occur, and when it is the null string, which never matches, the break lies at the end of the source. The piece before it runs to the end, and the next piece begins there, so each target after the pattern receives the null string, as for a null source does each target. A later string cannot match either. parse value 'alpha beta' with u ',' v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value 'alpha beta' with u 'a' v "" w
say '['u']['v']['w']'
parse value 'alpha beta' with u '' v
say '['u']['v']'
parse value '' with u ',' v 3 w
say '['u']['v']['w']' [alpha beta][]

say rest

say rest

262.body:
[parse.patterns.variable] An expression in parentheses is evaluated when the template reaches the end of the piece that it ends, which is after the targets of the earlier pieces are assigned and before the targets of that piece are . Its value is a string trigger as the string rule describes. A value that is an object and not a string is replaced by its string, as the conventions say. The value is used as the string that it is, so a value that looks like a number is still the characters to find, and a value that is the null string is the null string, which never matches . The expression may be as long as any expression, with operators and function calls. sep = ','; n = 4; none = ''
parse value 'ab,cd,ef' with u (sep) v
say u'|'v
parse value 'abc4efg' with u (n) v
say u'|'v

say '['u']['v']'

say '['u']['v']'

say u'|'v

say '['sep']['rest']'

say '['sep']['rest']' ab|cd,ef

263.body:
[parse.patterns.absolute] A whole number written as a trigger, or = followed by a whole number, puts a point at that position: the piece before it ends there and the next piece begins there. The characters before position n are the characters numbered below n, so u 4 v gives u the first three. A position beyond the end of the source puts the point at the end, and position 0 is the same as position 1, so a source of L characters has the points 1 to L+1. The = form says the same as the bare number. Only the = form can take the position from a variable or an expression, written in parentheses, as the bare parentheses are a string trigger. parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 4 v

The next piece begins at the position, so the text from there on is shared out again. This is the way a template reads part of the source twice. parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 8 v 3 w

That start is the start of the matched characters for a string, the position itself for a position, the beginning of the source before any break, and the end of the source after a break that found nothing. The point is limited to the positions from 1 to the end of the source. A relative position does not begin the piece that precedes it where the previous break ended, as other triggers do, but where that break began, so the characters of a matched string are part of that piece. A point that is not after the start of that piece makes it run to the end of the source, as for any position . +0 and -0 put the point at the start of the previous break. parse value 'abcdefghij' with u +3 v +3 w +3 y

At 0 they differ: the piece before >0 ends at once, where the previous break starts, so it is empty, and the next piece begins there, while +0 makes the preceding piece run to the end of the source. parse value 'abcdefghij' with u >3 v >3 w
say u'|'v'|'w
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'c' v >0 w
say '['u']['v']['w']'
parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'c' v +0 w
say '['u']['v']['w']'

say '['u']['v']'
n = 2

abcde|de|de|fghij [parse.patterns.length.before] <n puts the point n characters before the start of the previous break, limited to position 1, and it does not leave the targets between the previous break and <n the piece that the earlier triggers gave them. Those targets receive the n characters that lie just before the start of the previous break, or the characters from position 1 when fewer lie there, and the next piece begins at the point. So <n reads again the text before the break that precedes it. It is not the same as -n, which leaves the preceding piece to run to the end of the source. When no break precedes it, the start is position 1 and the targets before <n receive the null string. parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 'f' near <3 rest
say u'|'near'|'rest

[parse.patterns.number] The number of a position is a constant written in the template, or the value of an expression in parentheses after a sign, =, > or <. Blanks may separate the sign, =, > or < from the number or the parenthesis. The number, whether constant or expression, must be whole: a constant may be written in any form whose value is whole, such as 03, 4.0 or 1e1, and 3.5 is not. It must have no more digits than the current NUMERIC DIGITS allows, so 1e9 is accepted only when that setting is at least 10, counted on its value (0999 passes under 3 and 0.1e4 does not), and it must not be negative. A number that fails any of these checks raises SYNTAX 26.4 when the clause runs. A fraction, text, the null string and a negative value of an expression all raise it; the direction of a relative position is the sign in the template. A constant that is a symbol is checked the same way when the clause runs, so 3.5 and 3a raise SYNTAX 26.4 then and not when the program is read. A value of an expression that is an object and not a string is replaced by its string, as the conventions say, and that string is then checked; this holds after =, +, -, > and <. parse value 'abcdefghij' with u 03 v 4.0 w 1e1 y

numeric digits 12
call lit 'u 1e9 v'
exit

(A - that ends a line is a continuation and not a template token.) A program file that holds any of these does not run at all, and its exit code is 218. The text of INTERPRET raises the same error when it is read . say 'never shown'

call try 'u >> v'

call try 'u <'
exit

265.body: ANSI: 8.3.17; rexxref: Parsing > Advanced Topics in Parsing > Parsing Several Strings, Parsing > Using UPPER, LOWER, and CASELESS This page covers the two features that act on a whole parse and not on one template: the comma that moves to the next template and the next source string, and the options UPPER, LOWER and CASELESS that decide how the source is read. The instructions chapter specifies the keywords of PARSE, ARG and PULL that give a source and select an option. This page specifies what the options do to a parse.
265.breadcrumbs: Parsing » Several strings and case » Several strings and case
265.title: Several strings and case

266.body:
[parse.multiple.comma] A comma ends the template before it and begins the next one, and the next template parses the next source string. Each template starts afresh on its own string: its first piece begins at the first character, and a relative position before any trigger counts from there. The instructions that take their source from the arguments of a call, ARG and PARSE ARG, have one string for each argument, in order. An argument that was omitted is the null string. call show 'ab cd', 'ef=gh', 'ij kl mn'
call show 'ab cd', , 'ij kl mn'
exit
show: parse arg u v, w '=' y, z +2 q say u'|'v'|'w'|'y'|'z'|'q return ab|cd|ef|gh|ij| kl mn
ab|cd|||ij| kl mn [parse.multiple.single] A source of any other kind, such as a VALUE or a VAR, is one string. Its first template parses it. A template with no string left to parse, whether it follows such a source or the last argument, parses the null string, so each target of it receives the null string and a pattern in it finds nothing. parse value 'ab cd ef' with u v, w y, z
say '['u']['v']['w']['y']['z']'
data = 'one two'
parse var data first, second
say first'|'second'|' [ab][cd ef][][][]
one two|| [parse.multiple.counts] A source string with no template after the last comma is not parsed, and no variable sees it. A template that is missing, for example the one before a leading comma, assigns nothing and still uses up its string. call one 'ab', 'cd', 'ef'
call two 'ab'
call three 'ab', 'cd'
exit
one: parse arg u say u return
two: parse arg u, v, w say '['u']['v']['w']' return
three: parse arg , v say v return ab
[ab][][]
cd [parse.multiple.shared] The templates of one list are parsed from left to right, each after the one before it, so the variables assigned by an earlier template are in place for the later ones. The order rule applies across the commas as well. call mark 'a-b', 'x-a-z'
exit
mark: parse arg first '-' second, third (first) fourth say first second third fourth return a b x- -z

266.title: Several templates

267.body:
[parse.multiple.convert] The options UPPER and LOWER change the source before any matching: UPPER makes each of the ASCII letters a to z upper case, and LOWER makes each of A to Z lower case, and no other character changes. Every source string is changed, so a parse with several strings changes them all. The values assigned are pieces of the changed string. The patterns of the template are not changed, so a literal pattern must be written in the case that the option produces, or it will not match. s = 'Alpha-BETA-gamma'
parse upper var s u '-' v '-' w
say u v w
parse lower var s u '-' v '-' w
say u v w
parse upper var s u 'beta' v
say '['u']['v']'
parse upper var s u 'BETA' v
say '['u']['v']'
parse lower value 'ABC É' with u v
say u v
call two 'Ab-Cd', 'eF-gH'
exit
two: parse upper arg p '-' q, r '-' s say p q r s return ALPHA BETA GAMMA
alpha beta gamma
[ALPHA-BETA-GAMMA][]
[ALPHA-][-GAMMA]
abc É
AB CD EF GH [parse.multiple.caseless] The option CASELESS makes the matching of string triggers ignore the case of the ASCII letters: a and A count as the same character, and so on for each letter. It applies to string patterns, and to the value of a variable pattern in the same way. The source is not changed, so the values assigned keep their case, and positions, words and the whitespace rules are as they are without it. Without CASELESS, matching is exact . A conversion and CASELESS may be given together, and then the conversion changes the source and the match ignores the case of what is left. s = 'Alpha-BETA-gamma'
parse caseless var s u 'beta' v
say u'|'v
parse var s u 'beta' v
say u'|'v
pat = 'bEtA'
parse caseless var s u (pat) v
say u'|'v
parse caseless var s u 'GAMMA'
say u
parse caseless value 'xyz' with u 'Y' v
say u v
parse upper caseless value 'Ab-cD' with u 'cd' v
say u'|'v Alpha-|-gamma
Alpha-BETA-gamma|
Alpha-|-gamma
Alpha-BETA-
x z
AB-| Note. The ANSI draft (8.3.17) has the option UPPER and no other: it has neither LOWER nor CASELESS, which ooRexx adds and this book follows.

268.body: rexxref: Directives A directive is a clause that starts with two colons. It does not run: it declares a piece of the program, such as a class, a method or a routine, and the interpreter acts on it before the program's own instructions run. A program is a package: a set of declared pieces, and the instructions that come before the first directive. This chapter specifies how a program is split by its directives, and the pages that follow specify each directive. The directives are ANNOTATE, ATTRIBUTE, CLASS, CONSTANT, METHOD, OPTIONS, REQUIRES, RESOURCE and ROUTINE. The pages of this chapter are: ::CLASS : a class, its superclass, metaclass and inheritance, and the order in which the classes of a package come into being. ::METHOD : a method of a class, the options that set its access and its kind, and a method that belongs to no class. ::ATTRIBUTE : the methods that read and write an attribute. ::CONSTANT : a constant of a class or of the package. ::ROUTINE : a routine of the package and whether other packages see it. ::REQUIRES : the program or library that a package needs. ::OPTIONS : the settings that the code of a package starts with. ::RESOURCE : a block of text that the package holds as data. ::ANNOTATE : the annotations on the package, a class, a method, an attribute, a constant or a routine. The classes that the directives create are objects too, and what their own methods do is specified in the classes chapter. This chapter says only what a directive makes and what the options on it mean. A note on the examples. A directive cannot be run by INTERPRET, and a fault in one of them ends a program file before it writes anything. Where an example shows which condition a directive raises, it builds the text of a package with the Package class and catches the condition that building it raises. That class has its own page in the classes chapter, so the examples use it for one thing only: .package~new(name, lines) translates the lines as a package, installs it as the installation rule says and runs its instructions before the next clause of the caller.
268.title: Directives

269.body:
[dir.index.directive] A clause is a directive when its first token is ::, which may be followed by blanks or comments before the keyword. The keyword is not case sensitive. A directive begins its clause at the start of a line or after a semicolon; after a label on the same line the :: is read as part of an expression and raises SYNTAX 35.1. A keyword that names no directive raises SYNTAX 99.916, and :: followed by nothing that is a symbol raises SYNTAX 20.916. The error is found when the program is read, so that a program file with such a clause writes nothing and exits with 256 minus the error number, 157 for 99.916, as the reading rule describes for any fault of the text. A directive cannot be part of the text of INTERPRET , which refuses it. call try '::class k1'
call try ':: /* a comment */ Class k2'
call try '::CLASS k3'
call try '::frob k4'
call try '::'
call try '::"class" k5'
call try 'lab: ::class k6'
exit
try: signal on syntax name e p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-kw', .array~of(arg(1))) say arg(1) '=> ok' return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code return ::class k1 => ok
:: /* a comment */ Class k2 => ok
::CLASS k3 => ok
::frob k4 => 99.916
:: => 20.916
::"class" k5 => 20.916
lab: ::class k6 => 35.1 say 'before'
::frob k [dir.index.end] A directive ends where a clause ends: at the end of the line or at a semicolon, and a comma at the end of a line continues it on the next line, as the clause rules say for any clause. A comment after the directive is part of the clause's white space. What follows the semicolon is the next clause, so a directive and the first clause of its body can share a line. src = .array~of('::class k', '::method one; return 1; ::method two; return 2')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-end', src)
src = .array~of('say .box~new~m', '::class box,', ' public -- a comment', - '::method m', ' return 3')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-end2', src) 3

27.body:
[lex.operators.special] The special characters are the comma, the semicolon, the colon, the parentheses ( and ), the brackets [ and ], and the tilde. Each is a token that ends the token before it. The tilde is the message operator ~, and two tildes ~~ are the cascade operator. As the characters of any operator may be, the two tildes may be separated by blanks and comments. say 'abc'~length 'abc'~~length 'abc'~ ~length 'abc'~/**/~length 3 abc abc abc [lex.operators.blank] A blank, or a run of blanks and tabs, between two terms is the concatenation operator. A blank next to an operator, a comma or a tilde has no effect. So does a blank after an opening ( or [ and one before a closing ) or ]. A comment is no blank . say 'a' 'b' 'a'||'b' 'a'/**/'b'
say 1+1 1 + 1
say left( 'abc' , 2 ) 'abc' ~ left( 2 )
a = .array~of(5, 6)
say a[ 2 ] a b ab ab
2 2
ab ab
6 [lex.operators.adjacent] A ( that follows a symbol or a string with no blank between them opens the arguments of a function call, and a [ that follows a term with no blank between them opens a subscript. A ( that follows the name in a message term in the same way holds the arguments of the message. A comment between them is no blank . With a blank, a ( starts a parenthesized term that is concatenated with the term before it, so that a message is sent without arguments, and a [ is an error, SYNTAX 35.1. A ( after a ) with no blank between them concatenates the two terms without a blank. say abs(-1) abs/**/(-1) abs (-1) abs /**/(-1)
say (1)(2) (1) (2) (1)/**/(2)
a = .array~of(5, 6)
say a[2] a/**/[2] 'abc'~left(2) 'abc'~left/**/(2)
signal on syntax name e
interpret 'say a [2]'
e: say condition('o')~code
signal on syntax name f
interpret "say 'abc'~left (2)"
f: say condition('o')~code 1 1 ABS -1 ABS -1
12 1 2 12
6 6 ab ab
35.1
93.903

270.body:
[dir.index.prolog] The clauses before the first directive are the prolog, the main code of the package. It runs once the package is installed, and its end is the end of the program: the interpreter never goes on into the code that follows the first directive, which is reached only through the routine or method that it declares. A file without directives is all prolog, and a file whose first clause is a directive has no prolog. An exit or return in the prolog ends the program there, and the directives have been installed all the same. say 'start'
say .box~new~m
say 'end of the prolog'
::class box
::method m say 'running m' return 'result of m'
say 'this clause is part of m' start
running m
result of m
end of the prolog say 'start'
exit
::class box
::method activate class say 'activated' activated
start [dir.index.section] The clauses after a directive, up to the next directive or the end of the program, are that directive's section. The section is the body of the method or routine that the directive declares, and the directive clause itself is not part of it. A directive that declares no code, such as ::CLASS, allows only comments and empty lines between it and the next directive. Any other clause there raises a SYNTAX error found when the program is read: 99.916 after ::class. The pages of the directives that take a body or are refused one say which subcode their own case raises. call try '::class k', '-- a comment', '', '/* another */', '::method m'
call try '::class k', 'say 1', '::method m'
call try '::class k', 'x = 2'
call try '::class k', '::method m', 'say 1', 'x = 2'
exit
try: signal on syntax name e src = .array~new do i = 1 to arg() src~append(arg(i)) end p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-sec', src) say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=> ok' return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code return ::class k / -- a comment / / /* another */ / ::method m => ok
::class k / say 1 / ::method m => 99.916
::class k / x = 2 => 99.916
::class k / ::method m / say 1 / x = 2 => ok [dir.index.unit] Each section, and the prolog, is a code unit of its own. Its labels are known only inside it, its variables are not shared with another unit, and a construct that it opens must end inside it: a DO, IF or SELECT that is still open at the next directive raises SYNTAX 14.1, 14.3 or 14.2, and an ELSE that has no instruction by then raises SYNTAX 14.4, all found when the program is read. A routine or method that needs a value of another unit receives it as an argument or through an object variable. x = 'prolog variable'
say r1()
call try 'do', '::class k'
call try 'if 1 then', '::class k'
call try 'select', '::class k'
exit
try: signal on syntax name e src = .array~new do i = 1 to arg() src~append(arg(i)) end p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-unit', src) say 'ok' return
e: say src~makestring('l', ' / ') '=>' condition('o')~code return
::routine r1 signal on syntax name lost say symbol('x') call own call prolog return 'not reached'
own: say 'own label' return

271.body:
[dir.index.install] The interpreter installs a package before it runs the prolog, in four steps. First the ::REQUIRES directives are processed in text order wherever they stand, except that the library rule processes the LIBRARY ones before the others, and each required package is installed and runs its own prolog before the next step. Then the package's routines become known and every class is created, in the order that the class rule gives, and each new class object is sent an INIT message. When all classes exist, each is sent an ACTIVATE message in the order of creation. Only then does the prolog run, so a class method that ACTIVATE runs sees every class and routine of the package, and the prolog sees every class already activated. A class is reachable by its name, as the environment symbol that is a period followed by the name, once its INIT message has returned. During the INIT of a class the classes created before it are reachable, and the class itself and the classes created later are not, so that their symbols have the symbol's own text as value. The routines of the package are known from the start. Every class is reachable by the time the first ACTIVATE message is sent. f = 'spec-dir-index-lib.tmp'
call sysfiledelete f
call lineout f, 'say "lib prolog"'
call lineout f, '::class libc public'
call lineout f, '::method activate class'
call lineout f, ' say "lib activate"'
call lineout f
src = .array~of('say "prolog"', - '::class one', - '::method init class', - ' say "init one"', - '::method activate class', - ' say "activate one, routine says" r()', - '::requires "'f'"', - '::class two', - '::method init class', - ' say "init two"', - '::method activate class', - ' say "activate two"', - '::routine r', - ' return "r"')
p = .package~new('spec-dir-index-main', src)
call sysfiledelete f lib activate
lib prolog
init one
init two
activate one, routine says r
activate two
prolog say 'prolog'
::class a
::method init class say 'init a sees' .b r() signal on syntax name e say 'init a sees' .a~id return
e: say 'init a self' condition('o')~code
::class b
::method init class say 'init b sees' .a~id signal on syntax name e say 'init b sees' .b~id return
e: say 'init b self' condition('o')~code
::method activate class say 'activate b sees' .a~id .b~id
::routine r return 'r' init a sees .B r
init a self 97.1
init b sees A
init b self 97.1
activate b sees A B
prolog [dir.index.failure] A fault found while the package is read stops everything: nothing is installed and no prolog runs. A fault raised while the package is installed, such as a class that cannot be found or a required file that does not exist, stops installation at that step, so that no class activates after it and the prolog does not run. The condition is SYNTAX in both cases, and a program file ends with 256 minus the error number as its exit status, 158 for 98.909, as the SYNTAX rule says. The classes created before such a fault have received their INIT message, as the next example shows, and have received no ACTIVATE message. A class that names itself, directly or through the classes it names, is an exception: the order rule finds it before any class is created, so no INIT message has been sent. call try '::class k public private'
call try '::class k', '::class l subclass nosuchsuperclass'
call try '::requires "spec-dir-index-nosuchfile-xyz.rex"'
exit

e: say 'caught' condition('o')~code return caught 25.901
caught 98.909
caught 43.901 say 'prolog'

272.body:
[dir.index.names] A name that a directive takes is a symbol or a string. A symbol names the element in upper case, and a string names it as written, so ::class Box creates the class BOX and ::class "Box" creates the class Box. A lookup of a class or a method by name ignores case, whatever the spelling in the directive, and two directives that name one class, or one method of a class, in different cases declare it twice. The pages of the directives say what each does with a duplicate. say .Widget~id .WIDGET~id .gadget~id .Gadget~id
::class Widget
::class "Gadget" WIDGET WIDGET Gadget Gadget
272.title: Names

273.body: ::CLASS name [METACLASS m] [SUBCLASS s | MIXINCLASS s] [PUBLIC | PRIVATE] [ABSTRACT] [INHERIT i ...] rexxref: Directives > ::CLASS Deviations: D32, D114 ::CLASS declares a class. The class comes into being when the package is installed, before the prolog runs, and the methods that the ::METHOD directives after it declare belong to it until the next ::CLASS. This page specifies the name of the class, the options that place it in a hierarchy and make it visible to other packages, and the order in which the classes of a package are made. What a class object does once it exists, the methods of Class such as new , id and superclass among them, is specified in the classes chapter; the examples here use those methods only to show what the directive made.
273.title: ::CLASS

274.body:
[dir.class.create] ::CLASS creates one class, named by a symbol or a string, and the class is reachable from every code of the package as the environment symbol that is a period followed by its name, from the point that the installation rule gives. The class's id is the name that the name rule gives, and .shown and .SHOWN are one class. A class declared with no SUBCLASS or MIXINCLASS option is a subclass of Object, and a class is a mixin class only when MIXINCLASS says so. [lex.clauses.label] A clause that holds only a symbol or a string and a colon is a label. Blanks and comments may stand before the colon, and the colon implies a semicolon, so another clause, or another label, may follow on the same line. A label does nothing when it is reached. A symbol label is read in upper case, and a string label keeps its characters as written, so a label written as a lower-case string is not found by a name that is written as a symbol. 3.body: ooRexx. The open-source C++ implementation of Object Rexx, version 5. interrexx is written to run ooRexx programs, and the book's examples are also run on ooRexx to measure where the two agree. Deviation. A declared difference between interrexx and ooRexx, numbered in the Deviations chapter . A page lists in its front matter the deviations that touch its element, and states each as a rule whose identifier ends deviation.N; a builtin's page puts these rules under a Deviations heading at its end. Every example on which interrexx and ooRexx answer differently belongs to such a rule; any other difference is a defect. String method. A method of the String class. Many builtins run as one, as the conventions define. Identity. Whether two values are the same object, as opposed to equal strings. It is observable only through identityHash, the identity collection IdentityTable and, on ooRexx, objectName= on a string, which Deviation 36 covers; the book says where it is not specified.

The next line is joined whole, so when it is empty the clause ends at its line end. At the end of a program, the character just ends the clause. A -- is a line comment and not a continuation, and a minus sign that is not the last token is an operator. say 1, 2

To continue a call after a separator, the separator is written first, so that the comma at the end of the line is the continuation. Two commas in a row at the end of a line are a separator and a continuation. say words(1, 2)
