A routine is private to its package unless PUBLIC makes it visible to the packages that require it. A call runs the body as a unit of its own, as the unit rule says: its variables and labels are its own, and the arguments are read with ARG and USE ARG . A routine returns a value with RETURN. A routine whose body is empty returns none, so a function call of it raises SYNTAX 44.1, and a CALL of it leaves RESULT dropped. The routine is installed before the prolog runs, as the installation rule says, so the prolog and the ACTIVATE method of a class can call it. say r1(2, 3)

308.body: ::REQUIRES name [LIBRARY | NAMESPACE ns] rexxref: Directives > ::REQUIRES ::REQUIRES makes the public classes and routines of another package known to this one. The other package is a Rexx program, which the interpreter installs and whose prolog it runs before the requiring package goes on, or a native library that it loads. A NAMESPACE option gives the required package a name that can qualify the classes and routines it supplies. This page specifies the directive, what a required package makes visible, the faults that requiring can raise and the two options. 314.body: ::OPTIONS option ... rexxref: Directives > ::OPTIONS Deviations: D103 ::OPTIONS sets the defaults that the code of its package starts with. The defaults are the three NUMERIC settings, the TRACE setting, whether a routine takes the NUMERIC settings of its caller, the way that six conditions are raised, and whether the prolog runs when another package requires this one. The settings themselves are specified with NUMERIC and TRACE , and the conditions with their own pages in the conditions chapter. This page specifies the form of the directive, what each option sets, and how far it reaches.
314.title: ::OPTIONS

315.body:
[dir.options.syntax] The words after ::OPTIONS are options. An option is a keyword, in any case, followed by its value, except PROLOG and NOPROLOG, which stand alone. Any number of options may be written in any order, on one directive or on several. When an option of one kind occurs twice, in one directive or in two, the one that stands later in the text wins, and options of different kinds all stay in force. A directive with no option does nothing. A word that is no keyword of an option, which a second value after a keyword also is, raises SYNTAX 25.924. The directive takes no code of its own: a clause after it that is not a null clause raises SYNTAX 99.916, as the section rule says. The faults are found when the program is read, so as the read rule says a program file with one writes nothing and exits with 256 minus the error number, 231 for 25.924. src = .array~of('say digits() fuzz() form()', - '::options digits 23 form engineering', - '::options fuzz 3 digits 15', - '::OPTIONS Digits 11')

[dir.options.numeric] DIGITS, FUZZ and FORM set the NUMERIC settings that the code of the package starts with. DIGITS and FUZZ take a symbol or a string that the NUMERIC instruction would accept as its value, so that "7", 05, 1e2 and 5.0 are whole numbers. FORM takes the symbol SCIENTIFIC or ENGINEERING in any case, and no abbreviation. A missing value or a string raises SYNTAX 20.925, and any other symbol 25.11. [dir.options.trace] TRACE sets the tracing setting that the prolog, every routine and every method of the package start with. Its value is a word that the TRACE instruction accepts, chosen by its first letter, so that Off and O are alike, and a letter that is not valid raises SYNTAX 24.1, which a string with a blank before the letter does too. A missing value, a sign and a parenthesis raise 19.919. The empty string is accepted and starts the code with N. The directive is stricter than the instruction in one respect: a number is not a setting and raises 24.1. The setting is what TRACE() returns when the code starts, and a TRACE instruction changes it for the running code only, as the scope rule says. A question mark before the letter is accepted, and what interactive tracing does is specified in the debugging chapter . What TRACE() returns when the code starts after a question mark with no letter after it is ?N, as the Deviation states. call try 'o'

[dir.options.condition] ERROR, FAILURE, LOSTDIGITS, NOSTRING, NOTREADY and NOVALUE each take the value SYNTAX or CONDITION; NOVALUE takes ERROR as well, with the meaning of SYNTAX. CONDITION is the default and leaves the condition as the conditions chapter specifies it. SYNTAX makes the condition that no trap answers raise a SYNTAX condition instead, with these codes: 98.970 for ERROR, 98.971 for FAILURE, 98.972 for LOSTDIGITS, 98.973 for NOSTRING, 98.974 for NOTREADY and 98.986 for NOVALUE. The clause that raised it ends there as the SYNTAX rule says, and RC is 98 in the trap that catches it. Without a trap the program ends as the rule for an untrapped SYNTAX says, with exit status 158. A FAILURE raised as SYNTAX is not passed on to the ERROR trap, as the second example shows. A FAILURE that no trap answers, which the untrapped rule would ignore, is answered as ERROR here, so with ERROR SYNTAX it raises 98.970 when FAILURE is left at CONDITION, as the third example shows. A missing value or a string raises SYNTAX 20.929 and any other symbol 25.927, ERROR for an option other than NOVALUE among them, both when the program is read. call try 'error'
call try 'failure'
call try 'lostdigits'
call try 'nostring'
call try 'notready'
call try 'novalue'
exit

[dir.options.prolog] PROLOG and NOPROLOG decide what a ::REQUIRES of the package does with its prolog: with PROLOG, the default, the prolog runs, and with NOPROLOG it is skipped, so that a package of routines and classes can be required without its start-up code. The last of the two in text order is used. The installation of the package is not affected, so its routines and classes exist all the same. The program that was started runs its prolog whatever the option says. Loading the text of a package with the Package class follows the same rule as a requirement, as the first example shows. The option acts on a package that is required or loaded as a package only: a file that a program calls as an external routine runs its code from the start, whatever the option says, as the third example shows. f = 'spec-dir-options-pro1.tmp'

32.body: ANSI: 6.2.2.35, 7.4; rexxref: Numbers and Arithmetic This chapter specifies what a number is, how a number is written when an operation produces one, and the limits on its size. Rexx has no numeric type: a number is a string whose characters have a certain form, and the same string is a number or not depending only on that form. Operations that need a number read the string, compute on its value, and write the answer as a new string. The chapter describes the strings and the answers, and leaves the operators and the settings that steer them to the pages named at the end. A value is checked against the form each time an operation needs a number, and no check or conversion happens before that. The pages of this chapter are: Formats : how an arithmetic result is written, with significant digits, zeros, exponential notation and engineering notation. Limits : the range of exponents, overflow and underflow, and the limits that whole numbers have. Arithmetic : the operators, the rounding to NUMERIC DIGITS, integer division, powers and the errors of each. Settings : NUMERIC DIGITS, FUZZ and FORM, how a program changes them and which part of the program a change reaches. Comparison : when two values compare as numbers, and how NUMERIC FUZZ widens equality.

321.body: ::RESOURCE name [END delimiter] rexxref: Directives > ::RESOURCE ::RESOURCE puts lines of text into a package. The lines are not code: the interpreter does not read them as clauses, and a program reads them back as data by the name of the resource. A resource is the way to carry a template, a table or a message text inside the file of a program. This page specifies the directive and where the data ends, the lines as they are kept, and the way that a program reaches them. The methods of the collection that holds the resources belong to the classes chapter, and the examples use only those that are needed to read an item.
321.title: ::RESOURCE

322.body:
[dir.resource.create] The directive clause names the resource, and the lines that follow it are its data, up to a line that starts with the end delimiter. The name is a symbol or a string. The delimiter follows the word END, in any case, and is a symbol or a string too. Without END the delimiter is ::END. A delimiter that is a symbol is taken in upper case, and one that is a string as written, so that end done stands for the text DONE and end "done" for done. The match is case sensitive and is made at the start of the line: a line ends the data when its first characters are the delimiter, wherever the line goes on after them, and a line that has the delimiter after a blank, or in another case, is data. The delimiter line is not part of the data, and the clause that follows it is the first clause after the resource. A semicolon after the directive ends the directive clause, and what follows it on that line is dropped and never becomes a clause. A comment may follow the directive. a = .resources~tune

324.body:
[dir.resource.access] The environment symbol .RESOURCES holds the resources of the package whose code reads it, unless an entry or a class of the same name is found first ( the order ). It is a collection indexed by the resource names in upper case, and each item is an array of the lines of that resource. It is there from the start of the prolog, and in every routine and method of the package. A package with no ::RESOURCE has no .RESOURCES, and the symbol has its own text as value . The index is looked up exactly, so that .resources['COBALT'] finds the resource named cobalt and .resources['cobalt'] finds nothing. The collection is each package's own: the resources of a required package are not in the .RESOURCES of the package that requires it, and the other way round, so that a routine of the required package reads its own. The arrays are shared by all code of the package: an item that one routine changes, or an array that it extends, is changed for every later read, in any routine or method of the package. say 'none:' .resources

say r()

325.body: ::ANNOTATE PACKAGE | CLASS name | METHOD name | ATTRIBUTE name | CONSTANT name | ROUTINE name {annotation value}... rexxref: Directives > ::ANNOTATE ::ANNOTATE attaches notes to the parts of a package. A note is an annotation, a name with a text as its value, and a program that holds the object of a package, class, method or routine can read the annotations that were declared for it. The interpreter does nothing with them: no annotation name has a meaning of its own, so they carry information for tools and for the program itself. This page specifies what the directive may name, the form of the names and values, and which annotations a program finds. The methods that read and change annotations belong to the classes chapter, and the examples use only ANNOTATION and ANNOTATIONS, and the methods that reach an object.
325.title: ::ANNOTATE

326.body:
[dir.annotate.syntax] After the directive word comes a kind word, in any case: PACKAGE, CLASS, METHOD, ATTRIBUTE, CONSTANT or ROUTINE. Every kind but PACKAGE then has a target name, a symbol or a string, and the rest of the clause is a list of annotations, each a name and a value. The list may be empty. A missing kind raises SYNTAX 20.924, a word that is no kind 25.928, and a missing target name 19.925. The directive takes no code: a clause after it that is not a null clause raises SYNTAX 99.916, as the section rule says, so that the directive ends the code of the method or routine before it. These faults are found when the program is read, so as the read rule says a program file with one writes nothing and exits with 256 minus the error number, 236 for 20.924. call try '::annotate'

The value is a string, a symbol or a number with an optional sign, and is kept as text: a string as written and a symbol in upper case, which includes a number that is written as a symbol such as 1e3. 328.body:
[dir.annotate.read] The annotations of an element are kept with its object. The ANNOTATION message of the object of a package , class , method or routine , with an annotation name, returns the value as a string, or .nil when the element has no annotation of that name, and the name is looked up in upper case. The ANNOTATIONS message returns a table of all of them indexed by name. The annotation of an attribute is found on both of its methods, and that of a constant on the method of the constant. An annotation is not inherited: a class that names an annotated class as its superclass has none of its annotations, and the same name on a class and on its method are two separate annotations. A copy of an annotated routine or method keeps its annotations. p = .context~package

329.body: ANSI: 8.2.1, 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Not Trapped A condition is an event that a program can ask to be told about. The interpreter raises one when a command fails, when an unset variable is read, when an error is found in a running clause, when a stream cannot deliver, and when the program asks for one itself. What happens next depends on the trap for that condition: a program switches a trap on or off with the instructions SIGNAL and CALL , whose pages specify the syntax of those forms. This chapter specifies the conditions, what a trap does when its condition is raised, and what a program can learn about the condition afterwards. The pages of this chapter are: Condition traps : which trap answers a condition, what SIGNAL ON and CALL ON each do, the delayed state, and how far a trap reaches. Condition information : the condition object, the variables RC and SIGL, and how an error reaches the caller of the code that raised it. SYNTAX , ERROR and FAILURE , HALT , NOVALUE , NOSTRING , NOMETHOD , NOTREADY and LOSTDIGITS : one page for each condition, with when it is raised, what it carries and which traps answer it. USER conditions : the conditions that a program names itself. Error numbers : the numbers of the SYNTAX conditions and what each means. The RAISE instruction, which raises a condition on purpose, has a page of its own among the instructions. The CONDITION builtin owns what a program reads back from a trapped condition, and this chapter links its rules.

331.body:
[cond.index.state] Every condition has a trap with one of three states: OFF, ON and DELAY. A program starts with every trap OFF, and the instructions SIGNAL ON, CALL ON, SIGNAL OFF and CALL OFF set the state of the trap of their condition, which is what the S option of CONDITION reads back. DELAY is the state of a CALL trap while its handler runs, and the delay rule specifies it. The state of each condition is its own, and the trap of ANY has a state of its own beside those of the conditions it catches. A condition whose trap is OFF, and which no ANY trap catches, is untrapped, and the untrapped rule says what then happens. address system

332.body:
[cond.index.untrapped] When a condition is raised and no trap answers it, as the choice rule decides, ERROR, FAILURE, LOSTDIGITS, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE and the user conditions are ignored: the clause goes on as if nothing had happened, and the trap stays OFF. The exceptions are the FAILURE of a command, which the fallback rule says the ERROR trap answers, and the six conditions that the package's ::OPTIONS makes a SYNTAX condition. HALT and NOMETHOD are not ignored. An untrapped HALT raises SYNTAX 4.1 instead, and an untrapped NOMETHOD SYNTAX 97.1, or SYNTAX 97.2 when the message went to a private method that its sender may not run, as the NOMETHOD rule says. That SYNTAX condition is raised at the same place, so a SYNTAX trap catches it with CONDITION('C') answering SYNTAX. An ANY trap catches HALT and NOMETHOD before they would become SYNTAX, so the program sees their own names then. SYNTAX itself is not ignored, and the next rule says what it does. address system

333.body: ANSI: 8.2.4, 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped Deviations: D64, D75, D104 A trap is the setting that tells the interpreter what to do when a condition is raised, and there is one for each condition. A SIGNAL trap moves control to a label as SIGNAL does and abandons the clause that raised the condition. A CALL trap lets the clause finish and then calls a routine, which returns to the clause after it. This page specifies which trap answers a condition, what each kind of trap does, the state that keeps a CALL trap from calling itself, and the code that a trap reaches. What the program learns about the condition is on the information page , and the syntax that sets a trap is on the pages of SIGNAL and CALL .
333.title: Condition traps

334.body:
[cond.traps.choice] When a condition is raised, the trap of that condition answers it if its state is ON or DELAY. When it is OFF, the ANY trap answers instead if its state is ON or DELAY. When neither is on, the condition is untrapped , except that the FAILURE of a command then goes to the ERROR trap, as the fallback rule says. A trap that answers a condition changes only its own state, so every other trap, ANY included, stays as it was. The two kinds of trap are equal in this: a CALL trap for the condition wins over a SIGNAL trap for ANY, and a SIGNAL trap for the condition wins over a CALL trap for ANY. A condition that the ANY trap catches is still itself: CONDITION('C') answers its own name, and the default label or routine of an ANY trap is ANY. A condition whose own trap was switched off explicitly does not keep ANY from answering. A CALL trap for ANY answers only the conditions that CALL can trap, and a SIGNAL trap for ANY answers all of them. A user condition is answered by the trap of its own name, and the ANY trap catches the user conditions that have none. call on any name a

[cond.traps.signal] When a SIGNAL trap answers a condition, the clause that raised it ends at once, so that an assignment is not made, and a command whose string was being evaluated is not sent. A command whose return code raised ERROR or FAILURE has already run, and RC holds its return code. The state of the trap becomes OFF, the condition is recorded as the information page says, and control goes to the label of the trap as SIGNAL goes to a label, ending the open DO, LOOP, SELECT and IF constructs of the routine as that rule says. The label is the one that the NAME option gave, and the name of the condition when there was none. The trap is OFF at the label, so a second condition of the same kind that the code there raises is not trapped unless that code switches the trap on again or an ANY trap is ON, which the answer did not change. signal on syntax

335.title: SIGNAL traps

336.body:
[cond.traps.call] When a CALL trap answers a condition, the clause that raised it finishes first, so that a command has run and an assignment has been made. The state of the trap becomes DELAY, the condition is recorded, and a routine is called before the next clause starts. The next clause is the one after it in the same place, so the call is made inside a DO, a SELECT or an IF that holds the clause, and between the clauses of the text of an INTERPRET. When the clause that raised the condition ends the program, as an EXIT in the main program or the last clause does, the routine of the trap is called before the program ends. When it is the RETURN of a routine, the routine of the trap is called after the value of the RETURN is computed and before the caller goes on, and it sees the variables of the routine that returned. The caller then goes on with the clause after the CALL, or with the rest of the expression of the clause that invoked the routine as a function. What an EXIT inside an internal routine does with a pending CALL trap is a Deviation . The routine is the one that CALL finds for the name of the trap, which is the name of the condition when there was no NAME. It gets one argument, the condition object . The call does not change RESULT, and what the routine returns is dropped. When the routine returns, the trap is ON again, and the clause after the one that raised the condition runs. When the routine is an internal routine, SIGL is set as a CALL sets it, to the line of the clause that raised the condition, which for a RETURN or an EXIT is that clause itself and not the CALL. A routine without PROCEDURE shares the variables of the caller, RC among them. When the routine is a ::ROUTINE, a built-in function or an external routine, SIGL is not set, and it keeps the value it had. address system

337.body:
[cond.traps.delay] While the state of a CALL trap is DELAY, a condition that is raised for it again does not call the routine. ERROR, FAILURE and NOTREADY raised again are ignored. Every other condition that is raised is held, and the held ones are answered in the order raised when the state of the trap changes. A CALL OFF or SIGNAL OFF for the condition drops them. A CALL ON or SIGNAL ON for the condition answers them at the end of that instruction, with the trap that the instruction set. When the routine returns, the CALL trap answers them by calling the routine again. A SIGNAL trap is never DELAY. The held conditions are Deviation 75 . address system

338.body:
[cond.traps.scope] The states of the traps belong to the code that runs, which is the main program, a routine, a method or an internal routine, and each starts with states of its own. An internal routine, which a CALL or a function call reaches by its label, starts with a copy of the states of its caller, names, kinds and DELAY included, and what it does to the copy is not seen by the caller after it returns. A ::ROUTINE, a method and a routine made from other source text start with every trap OFF. The text of an INTERPRET runs in the code that holds it and shares its states, so a trap that the text switches on stays on after it. Because an internal routine has a copy, a SIGNAL trap that answers a condition in it jumps to a label of the code that holds the routine, and a RETURN there returns from the routine, as the SIGNAL rule says. signal on syntax name h

34.body: ANSI: 7.4.10; rexxref: Numbers and Arithmetic > Exponential Notation An operation that answers with a number writes it as a new string, and that string is the only trace of the computation: nothing remembers how many digits the operands had or which operation made the result. This page says what the written string looks like. The rules for rounding a number to a count of significant digits and for choosing plain or exponential notation are stated once, with the built-in functions, and this page applies them to the results of arithmetic and adds what is particular to those results.

340.body: ANSI: 8.4.1, 9.5.3; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Condition Object When a trap answers a condition, the interpreter records what it knows about the condition, and the code that the trap reaches can read it. The record holds the name of the condition, the kind of the trap, its state, a description, and an object that some conditions carry. It is read with the CONDITION builtin, which owns what each option answers, and as a condition object, a directory with one entry for each piece of information. The trap also sets the variables RC and SIGL, and an error that no trap in the code that raised it answers goes on to the code that called it. This page specifies the record, the condition object, the two variables and that journey, and the traps page specifies when a trap answers.
340.title: Condition information

342.body:
[cond.information.object] The condition object is a directory with these entries, whose names are in capital letters. CONDITION, DESCRIPTION, INSTRUCTION and ADDITIONAL are the entries that the object rule of CONDITION names. PACKAGE is the package that holds the code that raised the condition, and PROGRAM its name. POSITION is the number of the line on which the clause that raised the condition starts, in that code, and a NOTREADY that the interpreter raised has none. PROPAGATED is 1 when the condition left the level that raised it and 0 otherwise, as the propagated rule specifies. STACKFRAMES and TRACEBACK are lists with one item for each active level of code at that time, the main program's included, and the text of a traceback line is not specified. ADDITIONAL is present for a SYNTAX, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING or NOTREADY that the interpreter raised. A condition that a RAISE instruction raised has POSITION, and has ADDITIONAL exactly when the instruction gave one, whatever the name of the condition, as the options rule of RAISE says. The exception is a SYNTAX, which always has an ADDITIONAL array, empty when the instruction gave none, as the SYNTAX rule of RAISE says. SYNTAX adds CODE, the error number with its subcode as 41.1, RC, its major number, ERRORTEXT, the text of the error that the ERRORTEXT builtin answers for RC, and MESSAGE, the text with the details of this occurrence. ERROR and FAILURE have RC, the return code of the command. The texts of the messages are not specified, and the entry RESULT is not specified here. address system

345.body: ANSI: 8.4.1, 8.4.2, 9.2.4; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Condition Object; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > The Special Variable RC SYNTAX is the condition of an error in the program as it runs. It is raised by a clause that cannot be carried out: arithmetic on a value that is no number, a call with a wrong argument, a routine that does not exist, and the other faults that the error numbers describe. It is also the condition that HALT and NOMETHOD become when nothing answers them, and it is never ignored: a trap answers it, or the program ends. This page specifies what raises SYNTAX, what identifies the error, which traps can answer it and what a program sees after one has. The numbers of the errors are listed on the pages of the clauses that raise them and in the error numbers chapter, and the traps page and the information page specify what any trap does and what it records.

[cond.syntax.raise] An error that is found while a clause runs raises SYNTAX at that clause. The clause ends at the point of the error, so that an assignment it would have made is not made, a command it would have sent is not sent, and output that it would have written after the point is not written, while the effects it had before the point, such as the output of a function that the expression called, stay. The error can come from an expression, from a builtin function or a method, from a call that finds no routine, from the text of an INTERPRET instruction, from a trap that has no label, and from a RAISE instruction that names SYNTAX, as the last two examples show. A fault in the text of an INTERPRET is found when that text is read as a whole, as the whole-text rule says, so none of its clauses has run then. An error found while the program itself is read is not a condition, as the reading rule says. total = 10

350.body: ANSI: 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Not Trapped ERROR and FAILURE are the two conditions of a command. After an environment of the host has run a command, or has failed to, the interpreter looks at the return code and raises one of them; a command that a handler written in Rexx runs raises them only as the ERROR rule says. ERROR means that the command ran and answered with a return code that is not zero, and FAILURE means that the command could not be run at all. A program that wants to react to a failing command traps one or both. This page specifies when each is raised, what the condition records, and the way a FAILURE that nothing answers reaches an ERROR trap. How a command is sent, and how it sets RC, is on the command page .
350.breadcrumbs: Conditions » ERROR and FAILURE » ERROR and FAILURE
350.title: ERROR and FAILURE

351.body:
[cond.error.raise] A command that an environment of the host has run, and whose return code is not zero, raises ERROR at the end of the clause that sent it, so that the command has run and RC holds its return code before the trap answers. A return code of zero raises nothing. The record of the condition has the command string as its description, and the RC entry of the condition object holds the return code, which is also the value of RC in the code of the trap. The POSITION entry and SIGL are the line of the command clause. A SIGNAL trap goes to its label after the command has run, and a CALL trap calls its routine and then goes on with the clause after the command. The status .RS of the command is 1 for a command that raised ERROR, as the status rule says. A command that a CommandHandler written in Rexx runs raises ERROR or FAILURE only when the handler asks its context for it ( the raise rule ), or when it forwards the command to a native environment that raises one ( the forwarding rule ), whatever its return code. address system

'exit 0'
say 'zero' rc .rs
'exit 3'
say 'after' rc .rs
cmd = 'exit' 2 + 5
cmd

say 'not reached'

signal 4 ERROR OFF SIGNAL [cond.error.untrapped] An ERROR that no trap answers is ignored, as the untrapped rule says, unless the package's ::OPTIONS makes it a SYNTAX condition: the clause is over, RC holds the return code, .RS is 1, and the program goes on. The traps that answer it are the ones of the code that sent the command, which for an internal routine are its copy of the traps of its caller, as the scope rule says. The condition is not passed on to the next level, as the propagation rule says, so a routine that has its trap off ignores the ERROR although its caller has the trap on. address system

say 'back' rc

351.title: ERROR

352.body:
[cond.error.failure] A command raises FAILURE, and not ERROR, when it could not be run. That is the case when the current environment does not exist, as the status rule says, whatever the command is. On a POSIX host it is also the case when the return code is 127, in every native environment ( the return code rule ), whether the command was not found or exited with that code. No other return code of such an environment is a failure: 126 raises ERROR, and so does a negative one, which is not the failure of classic Rexx here. FAILURE, like ERROR, waits for the clause to end, and its record has the return code in RC, the command string as its description, and .RS is -1. A trap for ERROR does not answer a FAILURE as such, so it needs the fallback of the next rule , and a trap for FAILURE does not answer an ERROR. address system

signal on error name e
'exit 127'
say 'after' rc .rs
address nosuch
'exit 0'
say 'after env' rc .rs
address system
'exit 126'
say 'not reached'
f: say 'F' rc '['condition('d')']' condition('o')~rc sigl, condition('c') return
e: say 'E' rc .rs condition('c') F 127 [exit 127] 127 4 FAILURE
after 127 -1
F 30 [exit 0] 30 7 FAILURE

E 126 1 ERROR address bash

call on error name e
'exit 127'
address sh 'exit 127'
address command 'exit 127'
address path 'nosuchprogram_interrexx_spec'
'kill -9 $$'
exit
f: say 'F' rc .rs; return
e: say 'E' rc .rs; return F 127 -1
F 127 -1
F 127 -1
F 127 -1
E -9 1 [cond.error.fallback] The FAILURE of a command that its own trap and the ANY trap do not answer is answered as an ERROR by the ERROR trap, when that is on, as the untrapped rule and the choice rule also say. The condition is then ERROR for everything that reads it: CONDITION('C') answers ERROR, and the record holds the same return code and command string. .RS stays -1, because the command failed. A FAILURE trap that was switched off explicitly does not prevent this. An ANY trap that is on answers the FAILURE under its own name, so the ERROR trap is reached only when neither of the two is on. When no trap of the three is on, the FAILURE is ignored and nothing else is raised. A FAILURE that the RAISE instruction raised does not fall back: when its own trap and the ANY trap do not answer it, it is ignored, and the ERROR trap does not see it, as the untrapped rule of RAISE says. The second example shows both. address system

'exit 127'

'exit 127'

'exit 127'

'exit 127'

exit

353.body: ANSI: 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Not Trapped HALT is the condition of a request to stop the program from outside its own flow of clauses. A user of a terminal asks for it with an interrupt key, and a host program asks for it through an interface, and the interpreter raises it between two clauses. A program that traps HALT can tidy up and end on its own terms. This page specifies what a program sees of HALT, the effect of each kind of trap and what happens when none is on. The interrupt keys, the signals and the interfaces are of the host and not specified, so every example on this page raises HALT with a RAISE instruction, which has its own page in the instructions chapter.
353.title: HALT

354.body:
[cond.halt.raise] HALT is raised by a request that the host makes, and by a RAISE instruction that names it. Which host requests exist, and at which clause boundary one is noticed, is not specified. On Linux, SIGINT and SIGTERM are such requests ( the signal rule ). The condition has no description unless the RAISE instruction gave one with DESCRIPTION, so CONDITION('D') answers the null string otherwise. Its condition object has the entries that every condition has and POSITION, and neither RC, CODE nor ADDITIONAL, as the entries rule lists them. A HALT that the host raises is not passed on to the caller of the code that was running, as the propagation rule says for every condition but SYNTAX. Which level a RAISE instruction raises HALT in, the one that runs it or the caller of that one, is specified with that instruction. The examples whose trap answers HALT raise it with RETURN, which raises it in the caller. call on halt name h
call plain
call with
exit
h: o = arg(1) say 'HALT' condition('c') '['condition('d')']' condition('i'), condition('s'), o~hasindex('POSITION') o~hasindex('RC') o~hasindex('CODE'), o~hasindex('ADDITIONAL') return
plain: raise halt return
with: raise halt description 'asked to stop' return HALT HALT [] CALL DELAY 1 0 0 0
HALT HALT [asked to stop] CALL DELAY 1 0 0 0
354.title: Raising it

355.body:
[cond.halt.signal] A SIGNAL trap for HALT ends the clause that was running and goes to the label, ending the open DO and SELECT constructs as the SIGNAL trap rule says. A program uses it to leave a loop that has no other end. The trap is OFF at the label, and a second HALT is untrapped unless the program enables the trap again. signal on halt
n = 0
do forever n = n + 1 call check n
end
halt: say 'stopped at' n '['condition('d')']' condition('c') condition('s')
::routine check use arg n if n = 3 then raise halt description 'enough' return stopped at 3 [enough] HALT OFF n = 0
signal on halt name h
call stop
say 'not reached'
h: n = n + 1
say 'halt' n
if n = 1 then signal on halt name h
call stop
say 'not reached either'
::routine stop raise halt return halt 1
halt 2 [cond.halt.call] A CALL trap for HALT lets the clause that was running finish, calls its routine, and goes on with the next clause when the routine returns. The state of the trap is DELAY in the routine, as the delay rule says. A program that wants to stop in the routine ends it with EXIT. call on halt name h
say 'one'
call stop 'first'
say 'two'
call stop 'second'
say 'three'
exit

handler first DELAY

handler second DELAY
355.title: The traps

356.body:
[cond.halt.untrapped] A HALT that neither its own trap nor the ANY trap answers is not ignored. As the untrapped rule says, it becomes the SYNTAX condition 4.1 at the same clause, which a SYNTAX trap sees under the name SYNTAX, and the SYNTAX rule says what follows when none answers. That condition has CODE 4.1, RC 4 and no description, whatever description the RAISE instruction gave. say 'before'
raise halt
say 'not reached' before signal on syntax name s
raise halt description 'ignored text'
s: o = condition('o')
say condition('c') o~code o~rc '['condition('d')']' SYNTAX 4.1 4 []

357.body: ANSI: 8.4.1; rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped NOVALUE is the condition of reading a variable that has no value. A variable that was never assigned, or that was dropped, is not an error in Rexx: its symbol then stands for its own name, as the variable rule says. A program that wants to find such reads traps the condition, which turns a misspelled variable into a stop with the name in hand. This page specifies which uses of a variable raise NOVALUE, which do not, what the description holds, and which traps can answer it. The ::OPTIONS directive can make an untrapped NOVALUE into an error, and its rule specifies that.
357.title: NOVALUE

358.body:
[cond.novalue.raise] NOVALUE is raised when the value of a simple or compound variable symbol is needed and the variable has no value. That is so for a term of an expression wherever an expression is evaluated, among them the right side of an assignment, the condition of an IF or a WHEN, the bounds of a DO, an argument of a call and the value of a NUMERIC setting; for the variable that PARSE VAR reads; for a pattern in parentheses in a template; for a variable that names the override class of a message term; and for a variable that names a list in parentheses in DROP, in EXPOSE or in PROCEDURE EXPOSE. The clause ends at that point, so an assignment it would have made is not made. The stem symbol alone, as in st., is never without a value, as the stem rule says, so reading it raises nothing. A variable that is only assigned, dropped or named in an EXPOSE list, with no parentheses, is not read. EXPOSE must be the first instruction of a method, so no trap can precede it, and the ::OPTIONS example below makes the read visible with NOVALUE SYNTAX, which turns the untrapped condition into an error. An environment symbol such as .foo that finds no object is not a variable, so it raises nothing and stands for its own name in upper case. A symbol in the tail of a compound symbol raises nothing, and stays as its own name in the derived name. SYMBOL and VALUE do not raise it, as the function rules say. do k = 1 to 16 call probe k
end
exit

359.body:
[cond.novalue.trap] NOVALUE is answered by SIGNAL ON NOVALUE and by SIGNAL ON ANY, and by no CALL trap: CALL ON NOVALUE is an error, as the CALL ON rule says, and a CALL ON ANY trap does not see it, as the choice rule says. With the trap OFF, and no ANY trap on, the symbol has its own name as value and the clause goes on, as the untrapped rule says. A SIGNAL trap ends the clause, so the value that the clause would have computed is not used. NOVALUE is not passed on, as the propagation rule says. The traps that answer it are the ones of the code that read the variable, which for an internal routine are its copy of the traps of its caller, as the scope rule says. A ::ROUTINE starts with every trap OFF, and an internal routine that switches the trap off is not answered either. x = 'before'

36.body:
[num.formats.canonical] A written number has no whitespace and never starts with +. It has no leading zero, except the single 0 before the point of a magnitude below 1 and the number zero itself, and its decimal point stands between two digits, so it is never the first or the last character. Exponential notation is as the notation rule gives it. The leading zeros, the leading or trailing point, the plus signs and the whitespace that the operand had do not survive. say (' +007.250 ' + 0) ('.5' + 0) ('5.' + 0) ('0.5e1' + 0) ('-.5E+0' + 0), ('+ 3' + 0)
say ('00.00100' + 0) ('1e0' + 0) ('12E+01' + 0) ('125E-3' + 0) ('-1e-2' + 0) 7.250 0.5 5 5 -0.5 3
0.00100 1 120 0.125 -0.01 [num.formats.zero] A result that has the value zero is written as the single character 0, with no sign, no decimal places and no exponent. This holds however the zero came about: a product with a zero operand, a difference of equal numbers, a negation, or a zero written with decimal places or an exponent. No operation answers a negative zero. say (5 - 5.00) (0.00 * 7) (0 * -3) (-0.0 + 0) (-(0.00)) (1e5 - 1e5), ('-0' + 0) ('0e9' * 1)

0 0 0 0

360.body: rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Additional Object Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped Deviations: D30, D77 NOSTRING is the condition of needing the string value of an object that does not provide one. Most values a program handles are strings or answer as strings, and the interpreter converts them without notice. An object of a class that has no way to give a string is different: Rexx can still print it or join it to text, but it first tells the program, so that a program that trusts its values to be text can stop at the point where one is not. This page specifies which uses of an object raise NOSTRING, what the condition holds, which traps answer it and what a clause does when nothing does.
360.title: NOSTRING

361.body:
[cond.nostring.raise] NOSTRING is raised when a clause needs the string value of an object that is not a string, and request with the argument STRING, sent to the object, answers no string: an object with no MAKESTRING method does so, and so does one whose MAKESTRING or own request answers .nil or another object that is not a string, whatever its STRING method answers. An object whose request is private, or whose MAKESTRING or STRING method is private and would be sent, raises no NOSTRING at the uses listed below: the message is refused, as the conventions say for builtin arguments, and the clause raises SYNTAX 97.2. A string, a number and an instance of a subclass of String never raise it, and neither does an object whose request answers a string, as Object does with the answer of MAKESTRING. The uses that raise it include the three concatenation operators (the explicit ||, the abuttal and the blank), the operand of SAY, the source of PARSE VALUE, the text that INTERPRET runs, an operand of an arithmetic or comparison operator whose left operand is a string, the tail of a compound variable, and an argument of a builtin function that is to be a string, except for the builtins that link the native call rule , which raise SYNTAX 88.909 for it. Sending the message STRING to the object raises nothing, because the object is then not converted. Which other positions convert, such as the arguments of method calls, is not specified. What a builtin does with such an argument when no trap answers is the object rule of the conventions . The table below has one row for each object and one column for each of six uses, N where NOSTRING is raised and - where it is not. objs = .array~of(.object~new, .made~new, .string.sub~new('xy'), 42)

end

365.body: rexxref: Conditions and Condition Traps; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Descriptive Strings; Conditions and Condition Traps > Condition Information > Additional Object Information; Conditions and Condition Traps > Action Taken when a Condition Is Trapped NOMETHOD is the condition of a message that reaches an object with nothing to run for it. Sending a message is the way Rexx objects are used, and a message whose name is misspelled or meant for another class has no method to find. A program traps NOMETHOD to learn which message was lost and to which object it went. This page specifies when the condition is raised, what it holds, which traps answer it and what becomes of it when none does.
365.title: NOMETHOD

366.body:
[cond.nomethod.raise] NOMETHOD is raised when a message is sent to an object, the object has no method of that name that the sender may run, and the object has no UNKNOWN method that takes the message instead. A private method sent from code that may not run it, such as a routine or a method of an unrelated class, counts as missing : the message goes to UNKNOWN when the object has one and otherwise raises NOMETHOD with the name of the method. The access rule says which senders may run a private method, among them methods of the class, of its subclasses and of their instances, and class methods. The message may be written with ~, with ~~, or with a scope override such as ~name:super, as the information rule shows, and it may be sent by the SEND method of an object. The arguments of the message are evaluated before the lookup, so the clause has evaluated them when the condition is raised. The condition is raised in the code that sent the message, and the clause ends there when a SIGNAL trap answers. The exception is a message that FORWARD sends without CONTINUE, which the FORWARD rule raises in the caller of the forwarding method. A class with an UNKNOWN method raises nothing, because that method receives the message. The UNKNOWN method and the way a class defines methods belong to the classes chapter. do k = 1 to 5 call probe k
end
exit

[cond.nomethod.untrapped] A NOMETHOD that neither its own trap nor the ANY trap answers is not ignored. It becomes the condition SYNTAX 97.1 raised at the same clause, as the untrapped rule says, and a SYNTAX trap answers it under the name SYNTAX. NUMERIC DIGITS sets how many digits an operation works with, and an operand written with more of them is cut before the operation starts, so the program's result is not the one its text suggests. Nothing is wrong enough to stop the program, and the condition is how a program that cares about exact input finds out. The rules for which operands raise it, and how the cut is made, belong to the chapter on numbers: the arithmetic rule and the comparison rule . This page specifies what the condition holds, which traps answer it and how far it reaches.

The interpreter never raises one, so a program can use it for its own events, such as a missing record or a parse that found nothing, and give the code that deals with it the same trap machinery that the built-in conditions have. Every user condition has a name that the program chooses, and the name makes the condition. This page specifies the names, the traps that answer a user condition and what it holds. A user condition is raised with the RAISE instruction, whose page is RAISE , and the examples here raise them with raise user name.
378.title: USER conditions

379.body:
[cond.user.name] A user condition is raised by RAISE USER and a name, and by nothing else. The name is a symbol that is read as a constant in upper case, whatever it holds as a variable and whatever the spelling of its tail: foo.bar is the name FOO.BAR and does not take the value of bar. The condition is called USER and the name, joined by one blank, and CONDITION('C') answers that. Names are compared as text after the change to upper case, so Foo and FOO are one condition, and the numbers 1.5 and 1.50 are two. A user condition is a condition of its own, so it is not the built-in condition that has the same name, as the names rule says. bar = 'x'

This page gives the range, what a string outside it is, and the conditions that +, -, *, / and ** raise when a result leaves it. The integer division and the remainder have their own conditions . The page also separates this range from the smaller limit that a whole-number argument has.

It has a page for each class, or for a few classes that belong together, and a page, the method search , for how a message finds the method that runs it. The chapter index holds what is true of all of them: how a class page is laid out, how the classes are related, what a method does with a wrong argument, what new does, and what the string value of an object is. Where this chapter says that a program declares a class, the declaring is done by the ::CLASS directive, and the methods of that class by ::METHOD . The chapter does not repeat what those pages say about the options of the directives. It specifies the methods of Class that make and change classes while a program runs.
390.title: Classes

391.body: A class page opens with its front matter, then a title and an overview paragraph, and then the sections below, in this order. A page leaves out a section it has nothing for. The class : rules about the class as a whole: how an instance is made, its string value, how two instances compare, what it inherits. Class methods : the methods of the class object itself, the class side, such as new and of. Each is a rule group. Methods : the methods of an instance, the instance side, grouped by what they do. Each method is a rule group, and a group may cover several methods that share a rule. Deviations : the rules that state a Deviation , as every page does. A method that the class inherits from a superclass or a mixin class is specified on the page of that class. The page of a class links to it and states only what the class adds or changes. A method whose behavior is shared by the classes of a family, such as the collection classes, is specified once on the page of the class it belongs to, and the pages of the other classes link to it. The front matter names the element (the class, by its id), kind: class, the sections of the reference manual that describe it, the ANSI section when the ANSI draft has the class, and the Deviations that touch the page.
391.breadcrumbs: Classes » How a class page is laid out
391.title: How a class page is laid out

392.body: A rule on a class page is named class. followed by the page, which is the class name in lower case, and then the following words. On a page that holds several classes, the class name in lower case follows the page, as in class.comparators.numeric.compare. class.<page>.<method> is the main rule of a method, with the method name in lower case: class.array.append. class.<page>.<method>.<aspect> is a further rule of the same method, such as an error or a default. class.<page>.<topic> is a rule about the class as a whole, such as creation or comparison. A topic never takes the name of a method of the class: when the class has a method of that name, the main rule of the method is the rule about it, so for a class with a string method the rule about its string value is class.<page>.string. class.<page>.<method>.sends is the rule that states the messages the method sends, as the sends rule says. A class method and an instance method of one class never share an identifier. When a name exists on both sides, the instance method has the plain name, and the class method has the aspect class-side; a further aspect of the class method follows it, as in class.properties.load.class-side.error. The prefix form of - and +, which is the same method sent with no argument, takes the aspect prefix: class.<page>.minus.prefix. A method that is written as a symbol takes a word in place of the symbol: eq for =, seq for ==, ne for \=, sne for \==, ltgt for <>, gtlt for ><, gt, lt, ge and le for >, <, >= and <=, ngt and nlt for \> and \<, sgt, slt, sge and sle for >>, <<, >>= and <<=, nsgt and nslt for \>> and \<<, plus, minus, times, divide, intdiv, remainder and power for +, -, *, /, %, // and **, concat, blank and abuttal for ||, the blank and the abuttal, and, or, xor and not for &, |, && and \, brackets for [], and iif for ?. A method whose name ends in =, an attribute that is assigned, takes the name without it and -set: objectname-set for objectName=, and brackets-set for []=. Every method that a class defines has a rule on its page, and the identifiers never change once they are in the book. A method that the class only inherits has no rule on its page: the page links to the rule on the page that defines it, in a sentence that is not itself a rule and has no identifier. A method that the class defines but whose behavior another page owns, such as a String method that a builtin function runs, a Stream method that a stream builtin uses, or an operator method, is covered by one grouped rule per page and group. The identifier of a grouped rule is class.<page>.builtins for the methods that builtin functions run or use, as class.string.builtins and class.stream.builtins, and class.<page>.operators for the operator methods, as class.string.operators; it is a topic in the sense of the list above. The grouped rule lists each such method with a link to the rule that owns its behavior, and has one example that sends several of them as messages. It covers the inventory rows of those methods. Such a method has a rule of its own, in addition, only where something differs when it is sent as a message.
392.title: How rules are named

4.body: Every statement the book makes about behavior is a rule. A rule has an identifier of dotted lowercase words, and it is a single short paragraph. An identifier names the page that holds its rule, so a reader of the raw Markdown finds any rule from its identifier alone. The first word names the chapter: bif for built-in functions in builtins/, instr for instructions/, expr for expressions/, parse for parsing/, cond for conditions/, class for classes/, lex for lexical/, num for numbers/, dir for directives/, util for rexxutil/, env for environment/ and conc for concurrency/. The second word is the page's file name: bif.substr.pad is in builtins/substr.md, and the rules for a whole chapter, such as bif.index.call.count, are in its index.md. The conventions are one page, conventions.md, and every conv. rule is there. The checker rejects a rule on any other page. Identifiers never change and are never reused. Other pages refer to a rule by that identifier, and so do comments in the test sources: a test that exercises a rule cites it, and the checker reports any rule that has neither a cited test nor an example.
4.title: Reading a rule

400.body: rexxref: Objects and Classes > Default Search Order for Method Selection; Objects and Classes > Changing the Search Order for Methods; Objects and Classes > Defining an UNKNOWN Method; Objects and Classes > Mixin Classes; Objects and Classes > Metaclasses; Objects and Classes > Defining Instance Methods with SETMETHOD or ENHANCED; Objects and Classes > Public, Package-Scope, and Private Methods; Special Variables > SUPER; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Object Class > setMethod; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Object Class > unsetMethod; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > define; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > defineMethods; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > delete; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > enhanced; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > inherit; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Class Class (Metaclass) > uninherit Deviations: D32, D105, D110, D117 Every message goes to an object, and the object's class decides which method answers it. This page specifies the whole search: which methods an object has of its own, in which order its class and the classes it descends from are looked at, how a message can start the search part of the way down, what UNKNOWN receives when nothing is found, how a class object finds the class methods it answers, and what a change to a class does to objects that already exist. The pages of the classes Object and Class specify the arguments of the methods that make these changes; this page specifies what the changes do to the search. The classes chapter lists which class inherits which. The directives that create classes and methods are in ::CLASS and ::METHOD , and the search rule of the first gives the simple cases. Two words are used throughout. The method table of a class is the list of names the class itself holds: the methods that its ::METHOD directives declare and that define and defineMethods add. An entry of a table is either a method or a mark that hides the name (see hidden names ). The order of a class is the list of classes whose tables a message to one of its instances is looked up in.
400.title: Method search

[class.methods.order] The order of Object holds only Object. The order of any other class C starts with C itself and goes on with the orders of the classes in the list of superclasses that C holds, the list its superClasses method reports, one after the other, in the order of that list: the superclass and then the mixin classes in the order they were inherited, except that a mixin class that inherit placed in front of another class of the list, the superclass included, stands there ( the change rule ). A class that this makes occur more than once keeps only its last place. The order therefore ends with Object, and a class stands after every class that has it as a superclass or inherits it. The list is read from what the class holds, and no message is sent to a class for it: the search, isA, isInstanceOf, inherit and uninherit send none of superClasses, isSubclassOf, queryMixinClass or baseClass, so a metaclass that overrides them changes what a program that sends them gets and nothing else. In the second example the metaclass META announces each of those messages and answers falsely; the only announcement is the one for the superClasses that the program sends itself. Note. The first example prints the order of two classes. Each who method names its own class and sends who on to the class that follows it, using the special variable SUPER, which the SUPER rule specifies, so that the line shows the classes of the order in turn, Object left out. 402.body:
[class.methods.search] A message to an object is looked up in this sequence. First come the object's own methods, those that setMethod gave it and those that enhanced made it with. Then come the tables of the classes of the order of the object's class, one after another. The name of the message is compared in upper case. The first table that has an entry for the name decides: when the entry is a method that the sender may run, that method runs; when the entry hides the name, or the method is one the sender may not run, the name counts as not found and the search for the name ends, without going on to the classes behind. A name that counts as not found goes to UNKNOWN, as the unknown rule says. The same sequence serves send and the other methods that send a message, and the operators, which are messages. The first example shows each step: a table that is reached first wins, a superclass before a mixin class, and an object's own method before all of them. The message name is written in several cases. The second example sends operators, which find their methods in the same sequence, also when the message is written with a scope or an object has set the operator itself; an operator that finds no method goes to UNKNOWN like any message, with an array of one item for the infix form and an empty one for the prefix form ( the operator messages ). o = .sub~new

o~put('four', 'return "object four"')

say .sub~new~one '|' .sub~new~four

[class.methods.object] setMethod gives the receiving object a method of its own, found before any class. Its first argument is the name, which is used in upper case, and its second is the method: a method object, a string that is the source of the method, or an array of strings, one for each line, from which a method is made. A second setMethod of the same name replaces the method; the call with no second argument hides the name for the object, so that the search stops there and the message goes to UNKNOWN. unsetMethod takes the name off the object again: the name is looked up in the classes as if setMethod had never been sent, and unsetMethod of a name the object has not set is not an error. setMethod and unsetMethod are private methods with a further restriction, which the next rule gives. A define of the same name that is sent to the class afterwards is not seen while the object's own method of that name stands, and is seen after unsetMethod, as the rule on changes says; the second example shows the object's own method and the class's method of the same name. Deviation 110 has the example for the define that is seen after unsetMethod. o = .k~new
o~put('m', 'return "from a string"')
o~put('a', .array~of('parse arg x', 'return x * 2'))
o~put('n', .method~new('n', 'return "from a method object"'))
say o~m '|' o~a(21) '|' o~n '|' o~old
o~put('m', 'return "replaced"')
say o~m '|' o~old
o~put('old')
say t(o, 'old')
o~unset('old')
o~unset('m')
o~unset('never_set')
say o~old '|' t(o, 'm')
exit

404.body:
[class.methods.late] An object follows every change made to the methods that its class finds, at any time. A define, defineMethods or delete sent to a class C, an inherit or uninherit sent to C, and a change to the table of a superclass of C or of a mixin class in the order of C, all change what the instances of C answer: the instances made before the change as well as those made after it, however many changes came before, and also an object that has methods of its own from setMethod or enhanced. The own methods stay first in the search ( the object rule ). Deviation 110 gives the examples of the changes to the table of C itself. Note. In the example, A is an instance of K and S is an instance of a subclass. Both are made first, and each line gives, for each name, what A and S answer after a change to the superclass or to a mixin class, or after inherit or uninherit, with - where the name is not found. a = .k~new

405.body:
[class.methods.scoped] A message written object~name:scope starts the search at a class. The scope is a variable symbol, simple or compound, or an environment symbol such as .base, and its value is evaluated like that of any term; a string, a number or a parenthesized expression there makes the program unreadable with SYNTAX 20.917. The value must be a class that stands in the order of the object's class, that is the class itself, a superclass, an inherited mixin class or Object. Another value raises SYNTAX 88.914 when it is not a class, and 93.957 when it is a class that does not stand in the order. The object's own methods are not looked at, except a method that setMethod gave it with the scope OBJECT, which counts as an entry of the table of the object's class and is found ahead of that table's own entry when the search starts at that class, as the scope rule says. The search begins with the table of the named class and goes on through the classes that follow it in the order of the object's class, whichever class the sending method belongs to. It ends as the search rule says, and a name that is not found goes to UNKNOWN through the plain search for that name, and without one raises NOMETHOD, SYNTAX 97.1 when untrapped. A scoped message can be sent from any code, and the object need not be SELF. Note. In the first example o has a method of its own, and the scoped messages skip it. ONLYMX is held by a mixin class that stands behind BASE, so a search that starts at BASE reaches it, and ONLYBASE is held by a class in front of MX, so a search that starts at MX does not. o = .leaf~new

say o~hello '|' o~hello:.leaf '|' o~hello:.mid '|' o~hello:.base
say o~hello:.mx '|' o~onlymx:.base '|' o~onlymx:.mx
call try 'say o~onlybase:.mx'
call try 'say o~onlybase:.base'
exit

406.body:
[class.methods.forward] The CLASS option of FORWARD names the class that starts the search, and it starts it as the scope of a scoped message does: the object's own methods are skipped as for a scoped message, the table of the named class comes first, and the classes behind it in the order of the receiver's class follow. forward class (super) therefore runs the method that the running one overrides. The class must be one the receiver is an instance of, or the instruction raises 93.957 as the FORWARD page says. In the example, GO3 of the first mixin class forwards to the class behind it in the order of LEAF, which is the second mixin class, and GO4 of LEAF forwards to the second mixin class by name. o = .leaf~new

407.body:
[class.methods.unknown] When the search for a name ends without a method, because no table holds it, a mark hides it, or the sender may not run the method that was found, the search is made again for the name UNKNOWN, over the object's own methods and then the order of its class, whatever scope the first message had. The search for UNKNOWN makes no access check: a PRIVATE or PACKAGE UNKNOWN runs for any sender, and a mark that hides UNKNOWN ends the search as if there were none. The first UNKNOWN found runs, with two arguments: the name of the message in upper case, and a new array that holds the arguments of the message at their positions. The array has as many places as the position of the last argument that was not omitted , and a place of an omitted argument holds nothing; for a message with no arguments the array is empty and has dimension 1. The answer of UNKNOWN is the answer of the message, and a message to an UNKNOWN that answers nothing answers nothing, so that using it as a value, as SAY does, raises SYNTAX 91.999. A class in front of another in the order wins also here, so an UNKNOWN of a superclass hides the one of a mixin class and the object's own UNKNOWN hides both. When no UNKNOWN is found, NOMETHOD is raised . A message to a class object is looked up in the class-side order the same way. The second example sends to objects whose UNKNOWN is PRIVATE, is PACKAGE and is hidden, once from the code of another package; the third gives the dimension of the array. o = .c~new

408.body:
[class.methods.class-side] A message to a class object is looked up the same way as one to an instance, with a class-side order in place of the order. The class-side order of a class C starts with C, standing for the class methods that C declares with CLASS. It goes on with the order of the metaclass of C, each class of it standing for its instance methods, which are class methods of C; then the class-side orders of the superclass of C and of its inherited mixin classes, in the order of superClasses. A class that occurs more than once keeps its last place. The metaclass of C is the one METACLASS names, otherwise that of its superclass, otherwise Class, and the order of a metaclass is an ordinary order that ends with Class and Object. When a subclass has the metaclass of its superclass, the class methods of the subclass come first, those of the superclass next, then the methods of the metaclass, and last those of the inherited mixin classes. Naming another metaclass for the subclass puts that metaclass in front of the class methods of the superclass and keeps the metaclass of the superclass behind them. In the example, SUB inherits MIX and has the metaclass of BASE, SUB2 names a metaclass of its own, and SUB3 declares nothing, so it answers with the class method of BASE and then the method of the metaclass. call show .sub, .sub2, .sub3
exit

[num.limits.overflow] A result of +, -, * or /, or of the prefix + or -, whose first digit stands at a power of ten above 999999999 raises SYNTAX 42.901, and no value results. The test is made on the result after it is rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS, so a result that carries into a digit above the range when it is rounded raises it too. The operands may all be in range and the result still out of it. A prefix operator can only overflow, because its rounding shortens the digits and never moves them below the range, and a prefix operator on an operand that is out of range raises SYNTAX 41.1 for the operand. signal on syntax name a

The last digit is that of the result rounded to NUMERIC DIGITS digits, taken before the zeros that end a division or power result are removed. The test is therefore not made on the written result: 1 / 9.99999999e999999998 is written 1E-999999999 when it answers, yet under DIGITS 2 to 12 the rounded value, such as 1.0 for DIGITS 2, ends at -1000000000 and the division raises. The copy has the object variables of the receiver, each holding the same object that the receiver's variable holds, so the copy is shallow, and it has the same methods, the receiver's own methods included, and the same name. The copy has its own table of the object's own methods, holding the same method objects, and the variables of those methods are copied as the others are, so a change to one object's own methods or to those variables does not reach the other. It does not send init, and takes no argument: with one it raises SYNTAX 93.902. 418.body:
[class.object.request] request answers the receiver converted to the kind of object that its argument names, or .nil. The argument is a string, taken in upper case. The method first asks whether the receiver has a method named MAKE followed by that name; if it has, request sends that message to the receiver with no argument and answers what it answers, whatever that is, and the answer is not checked: a method may answer .nil or an object of another class. The message is checked for access as if the code that sent request had sent it, as for send : a PRIVATE method runs when request is sent by code that the access rule lets send it, a method of a subclass included, and raises SYNTAX 97.2 otherwise, and a PACKAGE method raises 97.3 when request is sent from another package. When there is no such method, UNKNOWN plays no part, the method compares the name with the id of the receiver's class, without regard to case: when they are equal it answers the receiver itself, and otherwise .nil. The id is that of the class of the receiver only, not of its superclasses. The argument is checked as for hasMethod: none raises 93.903, .nil and objects without a string value 88.909, and a second argument 93.902. o = .doc~new
say o~request('string') '|' o~request('Array')~class~id '|', o~request('doc')~class~id

419.body:
[class.object.send] send sends the message that its first argument names to the receiver, with the remaining arguments as the arguments of that message, in order, and answers what the message answers. An omitted argument stays omitted in the message, and omitted places at the end add nothing to the argument count. The message is an ordinary one: it is found by the search rule and so also goes to UNKNOWN when nothing is found, raises NOMETHOD (SYNTAX 97.1 when untrapped) when there is no UNKNOWN, and is checked for access as if the code that called send had sent it, so send('secret') from outside the class raises 97.2 for a private method that no UNKNOWN takes. The name is taken in upper case, and a number literal such as 12 names the message 12, as the same characters in quotes do ( Deviation 107 ). The first argument is a string, or an array of two items, the name and a class, which starts the search at that class as the scoped send rule says. An object that is not a string is sent request with the argument ARRAY, and the answer is used as the two-item form, whatever the class of the first argument is ( the sends rule ; an instance of a subclass of String is read as Deviation 109 states). .nil, and an object that answers .nil, raise SYNTAX 93.972, an answer that is no array and an array of another size 93.946, an array whose first item is missing 88.901 and one whose first item has no string value 88.909, and no argument 88.901. The null string is a name like any other: it names the abuttal method ( the joining rule ), so send('', 'x') joins and send('') raises that method's 93.903. An array whose second item is not a class raises 88.914. A message that answers nothing makes send answer nothing. o = .w~new

[class.object.setmethod] setMethod gives the receiver a method of its own, as the object method rule says, and answers no value. It is private, with the restriction that the access rule gives. The first argument is the name and is required (SYNTAX 88.901); an object that is no string and whose request with the argument STRING answers no string raises 88.909. The second is the method: a method object, a string that holds the source of a method, or an array, whose items are read as the source rule reads them, so an item that gives no string raises SYNTAX 93.952. These are instances of Method, String and Array themselves; an instance of a subclass of one of them, Method included, is converted as any other object is. Any other object is sent request with the argument ARRAY, and the array it answers is used; when it answers no array, it is sent request with the argument STRING, and a string answer is used as the source ( the sends rule ). .nil, and an object whose request with STRING answers .nil, raise SYNTAX 93.974, so a subclass of Method that declares neither MAKEARRAY nor MAKESTRING is refused. When that request answers an object that is not a string, the result is not specified. The method that the receiver gets runs the code of a method object that is given, with the scope that the scope rule says. It is not specified whether the method object that the receiver holds is the argument itself or a copy of it, and what scope the argument object answers afterwards is not specified either. The checks run in this order: the number of arguments, the name, the method, the scope. With no second argument the name is hidden for the receiver. The third argument is the scope, FLOAT or OBJECT as the scope rule says; another value raises 88.916, and .nil raises 88.909. A fourth argument raises 93.902. A source that does not translate raises the translation error from setMethod. The code of a method made from a source runs with the scope FLOAT, whose object variables are separate from those of any class: the methods that the receiver got by setMethod with FLOAT, by run and by enhanced share one set, which is kept for the receiver. o = .w~new

Its instance methods are therefore what every class object understands: the methods that make and change classes (subclass, mixinClass, define, inherit and the others), that answer questions about a class (id, superClasses, method) and that make objects (enhanced). Class is a subclass of Object, so a class also understands the methods of Object . Its class method new makes a new class. The chapter index lists how the library classes are related and what new and defaultName do. The method search specifies what define, inherit and the other methods that change a class do to the order in which methods are looked up; this page specifies their arguments, their checks and their errors. 423.body:
[class.class.new] The class method new of Class makes a class. It is a class method of Class and so of every metaclass, a subclass of Class, and it is not the new that makes the instances of an ordinary class ( the Object rule specifies that one). Its first argument is the id of the new class: a string, or an object whose request with the argument STRING answers one, and the null string and a number are allowed. The new class has Object as its superclass, is not a mixin class and not abstract, and is an instance of the class that received new, which is also its metaclass; its package is the package of that class, so .class~new gives a class whose package is the one of the library and a user's metaclass gives one whose package is the package that declares the metaclass. new sends the new class the message init with the arguments that follow the id, in order, and answers the class. The class answers no new of its own: a message new to it raises SYNTAX 97.1, but a subclass of it, made with subclass, has the new of every class. The id is required (SYNTAX 93.901, none), .nil and an object with no string value raise 88.909, and the arguments after the id are those of init, so Class itself, whose init takes none, raises 93.902 for one. f = .class~new('Foo')

[class.class.define] define gives the class an instance method, or hides a name, for every instance of the class, those that exist already included, as the rule on changes and the hidden-name rule say, and the search finds it as the search rule says, and answers no value. The first argument is the name, taken in upper case, and may be any string, a number included. The second is the method, in the forms that setMethod takes: a method object, a string that is the source of a method, or an array of strings, one for each line, converted as the setMethod rule says and with the messages of the sends rule . The method that the class holds runs the code of the method object that is given, with the class as its scope. It is not specified whether the method object that the class holds is the argument itself or a copy of it, and what scope the argument object answers afterwards is not specified either. A method replaces what the table held for the name. With no second argument the name is hidden; with .nil as the second argument the name is hidden from the search as well, but the table no longer holds an entry for it that method could answer. An object whose request with STRING answers .nil, as an instance of a subclass of Method that declares neither MAKEARRAY nor MAKESTRING does, raises SYNTAX 93.974, and a source that does not translate raises its translation error from define. A name is required (88.901), a name that is no string and has no string value raises 88.909, and a third argument raises 93.902. The number of arguments is checked first, then the class, then the name, then the method. The classes of the class library accept no define ( the library rule ), which raises 98.985 before any argument is checked. The examples use objects made after the change. .k~define('A1', 'return 1')

43.body: ANSI: 7.4.2, 7.4.3, 7.4.4, 7.4.5, 7.4.10; rexxref: Numbers and Arithmetic > Arithmetic Deviations: D53, D102 The arithmetic operators are the infix +, -, *, /, %, // and **, and the prefix + and -. Each reads its operands as numbers, works to the precision that NUMERIC DIGITS sets, and answers a new number. This page says how many digits an operation looks at in its operands, how it rounds, what each operator answers, and which errors an operation raises. How an answer is written is the business of the formats page , the size limits of the limits page , and the settings of the settings page . Where the operators stand in an expression is left to the expressions chapter .
