41.1 [num.arithmetic.digits] An operation works at NUMERIC DIGITS significant digits and rounds its result to that many, as the rounding rule of the builtins says and as the result rule applies to every operator. An operand is not rounded before the operation: it takes part with the digits it has, apart from the cut that the next two rules describe for the digits beyond DIGITS plus one. Under NUMERIC DIGITS 1 the product of 2 and 1.5 is therefore 3, where rounding 1.5 to 2 first would give 4, and rounding happens once, on the result. numeric digits 1
say (2 * 1.5) (1.5 + 1.5) (6 / 4) (0.4 + 0.4)
numeric digits 3
say (1 / 3) (2 / 3) (100 / 3) (1000 / 3) (10000 / 3) (2.5 * 2.5)
numeric digits 12
say (1 / 3) (2 / 3) (1 / 7) 3 3 2 0.8
0.333 0.667 33.3 333 3.33E+3 6.25
0.333333333333 0.666666666667 0.142857142857 [num.arithmetic.cut] Before *, /, % or // uses an operand that has more than DIGITS plus one significant digits, it cuts the operand to its first DIGITS plus one digits, counted from the first nonzero digit. The cut drops the later digits and does not round them. The digit kept beyond DIGITS takes part in the operation, so it shapes the digit on which the result is rounded. The two products and the two quotients below therefore differ from the exact ones, which would round to 4, 4, 1.0 and 0.32. numeric digits 1
say (1.19 * 3) (1.19 * 3.19)
numeric digits 2
say (1.499 / 1.5) (2.999 / 9.5) 3 3
0.99 0.31 [num.arithmetic.addsub] The result of + and - is rounded to DIGITS digits counted from the first digit of the operand whose first digit stands higher, and not from the first digit of the result. Let that higher digit stand at power of ten H, taking no account of an operand with the value zero. Both operands are first cut after the digit at H - DIGITS, which is one digit more than the rounding keeps. Their exact sum or difference is then rounded once, half up in magnitude, at the coarser of H - DIGITS + 1 and the DIGITS significant digits of that sum. So two close numbers can cancel down to zero, and a sum that carries into a new leading digit keeps one digit less after the point. numeric digits 3

say (1234 + 1) (1234 + 0) (0 + 1234) (1.234 - 0)

457.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > newFile (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > loadExternalRoutine (Class method); Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > []; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > annotation; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > annotations; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > call; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > callWith; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > package; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > setSecurityManager; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > source; The Security Manager Deviations: D41, D109, D111, D115, D118, D124, D134 A Routine object is a piece of code that is called with arguments and answers a value, as a routine of a program is. A ::ROUTINE directive makes one for each directive, and a program makes one of its own from source text with new, from a file with newFile, or from a native library with loadExternalRoutine. A routine object is called by the messages call, callWith and [], and every call is a call of an external routine: the code runs in a variable pool of its own, sees nothing of its caller's variables, and finds classes and routines through its package. The page specifies the class methods that make a routine, the messages that call it and ask about it, and the security manager that a routine can be put under. The routine that a directive makes is specified by ::ROUTINE , the annotations by ::ANNOTATE , and the instruction that calls a routine by name by CALL . A routine is made from source in the way a method is, so the rules of the Method page for the source and the context apply to new and newFile here, and this page states what is its own. newFile takes its file as the newFile rule says, and the library of loadExternalRoutine is found as the library rule says; the examples here name a file that they create themselves, or a library that every installation has. The examples that show an error use a routine try that sends the message in its argument and prints the answer, or the error code when the message raises one.

The arguments are the arguments of the message, and the argument count is the position of the last one that is not omitted : an omitted place before it stays omitted for ARG and use arg, and omitted places at the end add nothing. The code runs as the code of an external routine does: it has variables of its own and cannot see those of the program that called it, the classes and routines it names are those of its package, and exit ends the routine and answers the value it gives. [class.routine.source] source answers a new array that holds the lines of the routine's source, one string for each line, so changing the array changes nothing in the routine. A routine made by new has the lines of its source argument (an empty string and an empty array are a source of no lines), one made by newFile the lines of its file before the first directive, without a first line that begins with #!, and one that a ::ROUTINE directive makes has the lines of its section, which the rule of Method reads as it does for a method: the text after the ; of the directive is the first line, and an empty last line is left out, so a directive with nothing after its ; and no lines has an empty source. The last line of the source argument of new and of the file of newFile is left out when it is empty, too, and every read answers the same lines ( Deviation 134 ). [class.routine.setsecuritymanager] setSecurityManager gives the package that holds the routine's code a security manager, or with no argument removes the one that package has, and answers 1 ( the package rule ); a routine that new or newFile made has a package of its own. It is a protected method. The manager can be any object, .nil as well, and it is not checked when it is set; .nil is an object like any other and is sent the checkpoints, which it does not understand (SYNTAX 97.1), so only a call with no argument removes the manager. A second argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. While code of that package runs, the routine and its internal routines among it, the actions that the checkpoint rules name are offered to the manager first ( which code ). The code of other packages, and of the packages that the code makes, is not under the manager. A manager that is set or removed while code of the package runs is taken up by the calls that start after the change, except for the name checkpoints LOCAL and ENVIRONMENT, which the run that is going on takes up at once ( the run rule ). src = 'address system "echo hidden"; return "done"'
r = .routine~new('agent', src)
say r~setSecurityManager(.guard~new)
say r~call
say r~setSecurityManager
say r~call
say r~setSecurityManager(.nil)
call try 'r~call'
call try 'r~setSecurityManager(.guard~new, 1)'
exit

The rules for each name the entries of its information directory. The interpreter sends the manager the message of the checkpoint's name with one argument, a Directory that holds the entries; the manager answers 1 to say it handled the action, and the entries that the checkpoint reads from the directory are used, or 0 to let the action go on as it would. An answer that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.903, and an answer of no value raises SYNTAX 91.999. [class.package.new] new makes a package from a name and, optionally, a source and a context. The name is required (SYNTAX 88.901), and is a string or the string that its argument gives : an object that gives no string, .nil among them, raises 88.909. With a source, the name is only the name of the package, and the package is always a new object. With no source, the name is the name of a file, which new looks for and reads, as the file rule says, and there is no context: the arguments from the third on go to init. The context is the third argument. It is a Method, a Routine or a Package object, or omitted; any other value, .nil and PROGRAMSCOPE included, raises SYNTAX 93.953. The checks run in this order: the name, the context, the source (a source that is .nil raises 93.961), and then the source is translated, so that a source that does not translate raises its translation error, and new then installs the package as the install rule says. The arguments from the fourth on are passed to init of the new package, and so are the arguments from the third on when the source is omitted; the init of Object accepts none, and one argument raises SYNTAX 93.902 after the package is installed. [class.package.defaultoptions] defaultOptions reads and sets the options that a package gets when it is made without the corresponding ::OPTIONS. It takes an option name and optionally a value, and no further argument (SYNTAX 93.902). The name is required (88.901), an object that gives no string , .nil among them, raises 88.909, and only its first letter counts: D names DefineDefaultOptions and C names CountOverrides, in any case; another name raises SYNTAX 93.914. With no value the call answers the current value, and with a value it sets it and answers the previous one. DefineDefaultOptions is a string in the form of an ::OPTIONS directive, which is the same form that options answers; a string that is not one ::OPTIONS directive, in any case and after optional blanks, raises 93.900, as a string of two directives does, a string whose options the directive refuses raises the error of the directive (25.924 for an unknown option), and a directive with no options leaves every option at its initial value. The initial value names DIGITS 9, FORM SCIENTIFIC, FUZZ 0, NUMERIC NOINHERIT, each of the six condition options with CONDITION, PROLOG and TRACE NORMAL, as options lists them. CountOverrides is a whole number whose initial value is 0; a value that is not a whole number raises 93.905. While it is positive, every package that is made, by new and by the new and newFile of Method and of Routine, which make a package of their own, gets the default options in place of the initial ones and reduces the count by one; a package that gives an option in a directive keeps its own value for that option. A count that is 0 leaves the packages that are made with the initial options, and a negative count applies the defaults to every package that is made, and is reduced by one for each, so that it stays negative. say .package~defaultOptions('CountOverrides')

[class.package.findclass] findClass looks a name up as the environment symbol of the same name is looked up in the package's code, and answers what it finds, or .nil. The name is taken in upper case. The places that are searched, in this order, are the classes of the package, public or not; the classes that the package of its context finds, which are its own, public or not, the public ones of the packages it imports, and what its own context finds; the public classes of the packages it imports, the one imported first winning among equal names; the public classes of the library; the package's local directory; and then .local and .environment, so the answer may be an object that is not a class, such as .nil, .true or .local, and a name that nothing holds answers .nil. The first place that holds the name decides. The name is required (SYNTAX 88.901), an object that gives no string , .nil among them, raises 88.909, and a second argument raises 93.902. Any string is a name: a name with a blank or a period is found when addClass, addPublicClass or a directory holds it under that name. A name that has a colon is not looked up through a namespace: tg:shown and rexx:string answer .nil, even when a package that holds a public class SHOWN was added under the namespace TG. src = .array~of('return 1', '::class own public', '::class priv')

say p~findClass('rexx:string')~isNil p~findClass('rexx:')~isNil
call try 'p~findClass'
call try 'p~findClass(.nil)'
call try 'p~findClass("x", 1)'
exit

A program makes one with new, or gets one from the start and startWith methods of Object , and then decides when the message is sent. It can send the message and wait for the answer, start it so that another activity runs it while the sender goes on, or start a copy of it. Afterwards the object keeps what the message answered, or the error that ended it, and a program can ask for them, wait for them, or be told when they are there. The page specifies the class method that makes a message object, the methods that read what it holds, the methods that run it, the methods that wait for it, stop it or ask for a notification when it is done, and the three methods the class has because it implements the notification interfaces of MessageNotification and AlarmNotification . How an activity is scheduled, when a started message begins to run, and how it interleaves with the activity that started it is specified by the ordering rule and the waiting rule of the concurrency chapter. The examples on this page therefore show only results that no scheduling can change: they wait for a message with result or wait, or park the activity of the message on a guard that the example opens, before they print anything that depends on it. The methods that an example waits for, or that the waiting activity calls meanwhile, are UNGUARDED, so that the waiting activity and the activity of the message can both use the object ( the guard rule ). The examples that show an error use a routine try that interprets the clause in its argument and prints the clause with the error code, or with the class of the answer when no error is raised.

[class.message.send] send(target, argument, ...) sends the message in the activity of the sender and does not answer until the message has ended. It answers what the message answers, and nothing when the message answers nothing, so that a use of the answer as a value then raises SYNTAX 91.999. An error that the message raises is raised at the clause that sent send, as the error of an ordinary message would be, and is also kept: hasError answers 1 and result raises it again. The first argument, when it is not omitted, replaces the target of the message for this and every later run, and it may be .nil. When the call has more than one argument, as the count rule counts them, the arguments after the first replace the arguments of the message likewise; with only a target, or none, the message keeps its arguments. The message is found by the search rule in the target, goes to UNKNOWN when nothing is found, raises NOMETHOD (SYNTAX 97.1 when untrapped) when there is none, and is checked for PRIVATE and PACKAGE access as if the code that called send had sent it. A scoped name starts the search at its class, and raises 93.957 when the target is not an instance of that class; that error is raised to the caller of send, start or the other run methods before the message runs, and is not an error of the message. Each send is a new run: the message can be sent again, and the result, the error and the completion are those of the latest run. t = .t~new

When the message answered nothing it answers .nil, so that hasResult is the way to tell the two apart. What result does for a message that nothing will run, such as one that has never been sent or the original of a reply, is the case of Deviation 20 . t = .t~new

[class.message.notify] notify(target) asks for a notification when the message ends: the object target is sent the message messageComplete with the message object as its only argument. The target must be an instance of MessageNotification , a class that inherits it or a subclass of one; any other object, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 88.914, no target 88.901 and a second argument 93.902. notify answers nothing and can be sent any number of times: the targets are kept in the order of the calls, and each is sent messageComplete each time the message ends, in that order. A run of send or sendWith sends them before it returns, in the activity of the sender, and an error that a messageComplete raises is raised there, so that it ends the send clause; the targets after the one that raised it are not sent messageComplete, and when the message itself ended with an error, the sender sees the error of the messageComplete, while errorCondition keeps that of the message. The error does not become an error of a sent message, which has ended without one. When a message that has ended is given a target, the target is sent messageComplete at once, in the activity that called notify. For a started message the targets are sent it in the activity that ran the message; when that happens relative to the activity that waits for the message is a matter of scheduling. For a started message, an error that a messageComplete raises becomes the error of the message: hasError answers 1, errorCondition answers the condition of that error and result raises it, while hasResult keeps the 1 of the run. The targets after the one that raised it are not sent messageComplete, and the target that raised it is sent it that once ( Deviation 116 ). hasError answers 1 once the error has been recorded, which may be after wait has returned. 492.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > MessageNotification Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > MessageNotification Class > messageComplete (Abstract Method) MessageNotification is an interface class: a class that a program's class inherits to say that its instances can be told when a message has ended. An object that was given to the notify method of a Message as the target of a notification has to be an instance of it, and the library then sends that object the one message the interface names, messageComplete, each time the message ends. How the activities that run a message and its notifications are ordered is specified in the ordering rule of the concurrency chapter.

496.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > AlarmNotification Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > AlarmNotification Class > cancel; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > AlarmNotification Class > triggered (Abstract method) Deviations: D119 AlarmNotification is an interface class: a class that a program's class inherits to say that its instances can be told when an alarm goes off or is cancelled. An object that is given to an Alarm or a Ticker as the target of its notification has to be an instance of it, and the library sends that object triggered when the time comes and cancel when the alarm is cancelled. Message is an implementation, so a message object can be the target of an alarm. The classes Alarm and Ticker are specified apart from this page, the times at which an alarm or ticker goes off are specified with their init, and which activity runs the target by the timer rule of the concurrency chapter; the examples here wait on a guard that the notification opens before they print what it recorded.

5.body: An example is a short program followed by the exact text it writes to standard output. When the program ends with a non-zero exit code, the output is marked with that code. The checker runs every example with an empty standard input and compares the output byte for byte, so an example is evidence, not decoration. An example belongs to the rule above it. An output marked defect=#N (combinable with the exit code, as in output defect=#12 rc=1) is an example interrexx fails today because of open issue N. The output shown is still the specified one, and the checker accepts the mismatch on interrexx; when the example starts to pass, it reports that the marker is to be removed. An output marked escaped (combinable with the other markers) writes a character that cannot be shown as itself with an escape: \a or \x07 is the bell character, \xNN is the ASCII character of code NN in hexadecimal, and \\ is a backslash. The checker decodes the escapes before it compares, and any other backslash in such a block is an error.

They are not arguments of the operations and no number carries them, so the same expression gives different answers under different settings. This page says what each setting controls, how it is checked when a program changes it, and which part of a program a change reaches. It defines nineteen methods. Seven of them are abstract: they name what a collection has to be able to do, reading and writing an entry by its index and listing its indexes and items, and a class that inherits Collection declares them. The other twelve are written in terms of those seven and of the messages a collection answers for itself. They are the questions about an index, an item, the count and a supplier, and the set operations that combine two collections. A class that inherits only Collection gets all twelve working as the rules below say; a concrete class of the library may declare a method of the same name instead, and its page says what that method does. The page specifies the methods in that order. Where a method sends a message that a program can override, its .sends rule gives the message, the receiver and the order, as the sends rule asks. The argument of a set operation is read by a rule of its own, shared by the seven operations. OrderedCollection declares its own versions of five of the set operations, and MapCollection its own makeArray; the pages of the concrete collections link to this page for what they do not declare. The examples use the class box, a collection of strings in which the item and the index of an entry are the same string. It keeps its entries in a directory, answers the indexes and the items in sorted order, and declares put, remove and copy for the set operations; the rest it gets from Collection.

93.948 [class.collection.subset] subset(other) answers 1 when each item that the receiver's makeArray answers is equal to an element that the argument supplies, and 0 otherwise. The argument is read as the operand rule says, so for a plain or ordered argument the elements are its items, and a receiver with no items is a subset of every collection. An item and an element are equal as == compares strings: 1 and 1.0 differ, and so do a and A. For an argument that is read through allIndexes, the elements are its indexes, and an item of the receiver that is one of them must also have a matching entry: the receiver's entry at that index is sent \= with the argument's entry at that index, and an answer of 1 makes the result 0, so a receiver whose entries do not override \= compares them as = does, where 1 and 1.0 are equal and a and A are not. When isA says that the argument is a Set, its entries are not compared, because an index and its item are the same there. The answer of that isA is used as a logical value: a string that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.901, and an answer that is not a string, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 93.948 whatever its string value. The answer of \= is used as a logical value: what is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.6. a = .box~new('a b')

93.948 [class.collection.subset.sends] subset first reads the argument: it sends isA with OrderedCollection and, when that does not answer 1, isA with MapCollection, then allItems, allIndexes or makeArray as the operand rule says. For a map it then sends isA with Set. Then it sends copy to the receiver, items to the argument and makeArray to the receiver, each with no argument, and uses none of the first two answers. A copy that answers anything and an items that answers anything do not matter, but an argument that does not understand items raises SYNTAX 93.948. The answer of the receiver's makeArray has to be an Array of that class itself: an instance of a subclass of Array raises SYNTAX 98.913, and nothing is sent to it. subset reads its positions from 1 up to its last, a position that holds nothing giving the item .nil, and for each item, in order, subset sends hasItem with the item to the answer of the first step, and answers 0 at the first item for which that answers 0, sending nothing more. For a map that is not a Set, when hasItem answers 1 it sends [] with the item to the receiver and then [] with the item to the argument itself, and then \= to the receiver's entry with the argument's entry as the argument. 507.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > MapCollection Class; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > MapCollection Class > of (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > MapCollection Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > MapCollection Class > putAll Deviations: D33 MapCollection is the mixin class of the collections that map an index to an item: the directories, the tables, the relations, the sets and the other classes that the class hierarchy lists as inheriting it. It inherits Collection , and so has every method of that page, and it adds three: the class method of, which builds a collection from index and item pairs, and the instance methods makeArray, which answers the indexes where Collection answers the items, and putAll, which copies every entry of another collection in. The mixin also decides how a map is read when it is the argument of a set operation, which the operand rule states. A class that inherits only MapCollection has to declare put and allIndexes, which are abstract in Collection; the examples use the class store, which keeps its entries in a directory and declares those two, allItems and a string method that lists its entries in index order.

[num.settings.effect] NUMERIC DIGITS is the count of significant digits that arithmetic and numeric comparison keep, and it is also read by the builtins that round their numbers . NUMERIC FUZZ is the count of those digits that a numeric comparison ignores, so it acts only on comparison: every numeric comparison, the end test of a DO loop included, and the comparisons of the builtins that pick a number. NUMERIC FORM decides only how an exponent is written in a result that needs one, as the notation rule says. Each setting has a default that a program starts with: 9, 0 and SCIENTIFIC, unless a directive of the package gives another value. The builtins DIGITS , FUZZ and FORM answer the setting in force where they are called. say digits() fuzz() form()

It inherits Collection and declares twenty methods of its own. The ones that walk and change a sequence, first, firstItem, last, lastItem, next, previous, append, insert, delete and section, are abstract, and the four sorts are written in terms of other messages. The rest are appendAll and the set operations union, difference, intersection, xor and subset, which replace the versions of Collection for a class that inherits this mixin. disjoint and equivalent are not replaced: they are the methods of that page, and they use the set operations of this one through the messages they send. The set operations here treat the collection as a sequence that may repeat an item: a repeated item counts as many times as it occurs. They are built on messages that the receiver has to understand: removeItem, which no mixin defines, append, which this mixin declares abstract, and hasItem, which Collection defines. 522.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Collection Classes > SetCollection Class SetCollection is the mixin class that marks a collection as a set: one in which the index of an entry and its item are the same object. It declares no method. A class inherits it to say what kind of collection it is, and the classes of the library that do are Set and Bag, each of which also inherits MapCollection . The page says what the mixin is and what it changes for the programs that combine collections; the behavior of a set or a bag is on the pages of those classes.

526.body:
[class.array.new] new makes an empty array. The arguments say how large the dimensions are expected to be, and they are hints only: the array grows as entries are put into it. With no argument the array has no dimension yet; its dimension is 0 and its size is 0, and the first put gives it as many dimensions as the put has indexes. With one or more arguments, each a whole number that is not negative, the array has one dimension for each argument, of that size, and its size is the product of them, though it holds no item (items is 0). One argument that is an Array of such numbers gives the same dimensions as arguments would; an instance of a subclass is not such an array. An argument that is not a whole number that is not negative raises SYNTAX 93.906, and so does an array of sizes that holds one, or an instance of a subclass; an omitted argument followed by a given one raises SYNTAX 93.903, while omitted arguments at the end count for nothing. A size of 0 is allowed and makes a dimension with no room: new(0) has dimension 1 and size 0. A size is read as the index rule reads an index. a = .array~new

527.body:
[class.array.indexes] A method that takes an index takes it as one argument for each dimension, or as one Array that holds them all; at(2, 3) and at(.array~of(2, 3)) name the same entry. Only an instance of Array itself is such a list: an instance of a subclass is one argument like any other object. Each index is a whole number of at least 1, read from the string value of the argument ( the conversion rule ) as a whole-number argument of a builtin is ( the form rule , the digits rule ), so "2", ' + 2 ' and 2.0 are as good as 2 and NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part; an argument those rules refuse raises the error this rule names, not SYNTAX 40.12. The number of indexes must be the number of dimensions of the array: too few raise SYNTAX 93.925 and too many SYNTAX 93.926. An index that is not a whole number of at least 1 raises SYNTAX 93.907 when the array has one dimension, and SYNTAX 93.924 when it has more. No index at all, or an empty array of indexes, raises SYNTAX 93.901. An array that has no dimension yet (one made by new without arguments and not yet put into) has no entries, and a message that reads, with two or more indexes, answers as for an index that has no entry without checking them; with one index it is checked as for a one-dimensional array. [num.settings.block] A setting belongs to the routine that is running and not to a block of it. A NUMERIC instruction in the body of a DO loop, an IF or a SELECT changes the setting for the rest of the routine, including the clauses after the block, and a trapped condition that transfers control to a label of the same routine finds the setting as it was. A condition raised inside an internal routine whose trap names a label of the calling routine runs that label with the settings of the routine where the condition was raised, as the last lines of the example show. numeric digits 4
numeric fuzz 1
do 2 numeric digits 5
end
if 1 then numeric fuzz 2
select when 1 then numeric form engineering otherwise nop
end

exit

An internal routine changes only its own settings, and the caller has its own again when the routine returns, whether the routine is written with PROCEDURE or not. The value that the routine returns is a string like any other, written under the routine's settings, and the caller finds it as it was written. numeric digits 4

[class.array.sort] sort and stableSort put the items of the array in ascending order, in place, and answer the receiver; sortWith(comparator) and stableSortWith(comparator) do the same by the order the comparator gives. Items are compared by compareTo, which for strings is the string rule : 10 sorts before 9, and upper case before lower case. The comparator is any object that understands compare, and when it answers a negative number for two items the first sorts before the second, when it answers 0 they are equal, and when it answers a positive number the first sorts after. stableSort and stableSortWith keep items that are equal in their order; whether sort and sortWith do is not specified. The sorted items fill the slots from index 1 on in the order of the slots (in a multi-dimensional array the first dimension changing fastest), so an array whose items are not in the first slots, with an empty slot before an item, raises SYNTAX 98.975 before any comparison and stays as it was; empty slots after the items stay empty, and the size does not change. An array of fewer than two items is not compared; sortWith and stableSortWith then answer at once, before the slot check and without looking at the comparator, while sort and stableSort still make the slot check, so .array~of(, 5)~sort raises SYNTAX 98.975 and .array~of(, 5)~sortWith(.nil) does not. sort and stableSort take no argument: any raises SYNTAX 93.902. sortWith and stableSortWith take exactly one: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.903 and a second SYNTAX 93.902. [class.array.sends] No method that Array declares sends a message to its receiver: an override of at, put, append or any other of the methods is never asked by another method, and [] and []= do not use at and put. 543.body:
[class.list.indexes] An index of a list is a handle: the list hands one out when it creates an entry (append, insert) and answers it again as it walks the entries (first, last, next, previous, index, allIndexes, supplier). The handle names that entry for as long as the entry is in the list, whatever is inserted or removed around it. The page does not say what a handle is made of, which values a list hands out, in which order, or whether it hands out again the handle of an entry that was removed, and it says nothing of the handles of a list after empty, or of a copy. A program uses the handles that the list it asks has answered, and two handles are told apart by ==. A handle whose entry is not in the list, for instance one that was just removed, is not an error for the methods that look entries up: at, next, previous, delete and remove answer .nil and hasIndex answers 0. The methods that must have an entry, put, insert and section, raise SYNTAX 93.918 for any value that is not the handle of an entry of the list. Given to a method that looks entries up, a value that the list did not hand out either raises an error or is taken as a handle whose entry is not in the list; the page does not say which. .nil and the string x are no handle at all: every method that takes an index raises SYNTAX 93.918 for them, except that insert takes .nil to mean the front of the list ( the insert rule ). l = .list~new

[class.queue.indexes] An index of a queue is a whole number of at least 1, the position of an item counted from the head. A method that takes an index reads it from its string value ( the conversion rule ) as a whole-number argument of a builtin is ( the form rule , the digits rule ): "2", ' 2 ' and 2.0 are as good as 2, NUMERIC DIGITS plays no part, and an argument that those rules refuse, a number below 1, or .nil raises SYNTAX 93.907. [num.comparison.numeric] Two numbers compare as the sign of their difference. The difference is the one that the rule for - gives, calculated at NUMERIC DIGITS minus NUMERIC FUZZ digits, and the numbers are equal when it is zero, the first is the lesser when it is negative and the greater when it is positive. So the numbers are equal when that difference vanishes in the rounding, which tolerates a small difference in the digits beyond the precision, counted from the higher first digit of the two, and the values need not be exactly equal. The difference is taken as the rule for - computes it and its range is not checked, so a comparison raises no SYNTAX 42.901 or SYNTAX 42.902 and an overflow of the difference does not change the answer. 573.body:
[class.circularqueue.queue] queue(item, option) adds the item at the tail and push(item, option) at the head. When the queue already holds as many items as its size, the item at the opposite end is taken out first: queue takes out the item at the head and answers it, push takes out the item at the tail and answers it; when nothing was taken out, both answer .nil. A queue of size 0 holds nothing. The option is Normal by default; one whose first character is U, in either case, is Unique: before the item is added, every item that is equal to it by the strict == is taken out, and when that made room nothing else is. Any other option, a null string and one that begins with a blank included, is Normal, and option is read as the option rule says. [class.circularqueue.section] section(start, count) answers a new circular queue of the same class as the receiver, made by new with the size count, whose items are read from the receiver by position: the first at index start, the next ones at the indexes after it, wrapping from the size to the index 1, so that a section that runs past the tail goes on at the head. A position that holds no item gives .nil. count is at most the size of the receiver, and is the size of the receiver when it is omitted or larger; the new queue holds count items, .nil ones included. When start is above the size, the first entry is what [] answers for start, which is .nil, and the positions after it are 1, 2 and so on. The start is read as the Queue index rule says; count must be a whole number from 0 up, or SYNTAX 93.906 is raised, .nil raising SYNTAX 97.1. No start raises SYNTAX 93.901, and a third argument SYNTAX 93.902. The arguments are counted first. count is then checked with the messages and conditions of the new rule , after which its string value is read once more; that second value is the count, and one below 0 or not a whole number raises SYNTAX 93.906, so a count whose string value is -1 is refused even when its < answers 0. start is read last. The answer is not the receiver, and the receiver is not changed. q = .circularqueue~of('a', 'b', 'c', 'd')

[class.circularqueue.set] union, intersection and xor answer a new circular queue of the same class as the receiver, and the receiver is not changed. union(other) holds the items of the receiver followed by every item of the argument, so an item that both have is there twice; the size of the answer is the size of the receiver, or, when the receiver's number of items plus the argument's is greater, that number. intersection(other) holds the items of the argument in its order that the receiver has, each counting as often as the receiver has it, as the OrderedCollection rule says, and has the size of the receiver. xor(other) holds what the OrderedCollection rule says of the items that only one of the two has, receiver items first, and has the size of the receiver, or, when it holds more items, their number. difference, subset, disjoint, equivalent and appendAll are those of the mixins; difference answers a circular queue of the receiver's class and size, and appendAll answers the receiver and adds through append, so that the items that do not fit push the first ones out. An index is a string compared in full and by its exact characters, so ab and AB are two indexes, and an item is any object. A directory can also hold methods: a method that setMethod associates with a name runs when the name is read, and so makes a computed entry; a method named UNKNOWN answers every read of a name that has no entry. The class inherits MapCollection , and through it Collection ; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. Properties is its subclass, and StringTable is a sibling that has the same entry methods without the methods of a directory. A directory also gives its entries a second face: a message for which the method search finds no method, such as d~name, reaches the unknown method of the class, which reads or sets the entry of that name in upper case ( the unknown rule ). 6.body: Two documents are cited by section and are not copied: the ooRexx reference manual and the ANSI Rexx standard (X3.274-1996, cited from its final public draft, so the notes call it the ANSI draft). A page's front matter names the sections that describe its element. Both are informative: the rules are derived from them and from reasoning about the semantics, and where the two disagree the rule follows ooRexx and a note says how ANSI differs. Where both are silent, a rule matches ooRexx, and a note says so. The wording of this book is its own.
6.title: Sources

60.body: ANSI: 7.4, 7.4.1, 7.4.9; rexxref: General Concepts > Terms, Expressions, and Operators This chapter specifies how an expression is read and evaluated. An expression is one term, or several terms joined by operators, and it has one value when it has been evaluated. A term is a piece of the program that has a value of its own: a string, a symbol, a function call, a message, a parenthesized expression. The chapter covers what the terms are and how variables give a symbol its value, and then how operators combine terms. This page holds the rules that every operator shares: the precedence of the operators and the order in which an expression is evaluated. The pages of this chapter are: Terms : the kinds of term and the value of each. Variables : simple, stem and compound variables, and the value of a symbol that has none. Concatenation : the blank, the abuttal and ||. Arithmetic : + - * / % // and **. Comparison : the normal and strict comparisons. Logical : & | && and prefix \. Messages : the message operators ~ and ~~, and the rule that every operator is a message. The characters of the operators and the way a program is cut into tokens are in the lexical chapter , and the numbers that arithmetic works on are in the numbers chapter .
60.title: Expressions

The arithmetic, concatenation, comparison and logical operators on strings answer strings, so the value of such an expression is a string, written as the number rules say when the operator is an arithmetic one. From the tightest to the loosest they are: the message operators ~ and ~~ with the subscript [ ]; the prefix operators +, - and \; the power **; the multiplicative operators *, /, % and //; the additive operators + and - between two terms; the concatenation operators, which are the blank, the abuttal and ||; the comparison operators, normal and strict ones together on one level; &; and, loosest, | and &&. An operator takes as its operands the nearest terms to its sides that no tighter operator has claimed. say (2 + 3 * 4) (2 * 3 ** 2) (1 + 1~length)

So -2**2 is (-2)**2, which is 4, and a prefix operator before a comparison applies to the left operand alone. The right operand of an infix operator may itself start with a prefix operator, as in 2 ** -1, and prefix operators may follow one another, as in - - 1. say (-2 ** 2) (- 5 ** 2) (2 ** -1) (- - 1)

64.body:
ANSI: 7.4.1, 7.4.9; rexxref: General Concepts > Terms, Expressions, and Operators > Terms and Expressions A term is the unit that an operator works on: a piece of a program that has a value without an operator being applied. A program writes a term as a string, a symbol, a function call, a message, an expression in parentheses or a list in parentheses. The kind is set by the first token of the term and by the token after it, and not by the value. This page says what each kind of term looks like and what its value is, and leaves the way that terms are combined to the overview . [expr.terms.kinds] A term is one of these: a literal string , a symbol , a function call , a message term , an expression in parentheses , an array term or a variable reference term. ANSI: 7.3, 7.3.1; rexxref: General Concepts > Terms, Expressions, and Operators > Terms and Expressions A variable is a named place that holds a string, or any other object. A program names it with a variable symbol, of which the lexical rules distinguish three forms: the simple symbol, the stem symbol and the compound symbol. A simple symbol and a stem symbol name one variable each, and a compound symbol names the variable whose name the program works out when the symbol is evaluated. This page gives the value of each form, with the value of one that nothing has been assigned to, and the way a compound symbol becomes a name. [expr.variables.value] A variable symbol has the value that the variable was last assigned. A simple or compound variable that has never been assigned, or that has been dropped, is unset, and the value of its symbol is the name of the symbol, in upper case, or for a compound symbol its derived name . The SYMBOL function tells the two states apart: it answers VAR for a variable that has a value and LIT for one that has none. Reading an unset variable is what the NOVALUE condition reports when it is enabled, and the conditions chapter specifies it. A stem symbol is never unset in this sense, because its value is a Stem in every state, as the stem rule says: reading one that was never assigned raises no NOVALUE, and what SYMBOL answers for a stem symbol, which depends on whether it has been referred to, is specified with the function . say foo symbol('foo')

Assigning a value that is not a Stem to a stem symbol makes a new Stem with that value as its default, which discards the values that the compound variables of the stem had until then and sets their default . Assigning a Stem to a variable keeps that object, so a stem symbol assigned to another stem symbol shares the compound variables of one Stem with it, and the string value of a shared Stem is the name it was created with. The stem is used as written. The tail is split at its periods into components, and each component that is a symbol starting with a letter, !, ? or _ is replaced by the value of the variable of that name, or by its own name in upper case when that variable is unset. [class.relation.operand] union, difference, intersection, xor and subset take exactly one argument, the other collection: none, or an omitted one, raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second raises SYNTAX 93.902. The argument is read as a list of entries as the operand rule says: what its isA answers decides whether it is sent allItems, supplier or makeArray, and an answer that is neither 0 nor 1 raises SYNTAX 34.1. All five send supplier to a map, difference and subset included, and none of them sends items to the argument; in both the five differ from the operations of Collection . An element of a list is an index and an item at once, and an entry of a map is its own index with its own item. The answers of allItems and makeArray are read as the list rule says, an instance of a subclass of List included ( Deviation 118 ); one with no makeArray method raises SYNTAX 98.913. A supplier is sent available, and while that answers true index and item, then next: union, difference and subset send item before index, intersection and xor index before item. An argument that isA does not report as ordered or as a map and that has no makeArray method, .nil included, raises SYNTAX 93.948, and so does a supplier that is .nil. The five work on the object that copy of the receiver answers, and intersection and xor also on the one that new of its class answers ( their rule ), so the answers are instances of the class of the receiver unless a subclass overrides those; any object that understands the messages sent to it will do. A message that the copy, the new object or the supplier does not understand raises SYNTAX 93.948 when it is sent; an UNKNOWN method counts as understanding it. The entries are compared as pairs: an index is equal by the index rule and an item by ==. In the example each kind of argument records the message it is sent, then a map argument records the order of the messages to its supplier, and the last cases show errors. .local~log = .array~new

Members are found as a relation finds its indexes, by the hashCode and the == that they answer to; the methods that take an item compare by == as well. The class inherits MapCollection and SetCollection , and through them Collection ; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. Like Set it declares its own set operations, which read their argument as a list of members and not as a list of entries, and which count how often a member occurs. A bag has no unknown method: a message that the method search does not resolve raises NOMETHOD , as the error rule of the chapter says. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. [class.bag.members] A member is any object, .nil and the null string included, and the bag stores every object that was put, whether or not an equal one is there. A member is found by the lookup : hashCode answers the same string for the argument and for the stored object, and ==, sent to the argument with the stored object as argument, answers true. For an object that declares neither method that is the same object, and an Array is its own member only. A string is a member of its characters, compared by the strict comparison : case counts, a leading or trailing blank counts, and 5 and 5.0 are two members. A class that declares == has to declare hashCode so that equal objects hash alike, as the hash code rule says. A method that takes an index considers every member that is equal to the argument, and the bag does not merge them: the objects stay distinct, and allItems answers each of them. b = .bag~new

ANSI: 7.4.6; rexxref: General Concepts > Terms, Expressions, and Operators > String Concatenation Concatenation joins two values into one string. Rexx has three forms of it, which differ in what they put between the two values: the blank operator puts one blank, and the abuttal and the operator || put nothing. The blank is the form a program uses without noticing, as when it writes say 'total:' x. This page says when two terms are concatenated, what the joined string holds, and how concatenation ranks among the other operators. [expr.concatenation.blank] Two terms that are separated by one or more blanks or tabs, with no operator between them, are concatenated with exactly one blank in the result. The blanks of the program are not kept, and a tab becomes a blank, but the blanks that belong to the values are: a value that ends in a blank or begins with one keeps it. The null string takes part like any other value, so a blank remains on its side of the result. A blank next to an operator is no concatenation, as the blank rule says. say 'a' 'b'	'c'
say 'a ' 'b' ' c'
say '[' '' 'a' '' ']' a b c
a b c
[ a ] [expr.concatenation.abuttal] Two terms with nothing between them, or with only a comment between them, are concatenated without a blank. This is the abuttal. It joins a string and a symbol, as in x'%', two parenthesized terms, and the value of a function call with the term after it. A comment is no blank , so it does not stop the abuttal. x = 5
say x'%' x'<' (x)(x) x/**/x
say abs(-2)abs(-3) (1 + 2)(3)
say x /**/ x 5% 5< 55 55
23 33
5 5 [expr.concatenation.operator] The operator || concatenates the two terms with no blank, and blanks around it are dropped. A line end ends the clause even after the operator, so a || at the end of a line without a continuation leaves it without a right operand and raises SYNTAX 35.1. The second example shows that in a program file, which exits with 256 minus the error number , and the third shows it in the text of an INTERPRET instruction , where the end of the text ends the clause and the error is an ordinary condition. say 'a' || 'b' 'c'||'d'
say 'a' ||, 'b' ab cd
ab say 'before'
say 'a' || signal on syntax name e
interpret "say 'a' ||"
e: say condition('o')~code 35.1 [expr.concatenation.precedence] The three forms are on one level of precedence , below the arithmetic operators and above the comparisons. The operands of an arithmetic operator are therefore evaluated before the result is joined to a neighbour, and the concatenations of a run are applied from left to right. say 1+2 3*4
say 1 + 1 || 2 * 3
say (1 || 2 = 12) (1 2 = '1 2') 3 12
26
1 1 [expr.concatenation.operands] The operands are joined as they are, so a number is not put into its normal form, and 1.50 || 2.0 is 1.502.0. An operand that is an object other than a string is replaced by a string first, on either side of the operator, by the conversion rule . The result is a String also when an operand is an instance of a subclass of String, and that operand contributes its own characters. say 1.50 || 2.0 007 || 7

Members are found as a table finds its indexes, by the hashCode and the == that they answer to. The class inherits MapCollection and SetCollection , and through them Collection ; the hierarchy rule lists what it inherits. Unlike a table it declares its own set operations, which read their argument as a list of members and not as a list of entries. A set has no unknown method: a message that the method search does not resolve raises NOMETHOD , as the error rule of the chapter says. Examples that show an error use a small routine try, as the builtin pages do. Where several members qualify for a method that answers one, which one it answers is not specified, and the examples then hold one member or sort the answers ( the hash order rule ).

67.body: ANSI: 7.4.2, 7.4.3, 7.4.4, 7.4.5; rexxref: General Concepts > Terms, Expressions, and Operators > Operators > Arithmetic The arithmetic operators are + - * / % // and **, with + and - also usable in front of one term. This page describes them as part of an expression: which operands they take, in what order the operands are evaluated and checked, and which errors an operand that is not a number causes. What the operators compute, to how many digits and with which rounding, is in the arithmetic page of the numbers chapter , and this page links its rules rather than stating them again. Where an operator ranks among the others is in the precedence rule .

[class.set.members] A member is any object, .nil and the null string included, and the set stores the object that was put. A member is found by the lookup : hashCode answers the same string for the argument and for the stored object, and ==, sent to the argument with the stored object as argument, answers true. For an object that declares neither method that is the same object, and an Array is its own member only. A string is a member of its characters, compared by the strict comparison : case counts, a leading or trailing blank counts, and 5 and 5.0 are two members. A class that declares == has to declare hashCode so that equal objects hash alike, as the hash code rule says. When put finds an equal member, the set keeps the object it has as the index of the entry, and takes the new object as its item: at and allItems then answer the new object, and allIndexes and makeArray the old one. s = .set~new

An entry is a tail, a string, and the item stored at it; the stem also has a default, the value that every tail without an item has, and a name, which is the text that stands for the stem when it has no default. 97.1 [class.datetime.value] An instance holds a date and a time of day as the fields year (1 to 9999), month, day, hours, minutes, seconds and microseconds (0 to 999999), and an offset from UTC. The fields are the time as the people in that zone read it. No method changes an instance: every method that answers a different moment answers a new instance. [class.datetime.offset] The offset of an instance is the distance of its zone east of UTC, in whole minutes from -900 to 900. The method offset answers it as a TimeSpan , so an instance in a zone 5 hours and 30 minutes east of UTC answers 05:30:00.000000 and one in a zone 90 minutes west answers -01:30:00.000000. Every place that takes an offset takes the same two forms: a number of whole minutes in that range, or a TimeSpan that is a whole number of minutes in that range. The argument is sent isA with the class TimeSpan; only a TimeSpan is then sent totalMicroseconds and is converted to minutes, and any other value is read as a number ( the argument rule ) and sent the messages that the sends rule lists. A value outside the range, a number that is not whole as the form rule and the digits rule read it ( Deviation 130 ), such as 1.5, and a span that is not whole minutes raise SYNTAX 88.907 for new and, with a number or a span, for toTimezone, and SYNTAX 88.918 for today and for the from methods that read an offset, which are all but fromWeekNumberDate (it ignores the offset ) and fromUtcIsoDate (it has none); a value that is no number at all gets the same code from new, today and those from methods, and what toTimezone raises for it is in the zone rule . d = .datetime~new(2017, 6, 30, 5, 6, 7, 8, 330)

700.body:
[class.datetime.new] new makes an instance and sends init to it with the arguments it received ( the new rule ); the init of DateTime takes up to eight arguments, and the number of them that are given, counted as the count rule says, picks the form. With no argument the moment is that of the host's clock, whose value is not specified. With one argument or two, the first is the number of microseconds from 00:00:00.000000 on 1 January 0001 to the moment, a whole number from 0 to 315537897599999999, and the second, if present, is the offset. With three arguments or four they are year, month and day, the time of day is 00:00:00.000000, and the fourth, if present, is the offset: the four-argument form is not the three-argument form with an hour. With from five to eight arguments they are year, month, day, hours and minutes, then seconds, microseconds and the offset, where an omitted one of these three is 0 (the offset: the default ). Without an offset argument the instance has the default offset. An argument that the form needs and that is omitted raises SYNTAX 93.903; more than eight arguments raise SYNTAX 93.902. say .datetime~new(2017, 6, 30, 5, 6, 7, 8, 0)

The other five take the forms dd/mm/yy, d mon yyyy (the day has one or two digits, the month is the three letters of its name with a capital first letter), yy/mm/dd, yyyymmdd and mm/dd/yy. A two-digit year is the one that the century rule of DATE gives, so it depends on the current year. Each of the other five takes the field separator as its optional second argument, in place of the default that the output separator of the option has: the null string or one character that is no letter and no digit. 701.title: Class methods

702.body:
[class.datetime.fields] year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds and microseconds answer the field of that name as a whole number without leading zeros, so the microseconds of 10:00:00.012345 are 12345. dayMinutes, daySeconds and dayMicroseconds answer how many whole minutes, whole seconds and microseconds the time of day is past 00:00:00.000000. The offset plays no part in any of them. Each method takes no argument: one raises SYNTAX 93.902. d = .datetime~new(2016, 2, 29, 9, 8, 7, 12345, 120)
say d~year d~month d~day d~hours d~minutes d~seconds d~microseconds
say d~dayMinutes d~daySeconds d~dayMicroseconds
say .datetime~minDate~dayMicroseconds .datetime~maxDate~dayMicroseconds
say d~toUtcTime~hours d~toTimezone(-600)~day
signal on syntax name bad
say d~year(1)
bad: say condition('o')~code 2016 2 29 9 8 7 12345
548 32887 32887012345
0 86399999999
7 28
93.902 [class.datetime.calendar] weekDay answers the day of the week from 1 for Monday to 7 for Sunday, and dayName its English name; monthName answers the English name of the month. Both names begin with a capital letter. yearDay answers the number of the day in its year, from 1, baseDate the number of days from 1 January 0001 (day 0) to the day, and isLeapYear answers 1 when the year is divisible by 4 and not by 100, or is divisible by 400, and 0 otherwise. daysInMonth answers the length of the month in days and daysInYear the length of the year, 365 or 366. They agree with the options B and D of DATE and with the names of M and W. Each takes no argument. d = .datetime~new(2017, 6, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0)
say d~weekDay d~dayName d~monthName d~yearDay d~baseDate
say .datetime~new(1, 1, 1)~dayName .datetime~new(9999, 12, 31)~dayName

703.title: Writing a moment

704.body:
[class.datetime.add] Each of addYears, addWeeks, addDays, addHours, addMinutes, addSeconds and addMicroseconds answers a new instance, of the class of the receiver, that is the receiver moved by its argument; the receiver is not changed, and the offset is kept. addYears takes a whole number of years, read as the form rule and the digits rule say ( Deviation 130 ), and keeps month, day and time of day, except that 29 February moves to 28 February when the year it lands in is no leap year; a year past the range raises SYNTAX 88.907, and a number of years of 1000000000 or more in magnitude, or a value such as 1.5 or x, raises SYNTAX 88.903. The other six take a number, a negative one moves back, and a fraction is allowed: addDays(1.5) is a day and twelve hours. The new moment is the receiver's count of microseconds plus the amount in microseconds, rounded to 18 significant digits; a part of a microsecond that is left is dropped toward the earlier moment. So addMicroseconds of 1.5 adds 1 and of -1.5 subtracts 2, and on a date of 2016, whose count has 17 digits, of 0.96 adds 1 and of -0.04 adds nothing. A value that is no number raises SYNTAX 88.902; a moment outside the range of the class raises SYNTAX 40.19. A missing argument raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second argument SYNTAX 93.902. d = .datetime~new(2016, 2, 29, 9, 8, 7, 12345, 120)

say e~addMicroseconds(1.5)~microseconds e~addMicroseconds(-1.5)~microseconds, e~addMicroseconds(-0.5)~microseconds

704.title: Arithmetic

705.body:
[class.datetime.compare] compareTo takes one argument and answers -1 when the receiver is the earlier instant, 0 for the same instant and 1 when it is the later, comparing the instants in UTC, so that two instances with different fields and different offsets can be equal. The argument is sent isA with DateTime, and a DateTime is then sent utcDate; an argument that is no DateTime raises SYNTAX 88.914 as soon as isA has answered ( Deviation 126 ), and the comparison operators raise it for such an argument too, except that an operator whose argument is .nil does as the .nil rule says, without compareTo. The comparison operators =, ==, <, <=, >, >=, <>, ><, \=, \==, <<, <<=, >>, >>= and \<, \>, \<<, \>> are those of Orderable , which answer from compareTo of the receiver, strict and non-strict ones alike: == is as =. The text of the instances plays no part. d = .datetime~new(2016, 2, 29, 9, 8, 7, 12345, 120)
z = .datetime~new(2016, 3, 1, 10, 0, 0, 0, 0)
q = .datetime~new(2016, 2, 29, 7, 8, 7, 12345, 0)
say d~compareTo(z) z~compareTo(d) d~compareTo(q) d~compareTo(d~copy)
say (d < z) (d > z) (d = q) (d == q) (d \= q) (d <> q) (d <= q) (d >= q)
say (d << z) (d >> z) (d <<= q) (d >>= z) (d \== q) (d >< q)
say (d~string == q~string) (d = q)
say (d \< z) (d \> z) (d \<< z) (d \>> z)
call try 'd~compareTo'
call try 'd~compareTo(z, 1)'
exit

706.body:
[class.datetime.zone] toLocalTime, toUtcTime and toTimezone answer a new instance, of the class of the receiver, for the same instant with the fields of another zone: the fields move by the difference of the offsets. toLocalTime takes the default offset ( the default ), toUtcTime the offset 0, and toTimezone the offset that its argument gives ( the offset rule ), 0 when it has no argument. The instant does not change, so utcDate and the comparisons see the same moment. When the new fields fall outside the range of the class the methods raise SYNTAX 40.19. toLocalTime and toUtcTime take no argument, and toTimezone at most one. The argument of toTimezone that is not a TimeSpan is read as a number of minutes by multiplying it with 60000000 with *, so a string that is no number raises SYNTAX 41.1 and .nil, which has no *, SYNTAX 97.1; a number that is not a whole number of minutes in the range raises SYNTAX 88.907. d = .datetime~new(2016, 2, 29, 9, 8, 7, 12345, 120)

say d~toTimezone
say d~toTimezone(-90)~utcIsoDate d~toTimezone(90)~utcIsoDate
say d~toTimezone(120)~utcIsoDate d~toTimezone(900)~utcIsoDate
say d~toTimezone(.timespan~fromHours(-5))~utcIsoDate, d~toTimezone(.timespan~fromMinutes(-61))~utcIsoDate
say (d~toTimezone(-77) == d), (d~toTimezone(-77)~utcDate == d~utcDate) d~toTimezone(-77)~timeOfDay
l = d~toLocalTime
say (l == d) (l~offset == .datetime~new~offset) (l~utcDate == d~utcDate)
say d~toTimezone(60)~class~id d~toTimezone(60)~toUtcTime~isoDate
say .datetime~minDate~toTimezone(60) .datetime~maxDate~toTimezone(-60)
call try 'd~toTimezone(901)'
call try 'd~toTimezone(1.5)'
call try 'd~toTimezone(.timespan~fromSeconds(90))'

call try '.datetime~maxDate~toTimezone(60)'
call try '.datetime~minDate~toUtcTime'
call try 'd~toUtcTime(1)'
call try 'd~toTimezone(1, 2)'
exit

[class.datetime.sends.new] The class methods send new to the receiver, so a class that overrides its new sees them, and new sends init to the new instance with the arguments it got ( the new rule ); the init of DateTime sends nothing. minDate sends new with the four arguments 1, 1, 1 and 0, and maxDate with the eight arguments 9999, 12, 31, 23, 59, 59, 999999 and 0. today and every from method other than fromOrdinalDate and fromWeekNumberDate send new with two arguments: the number of microseconds from the start of 0001 to the moment, and the offset argument exactly as the caller gave it (a TimeSpan is not converted), or, without one, the default offset in minutes; fromUtcIsoDate, which has no offset argument, sends the offset of its string in minutes. fromOrdinalDate sends nothing to the receiver and answers a plain DateTime, whatever the receiver is. fromWeekNumberDate sends new with the three arguments year, 1 and 4, then sends that instance weeksInYear (which sends year), weekDay and addDays, and the answer of addDays is the result. The first example prints, for each call, the messages sent in order, with the number of arguments after NEW and INIT. The second example prints the second argument that init gets: a TimeSpan or a string that the caller gave arrives as it is, the offset of the string of fromUtcIsoDate as a number of minutes (150 for +02:30), and, without an offset argument, the default offset in minutes. An argument that is read as a number is sent more messages than the one that reads its string value ( the argument rule ). A year, month, day, hours, minutes, seconds or microseconds argument of new is sent >= and <= with the limits of its range and then right with the width of its field, 4 for the year, 6 for the microseconds and 2 for the others. An offset that is not a TimeSpan, the argument of new, today or a from method other than fromWeekNumberDate, is sent isA, read for its string value, and sent >= with -900, <= with 900 and * with 60000000. An amount of addDays, addHours, addMinutes, addSeconds and addWeeks is sent *, and addYears and addMicroseconds read the string value of their amount twice. A number argument of toTimezone is sent isA and *, then read for its string value and sent >= and <=; the new that toTimezone sends gets the argument itself, which is then handled as the offset of new is. A count of new and the argument of fromTicks and fromBaseDate are read for their string value only. The third example passes an object whose makeString answers a number and whose unknown sends every other message to that number, and prints the messages the object got. names = 'WEEKSINYEAR YEAR WEEKDAY ADDDAYS OFFSET'

Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TimeSpan Class > totalMinutes; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TimeSpan Class > totalSeconds Deviations: D109, D126, D127, D130, D131, D132, D133 A TimeSpan is a length of time: a signed count of microseconds, at most 3652058 days and 23:59:59.999999 either way, read as days, hours, minutes, seconds and microseconds. It is the difference of two DateTime moments and what is added to one ( the + rule ), and it can stand for the offset of a time zone ( the offset rule ). Its methods answer the parts and the totals of the span, write it as text, make another span from it by addition, multiplication and division, and compare it with another. The class inherits Comparable and Orderable, which give it the comparison operators on top of its own compareTo. Every method that answers another span answers a new instance; only init, sent again, changes one ( the new rule ). The examples build their spans from fixed values.

[class.timespan.new] new makes an instance and sends init to it with the arguments it received ( the new rule ); the init of TimeSpan takes from one argument to five, and the number of them that are given, counted as the count rule says, picks the form. With one argument it is the number of microseconds of the span, a whole number as the form rule and the digits rule read it ( Deviation 130 ), positive or negative. With two arguments they are hours and minutes, with three hours, minutes and seconds, with four days, hours, minutes and seconds, and with five days, hours, minutes, seconds and microseconds; a part that the form does not name is 0. The parts of the multi-part forms are never negative: a span below zero is made by the one-argument form or by negating a span. No argument raises SYNTAX 93.901, and more than five SYNTAX 93.902. [class.timespan.parts] days, hours, minutes, seconds and microseconds take no argument and answer the parts of the span as whole numbers that are never negative: they describe its size, not its sign. hours is from 0 to 23, minutes and seconds from 0 to 59, microseconds from 0 to 999999, and days the whole days. A span of 90 seconds has 0 days, 0 hours, 1 minute and 30 seconds, and the span of -90 seconds has the same parts. sign answers -1, 0 or 1 as the span is below, at or above zero. duration answers a new span that is not below zero and has the size of the receiver; this is stated for a span shorter than 1000 seconds, one whose count has at most nine digits, and what duration answers for a longer one is not stated here. It makes its answer by sending new to the class of the receiver ( the sends rule ). Any argument raises SYNTAX 93.902 for each of these methods. t = .timespan~new(3, 7, 41, 52, 250)
n = .timespan~new('-286912000250')
z = .timespan~new(0)
do s over .array~of(t, n, z) say s~days s~hours s~minutes s~seconds s~microseconds '|' s~sign
end

[class.timespan.add] Each of addWeeks, addDays, addHours, addMinutes, addSeconds and addMicroseconds takes one number and answers a new span, of the class of the receiver, that is the receiver lengthened by that many weeks, days, hours, minutes, seconds or microseconds, and shortened by a negative number; the receiver is not changed. A fraction is allowed: addDays(1.5) is a day and twelve hours. The new count of microseconds is the receiver's count plus the amount in microseconds, the sum rounded to 18 significant digits, and a part of a microsecond that is left is dropped toward zero, whatever the sign of the sum (a span of -5 microseconds that is given 0.5 microseconds becomes -4, and one of 5 given -5.5 becomes 0). A value that is no number raises SYNTAX 88.902, a sum outside the range of the value rule raises SYNTAX 40.19, and an amount of 1000000000000000000 microseconds or more in size raises SYNTAX 88.903. A missing argument raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second SYNTAX 93.902. t = .timespan~new(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)

714.body:
[class.timespan.compare] compareTo takes one argument and answers -1 when the receiver is the shorter (the lesser) of the two spans, 0 for two spans of the same count and 1 when it is the longer, comparing the signed counts, so that a negative span is less than any that is not. The argument is sent isA with TimeSpan, and a TimeSpan is then sent totalMicroseconds; the receiver is sent nothing. An argument that is no TimeSpan raises SYNTAX 88.914 as soon as isA has answered ( Deviation 126 ), and the comparison operators raise it for such an argument too, .nil excepted (see below). The comparison operators =, ==, <, <=, >, >=, <>, ><, \=, \==, <<, <<=, >>, >>=, \<, \>, \<< and \>> are those of Orderable , which answer from compareTo of the receiver, strict and non-strict ones alike: == is as =, and two spans of the same count are equal however they were made. The text of the instances plays no part. A missing argument raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a second one SYNTAX 93.902; an operator whose argument is .nil does as the .nil rule of Orderable says, and compareTo(.nil) raises SYNTAX 88.914. The sort methods order spans by this method ( the sort rule ). a = .timespan~new(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
b = .timespan~fromMicroseconds(a~totalMicroseconds)
c = .timespan~new(1, 2, 3, 4, 6)

z = .timespan~new(0)
say a~compareTo(c) c~compareTo(a) a~compareTo(b) a~compareTo(a)
say n~compareTo(z) z~compareTo(n) n~compareTo(.timespan~new('-6'))
say (a = b) (a == b) (a \= b) (a < c) (a > c) (a <= b) (a >= c) (a <> c)
say (a >< b) (a << c) (a >> c) (a <<= b) (a >>= c) (a \== c)
say (a \< c) (a \> c) (a \<< b) (a \>> b)
say (n < z) (n << z) (z > n) (n = z) (z = .timespan~fromMicroseconds(0))
say (a = .nil) (a \= .nil) (a == .nil) (a <> .nil)
l = .array~of(c, a, z, n, .timespan~fromDays(1))
say show(l~copy~~sort)
say show(l~copy~~sortWith(.descendingComparator~new))
say show(l~copy~~sortWith(.comparator~new))

call try 'a~compareTo(b, c)'

call try 'a \>> .nil'

715.body:
[class.timespan.sends.new] The class methods fromDays, fromHours, fromMinutes, fromSeconds, fromMicroseconds, fromNormalTime, fromCivilTime and fromLongTime send new to the receiver with one argument, the count of microseconds, so that a class that overrides its new sees them, and new sends init to the new instance with the arguments it got ( the new rule ); the init of TimeSpan sends nothing to the instance. fromStringFormat sends nothing to the receiver and answers a plain TimeSpan. The count is checked by init ( the checks of new ), so a count outside the range raises its error after new and init were sent. The first example prints, for each call, the messages sent in order, with the number of arguments after NEW and INIT. The numbers that a program passes are read for their string value, and are sent further messages ( the argument rule ). The one-argument form of new and fromMicroseconds read the string value of their argument three times and twice. In the other forms of new each argument is read, in the order of the arguments, and sent >= with 0 and, but for the days, <= with the greatest value of its range (23, 59, 59 and 999999), after which the days are sent * with 24, the minutes * with 60 and, in the form of two or three arguments, the hours * with 3600; the hours of the forms with days, the seconds and the microseconds are read for their string value once more. A value that is not a whole number, or a value for the days with more than nine digits, is refused after it is read and before >= is sent; a count of the one-argument form is refused after its first reading when it is no whole number or 1000000000000000000 or more in size, and after its second when it is outside the range. fromDays, fromHours, fromMinutes and fromSeconds read their argument and send it * with 24, 3600, 60 and 1000000. fromNormalTime, fromCivilTime and fromLongTime read the string once, and fromStringFormat once, and twice when it is refused. The second example passes objects whose makeString answers a number, and whose unknown sends every other message to that number, and prints the messages each object got. call probe 'new', '.spy~new(1, 2, 3)'

call probe 'fromDays x', '.spy~fromDays("x")'
exit

717.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Comparable Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Comparable Class > compareTo Comparable is a mixin class that stands for the objects that can be put in order. It holds one method, compareTo, which compares the receiver with another object and answers a number whose sign tells which one is the greater. A class that inherits it overrides compareTo with its own ordering; what the class holds itself is only a default that orders objects by their identity, which no program should rely on. The comparison operators are not part of it: Orderable has them. The class is the base of the ordering that sort uses and that the default comparator sends.
717.title: Comparable

The default compareTo sends identityHash to the receiver and then to the argument, and answers -1, 0 or 1 as the number that the first answered is less than, equal to or greater than the one that the second answered, compared to 18 significant digits whatever NUMERIC DIGITS the program has set. 719.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Orderable Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Orderable Class > compareTo; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Orderable Class > Comparison Methods Orderable is a mixin class that gives a class the eighteen comparison operators as methods, all of them answered from one method, compareTo. A class that inherits it and overrides compareTo with its own ordering can then be written on both sides of <, =, >>= and the rest, and sorted by sort . DateTime, TimeSpan and File are such classes; the comparison rule of DateTime , the one of TimeSpan and the one of File say what their compareTo answers, and that it raises SYNTAX 88.914 for an argument of another class ( Deviation 126 ), which the operators then raise too, but for a .nil argument ( the .nil rule ). The page of Comparable describes the class that holds the compareTo alone.
719.title: Orderable

72.body: ANSI: 7.4.7; rexxref: General Concepts > Terms, Expressions, and Operators > Operators > Comparison Deviations: D122 A comparison operator compares the values of two terms and answers 1 when the relation holds and 0 when it does not. Rexx has two families of them: the normal comparisons, which compare numbers as numbers and anything else as text with some leniency about blanks, and the strict comparisons, which always compare the characters exactly. This page lists the operators, gives the rules for comparing text in both families, and ties them to the rules for numbers. How two numbers compare, including NUMERIC FUZZ, is in the numeric comparison page .
72.title: Comparison operators

720.title: The class

721.body:
[class.orderable.compare] Each of the eighteen comparison methods takes one argument, sends compareTo to the receiver with that argument, and answers what the answer of compareTo answers to a comparison message that has the number 0 as its argument. That message is = for = and ==, < for < and <<, > for > and >>, <= for <= and <<=, >= for >= and >>=, and \= for \= and \==. So a strict operator is not strict here: the answer of compareTo is compared as the non-strict operator compares, and an answer of 1 (with blanks) is greater than 0 for >> as for >, one of 00 is equal to 0 for ==. An answer that is no number is compared as a string with 0, so that abc is greater and the empty string is less. What a method answers is whatever the sent message answers; an answer of compareTo that does not understand the message raises SYNTAX 97.1, as .nil does for every message here but = and \=. Four methods hand the work to another method of the receiver: \<, \>, \<< and \>> send >=, <=, >>= and <<= with their argument and answer what it answers, and <> and >< send \= the same way. So a class that overrides >= changes \< as well. The example prints, for answers of compareTo of -1, 0, 5, abc, the empty string, 1, 00 and .nil, what the eighteen methods answer, in the order of the list in the creation rule with compareTo left out. call show '-1', '-1'
call show '0', '0'

call show 'abc', 'abc'

call show '00', '00'
call show '.nil', .nil
exit
