It has one method, compare, which takes two objects and answers a number: negative when the first is to come before the second, 0 when the order does not tell them apart, and positive when the first is to come after. The sorting methods that take a comparator, such as sortWith , send it compare and need nothing else of it, so any object with such a method will do. This page describes Comparator and the seven classes below it: CaselessComparator, ColumnComparator, CaselessColumnComparator, DescendingComparator, CaselessDescendingComparator, InvertingComparator and NumericComparator. Each is made by new like any class; the compare of each hands the two objects to a method of the first or to a comparator that the instance holds, and says what it answers, so what a comparator answers for an object that is not a string depends on that object's own methods.

[class.comparators.creation] Comparator is a mixin class ( the mixin rule ) whose only superclass is Object; each of the other seven classes is a mixin class whose only superclass is Comparator. Every one of the eight defines its own compare. ColumnComparator, CaselessColumnComparator, InvertingComparator and NumericComparator define init as well; the other four have the init of Object and take no argument in new, so that an argument raises SYNTAX 93.902 ( the new rule ). [class.comparators.sends] Each compare sends the messages below, in this order, and no other but those that NumericComparator sends in reading the difference: nothing is sent to the second argument or to the comparators themselves, nothing is sent to the first argument but what is listed, and no argument is asked isA. Comparator sends compareTo to the first argument with one argument, the second. CaselessComparator sends caselessCompareTo the same way. ColumnComparator sends compareTo, and CaselessColumnComparator caselessCompareTo, with three arguments: the second argument, start and length. DescendingComparator sends compareTo with one argument and then the prefix -, which is the message - with no argument, to the answer, and CaselessDescendingComparator does the same with caselessCompareTo. InvertingComparator sends compare with two arguments, the arguments it got, to the comparator it holds and then the prefix - to the answer. NumericComparator sends - to the first argument with one argument, the second. The answer of the last message of each is the answer of compare, except that NumericComparator answers the sign of it, reading it as a number as the argument rule says. Where a String is a value, so that every operation answers a new string, a buffer is an object with an identity: append, insert, upper and the other changing methods alter the characters it holds and answer the buffer itself. Beside the characters a buffer has a size, the number of characters it can hold before it has to grow, which a program can read and set. A buffer is no String: it understands a part of the String methods, and for those it states only what differs, the rest being linked to the page that owns it.

737.body:
[class.mutablebuffer.sends] No method of the class sends a message to the buffer it works on: not length, string, makeString, append, insert, setText, substr, delStr, getBufferSize, setBufferSize or any other, so that a subclass that overrides one of these changes only the calls that name it. new sends init as the init rule says and copy sends nothing. What a method sends to its arguments is the reading of their string values, once for each argument that is present and in the order of the arguments, each reading followed at once by the check of that argument: the first argument that fails raises its error and the arguments after it are not read. The reading is the string-value rule 's: the argument is sent request with STRING, and the request of Object sends it makeString, so an argument that is a buffer of a subclass is sent both. append reads and appends one argument at a time. A call with too many arguments reads none. Nothing but that reading is sent to an argument. The first example prints, for each call, the messages that the subclass saw; the second passes objects that answer a string and log the reading, named by their first argument, and would log isA, string and class too; their request is that of Object. It prints the log in order, with the error that ended the call. The third example shows the request that comes before each makeString. b = .spy~new('Hello world', 40)

In ooRexx a collection after the growth reclaims the old storage, and the routine then reads garbage. A program in Rexx sees only that the characters survive the growth, which the example shows: the buffer grows several times and still holds what was appended before. b = .mutablebuffer~new('abc', 3)

754.body:
[class.file.new] new sends init ( the new rule ). init takes a path and an optional dir. The path is read as a string argument : a File given as path is read by its makeString, which is its absolute path, and an argument with no string value raises SYNTAX 88.909. A call with no argument raises SYNTAX 93.901, one with a third argument 93.902, and one with dir and no path 93.903 ( the argument rules ). The path that the instance holds is made in these steps. First path and dir each lose their trailing slashes, but a lone slash keeps its slash: a//b/// is a//b, /// is /, and the empty string stays empty; slashes anywhere else are kept. Then, when dir is omitted or .nil, the path is the path that is left. Otherwise it is dir, a slash and path, where the slash is left out when dir ends in one or path begins with one, and where both supply one a single slash stands. A dir that is the empty string counts as a dir, so a with an empty dir is /a. A dir that is a File is read as its absolute path, and any other dir as a string argument , with the error that a path has. The text of the path is kept as it was written, apart from these steps: path ( the path rule ) answers it, and a File made with a relative path or dir is relative to the current directory when it is made ( the absolute rule ). init sent to an instance again changes that instance as new made it, and answers nothing. say .file~new('a//b///')~path .file~new('///')~path '['.file~new('')~path']'

93.902 [class.file.searchpath] searchPath takes a file name and an optional path, and answers a new File, or .nil when nothing is found. The path lists directories. A string path is cut at every :, the class is sent pathSeparator, whose answer plays no part, and the empty pieces are dropped. Any other path is sent request with the argument ARRAY, and the items of the array it answers are the directories, each read as a string argument , so a .nil item raises SYNTAX 88.909; an answer that is not an array raises SYNTAX 98.913. An omitted path stands for the directories of the environment variable PATH. The directories are tried in order, and the answer is the first one that holds a file of that name, as new of File with name as path and the directory as dir would make it: the class of the answer is File, whatever the class that received searchPath. The name may name a file below the directory, as sub/c.txt. A directory that holds a directory of that name does not count, and a name that has a wildcard character * or ? finds nothing, nor does an empty name. No argument raises SYNTAX 93.901 and a third one 93.902. The name is read as a string argument , so an object whose makeString answers a name is searched for by that name and .nil raises SYNTAX 88.909. A name that begins with a slash is the absolute path of the file: the answer is a File for it when the file exists, whatever the directories. A relative directory is relative to the current directory, and the answer holds the absolute path of the file it finds, as the next rule shows. The environment symbol .CONTEXT answers the context of the code that names it. Its methods answer what the code was started with (its arguments, name and executable), what it has set (the NUMERIC settings, the status of the last command, the variables), where it is (the line, the call stack) and which run it belongs to. A program cannot make a RexxContext; it only receives them. Scheduling between activities belongs to the concurrency chapter , and the examples here use a second activity only to show that its context is another one. The condition object, TRACE and the CALL and SIGNAL instructions are specified in their own chapters, and this page links their rules.

778.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > activate (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > collector (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > collector= (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > counter (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > makeStringImpl (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > notify (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > notify= (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > option (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > option= (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > setMakeString (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > unsetMakeString (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > compareTo; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > TraceObject Class > makeString Deviations: D7, D50, D109 Every line that TRACE writes is first an object, a TraceObject: a StringTable whose entries describe the line, the code that produced it and the moment, and whose string value is the text of the line. The object, and not its text, is what the trace destination receives. The class lets a program choose how the text is formatted (the option), see every line as an object while the program runs (notify) or afterwards (collector), and replace the formatting altogether (setMakeString). The class methods live on the class object, as the attributes of a singleton do: .traceobject~option = 'S' sets one. The instance methods are makeString and compareTo; everything else an instance answers is that of StringTable and its entries. This page links the rules of the TRACE instruction for what a trace line says and for where it goes. Deviation 7 covers the order in which concurrent activities' lines arrive, and Deviation 50 a line the destination refuses. Deviation 109 applies to every argument below that is read as a string.

[class.traceobject.compareto] compareTo compares the receiver with its argument, usually another TraceObject, by their NUMBER entries and answers -1 when the receiver's is smaller, 0 when they are equal and 1 when it is larger. [class.validate.arguments] Every check takes the name of the argument as its first argument, the value as its second, and then its own further arguments. The name is only used in the error: it may be any string, a name or a text, and it is the first entry of the condition's ADDITIONAL array, whose other entries each rule below gives. The counts are fixed: two arguments for number and logical, two and an optional digits for the other number checks, three for classType and requestClassType, and four and an optional digits for the range checks. A call with fewer raises SYNTAX 93.901, one with more 93.902, and one that leaves out a required argument before the last one given 93.903; omitted arguments at the end count as not given. The ADDITIONAL array of the first holds the least number of arguments, that of the second the most, and that of the third the position of the first argument left out. The argument count is checked first, then digits, and the value last. Every value and bound is read as a string as the conversion rule says. [expr.logical.order] Both operands of &, | and && are evaluated, from left to right, before either is checked, so no operator stops early. A function call in the right operand runs even when the left operand has already decided the answer, and an error in the right operand is raised before a left operand that is not a logical value is found out. 790.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Singleton Class (Metaclass); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Singleton Class (Metaclass) > new (Class Method) Singleton is a metaclass for the programs that want a class with one instance. A class that names it in the METACLASS option of its ::CLASS directive makes one object, the first time it is sent new, and answers that same object to every later new. The class has no other use: a program that needs the object only has to ask the class for a new one. The place of Singleton in the hierarchy is stated in the hierarchy rule , and the mixin rule lists it among the mixin classes. This page specifies what it does for the classes that use it.

793.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Alarm Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Alarm Class > attachment; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Alarm Class > cancel; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Alarm Class > canceled/cancelled; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Alarm Class > init; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Alarm Class > scheduledTime; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Alarm Class > triggered Deviations: D109, D119, D135 An Alarm is a one-shot timer. It is made for a moment, a target that wants to hear of it and, if the program likes, an object to attach; when the moment comes it sends its target triggered, and when it is cancelled before that it sends the target cancel. The target has to be an implementation of AlarmNotification , which states what the target is sent and when; this page states how an alarm is made, what its time may be and what its own methods answer. By which activity the library runs the target is specified by the timer rule of the concurrency chapter, and the moment it is set for by the rules of init ( seconds , time of day , DateTime and TimeSpan ). The examples do not depend on it: they set an alarm for a time that the program does not wait for and cancel it, or they wait on a guard that the target opens, and they print nothing that varies with the clock.
793.title: Alarm

It may have private methods besides these; they are not part of this specification. Its only superclass is Object, it inherits no mixin class and is not itself a mixin class ( the hierarchy rule ). In particular an Alarm is not an implementation of AlarmNotification: it cannot be the target of another alarm. new is the one that Class supplies : it sends init the arguments of new, which the next rule states, and answers an instance of the class that received it, so a subclass of Alarm makes instances of itself. cancel and the readers canceled, cancelled and triggered are stated in the rules on cancelling . say .alarm~id .alarm~superclasses~items .alarm~superclass~id, .alarm~queryMixinClass

[class.alarm.init] new sends init(atime, target, attachment), and init sets the alarm up. It needs the first two arguments, so new with none or only the first raises SYNTAX 93.901 and an omitted first or second argument raises SYNTAX 93.903; a fourth argument raises SYNTAX 93.902. The checks of the arguments that are present are made in this order: first the target, which must be an implementation of AlarmNotification or SYNTAX 88.914 is raised, and then the time, which raises SYNTAX 93.951 for every value that the rules below do not accept, except the very large ones for which they name other errors. So a target that is no implementation is reported even when the time is wrong too, and a refused alarm is not set. attachment can be any object, and is .nil when it is omitted. The alarm is set when init ends normally. A subclass whose init does not send init to its superclass makes an alarm that is not set ( Deviation 135 ). A second init, sent after the one that new sent, is refused, as Deviation 162 says. n = .note~new

It is read as a number as the DATATYPE N rule reads it, so blanks at either end are allowed and a decimal point or an exponent is too, and it has to be zero or more: a string that is no number, the empty string and a negative number raise SYNTAX 93.951. The number is cut to the microsecond before its sign is checked, so -0.0000001 is a time of zero. A number with more than 18 significant digits is first rounded to 18, and the number is read in full whatever the NUMERIC DIGITS setting. A number of 10**12 or more, or of -10**12 or less, once it is rounded as said above, raises SYNTAX 88.903 instead, and one for which the date and time of the moment in the host's offset, as scheduledTime would answer it, would fall after 31 December 9999 at 23:59:59.999999 or before 1 January 0001 at 00:00:00.000000 ( the limits of DateTime ) raises SYNTAX 40.19, which is checked before the sign. The largest and smallest times accepted so depend on the host's offset, as they do for addSeconds of a DateTime of now. A TimeSpan that does so raises SYNTAX 40.19 too. The alarm is set for the moment that many seconds after init read the clock, to the microsecond. 799.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Ticker Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Ticker Class > attachment; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Ticker Class > cancel; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Ticker Class > canceled/cancelled; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Ticker Class > init; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Ticker Class > interval Deviations: D109, D119, D135 A Ticker is a repeating timer. It is made for an interval, a target that wants to hear of it and, if the program likes, an object to attach; at the end of every interval it sends its target triggered, until it is cancelled, and when it is cancelled it sends the target cancel. The target is an implementation of AlarmNotification , which states what the target is sent and when. A ticker is made as an Alarm is, with an interval in place of a time; it has no scheduledTime and no triggered of its own, and it asks for the target and the attachment as an alarm does. This page states how a ticker is made, what its interval may be and what its own methods answer. By which activity the library runs the target, and whether a triggered that is still running delays the next one, is specified by the timer rule of the concurrency chapter. The examples that wait use a guard that the target opens, and print nothing that varies with the clock.

41005A [conv.string.object] An argument that a page calls a string and that is an object other than a string is replaced by a string, and the builtin works on that string. The replacement is found by sending the object the message REQUEST with the argument STRING, and nothing else is sent first. When the answer is a string, it is the replacement. When the answer is .nil or another object that is not a string, the replacement is the answer of the object's public STRING method, and when that answer is not a string either, see Deviation 30 . The REQUEST of Object sends the object MAKESTRING when it has one and answers what that answers, and answers .nil when it has none. So an object with a MAKESTRING method is replaced by its answer, as for an Array or a MutableBuffer , and an object with only a STRING method by the answer of that method. A class that declares its own REQUEST method decides the answer itself: its MAKESTRING method is not used unless its REQUEST sends it, and a REQUEST that answers a string is used even when the class has a STRING method. A MAKESTRING that answers .nil or an object that is not a string is like a REQUEST that does. An instance of a subclass of String is a string here, whether it is passed directly or is what REQUEST answers: the builtin works on its own characters, and no message is sent to it for that ( Deviation 109 ). A builtin that reads several such arguments reads them from left to right, after it has checked the number of its arguments. An argument that a builtin reads as a whole number or as a number is read this way too, and the replacement must then be a number. A builtin whose page links the native call rule has no fallback to STRING, as that rule says, and the same holds for the string arguments of methods ( the method argument rule ). A REQUEST, MAKESTRING or STRING method that is private and would be sent is not one the replacement can use: the call raises SYNTAX 97.2. 80.body: rexxref: General Concepts > Terms, Expressions, and Operators > Operators ooRexx is object based, and the operators of an expression are part of that. The tilde ~ sends a message to the value of the term before it, the double tilde ~~ does the same and keeps the receiver as its value, and the brackets [ ] send the message []. An arithmetic, comparison, logical or concatenation operator is a message too, sent to its left operand with the right operand as its argument. This page gives the rules that make the operators and the message terms one mechanism. The syntax of a message term is in the terms page , and the classes, their methods and the messages every class understands are specified in the chapters about classes . The ANSI standard has no message operators.

804.title: Deviations

805.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Monitor Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Monitor Class > current; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Monitor Class > destination; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Monitor Class > init; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > Monitor Class > unknown Deviations: D118, D124 A Monitor stands in for another object. A message that the monitor does not have a method for is sent on to the object that is the monitor's current destination, with the same name and the same arguments, and what that answers is what the monitor answers. The destination can be changed while the program runs, and put back to the one before: a program that holds a monitor, or that has made one the value of a name such as .output that other code reads, changes where the messages go without that code noticing. A monitor is transparent only for messages that it does not itself understand: the methods of Object are the monitor's own, and the rule on them says which messages are not forwarded. The forwarding is the unknown method, which the method search runs when it finds no method.

808.body:
[class.monitor.unknown] unknown(name, arguments) forwards a message. It is run by the method search for a message the monitor has no method for, with the name in upper case and the array of the arguments that the search builds, and it can be sent directly with the same two arguments. It sends the current destination a message with that name and the items of the array as its arguments, and answers what that message answers; when the message answers nothing, unknown answers nothing. The arguments are passed on as they were sent: an omitted argument stays omitted, so that the destination counts the arguments by the last one present, and a trailing omitted argument is not counted. A condition that the destination's method raises is raised for the message to the monitor in the same way, an error number and subcode included. When the destination does not understand the name, or is .nil, SYNTAX 97.1 is raised; and a method of the destination that is PRIVATE or PACKAGE is not available to the monitor, which is not the destination and has not the destination's package: the message raises SYNTAX 97.2 or 97.3 as it would for any other sender ( the access rule ). A method that the destination has on its class side is not reached. A destination that has an unknown method of its own gets that message in turn, with the name in upper case. Called directly, unknown needs both arguments (SYNTAX 93.901), takes no more (SYNTAX 93.902), and needs the name to be present (SYNTAX 93.903). a = .target~new('A')

809.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > EventSemaphore Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > EventSemaphore Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > EventSemaphore Class > isPosted; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > EventSemaphore Class > post; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > EventSemaphore Class > reset; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > EventSemaphore Class > uninit; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > EventSemaphore Class > wait Deviations: D109 An EventSemaphore is a flag that activities can wait for. It is either posted or cleared. An activity that has to wait for something another activity does calls wait; the activity that does it calls post, and every activity that waits goes on. A semaphore that is posted lets wait return at once, until it is cleared again with reset. This page states what each method answers and checks, and what a timeout may be. How activities are scheduled, and so which of several waiters runs first after a post, is specified by the waiting rule of the concurrency chapter. The examples that use two activities start a message and wait on the semaphore from the program; the order of their output is forced by the semaphore itself.

[class.eventsemaphore.wait] wait(timeout) answers 1 when the semaphore is posted, at the call or before the timeout ends, and 0 when the timeout ended with the semaphore still cleared. The timeout says how long the caller is prepared to wait. Omitted or below zero, there is no limit, so the answer is 1, except for a wait that a signal's HALT ends ( Deviation 10 ). Zero is no wait at all, and the answer is the state at the call, as isPosted gives it. Above zero it is a limit in seconds. One post ends the wait of every caller that is waiting, however many there are; which of them runs on first is not specified. An activity that is about to enter a part of the program that only one activity may be in at a time calls acquire; when it leaves it calls release. While one activity owns the semaphore, another that calls acquire waits for the owner to let go, or gives up after a timeout. An activity that owns the semaphore can acquire it again without waiting, and then has to release it as many times. This page states what each method answers and checks, how the count of acquisitions works and what a timeout may be. How activities are scheduled, and so which of several that wait gets the semaphore next, is specified by the waiting rule of the concurrency chapter. The examples that use two activities start a message from the program and use event semaphores to force the order of what happens, so that nothing in their output depends on speed.

817.body:
[class.mutexsemaphore.acquire] acquire(timeout) gives the activity that calls it ownership, and answers 1, when no activity owns the semaphore and when the activity already owns it. It answers 0 when another activity owns it and keeps it for the whole timeout. The semaphore counts how many times its owner has acquired it: a call from the owner does not wait, adds one to the count and answers 1, and the semaphore becomes free only when release has taken the count back to zero. The timeout bounds the wait of a caller that does not get the semaphore at once. Omitted or below zero, there is no bound, so the answer is 1, except for a wait that a signal's HALT ends ( Deviation 10 ). Zero means no wait: the answer says whether the semaphore was free or the caller's already. Above zero it is a bound in seconds. When the owner lets go, one of the activities that wait gets the semaphore, which of them is not specified. The timeout is read as the next rule says, before the semaphore is looked at, so an invalid one raises its error whoever owns the semaphore. Ownership does not outlive the activity: when an activity ends, every count it held is dropped and the semaphore is free for others. In the first example one activity does all the calls, and in the second a message that the program starts owns the semaphore while the program calls. m = .mutexsemaphore~new

820.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandHandler Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandHandler Class > deregister (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandHandler Class > environments (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandHandler Class > handler (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandHandler Class > handlers (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandHandler Class > register (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandHandler Class > command Deviations: D109 A command that a program sends to an environment is run by whatever the environment is. CommandHandler is the mixin class for environments written in Rexx: an object whose class inherits it, registered under a name, receives every command that is sent to that name as a message, and answers with the return code of the command. The class methods register such an object, remove it, and list the environments of the interpreter, the native ones that run commands in the host's shell among them; the objects that stand for those are the NativeCommandHandler objects. While a command runs, the handler gets a CommandContext that describes it. This page states the class, how a command reaches the method command of the handler and what the handler answers, and the class methods. The environment chapter specifies the environments of the interpreter , how a command to a name that no environment has fails and what the native environments do ; this page says only where the class takes part. The examples register environments under names of their own, and use no environment that runs commands in the host.

[class.commandhandler.creation] CommandHandler is a mixin class: it has the one instance method command and the class methods deregister, environments, handler, handlers and register, besides the methods that every class has. Its superclass is Object, and it inherits no mixin of its own ( the hierarchy rule ). A class that inherits it gets the instance method command and the class methods too, so a program may send register to its own handler class as well as to CommandHandler, and all of them work with the same environments. A class method is not an instance method: an instance of such a class does not understand register. new sent to CommandHandler makes an instance, as it does for any class that is not abstract, and command sent to that instance is the abstract method that the command rule states. The class may have private methods besides these; they are not part of this specification. say .commandhandler~id .commandhandler~superclasses~items, .commandhandler~superclass~id .commandhandler~queryMixinClass

[class.commandhandler.register] register(name, handler) makes handler the handler in use for the environment name and answers the handler that it covers: the one that was in use for the name before, or .nil when there was none. Both arguments are required (SYNTAX 93.901) and a third raises SYNTAX 93.902. The name is read as the name rule says, and is kept in upper case, so a handler is found by the name in any case; a name with a blank is allowed, and the null string and an object that is not a string raise SYNTAX 93.900. handler must be an object of a class that inherits CommandHandler: the object is asked isA with .CommandHandler as the argument, once, after the name was read, and it is accepted when the answer is true; .nil, a class and an object of another class raise SYNTAX 93.900. The handler it covers is not lost: it comes back into use when this one is removed by deregister , and handlers lists it. The same object can be registered more than once, under several names and under one name again. A handler is the object registered, not a copy. The registration belongs to the interpreter instance, and a name that is already the name of a native environment is covered like any other. a = .echo~new('a'); b = .echo~new('b')

826.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > NativeCommandHandler Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > NativeCommandHandler Class > command; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > NativeCommandHandler Class > kind; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > NativeCommandHandler Class > name Some command environments are not written in Rexx: the environment SYSTEM, which runs commands in the host's shell, the environments that name a shell, and those that an application that hosts the interpreter adds. A NativeCommandHandler is the object that stands for one of them, so that a program can list it, register it again under another name, remove it, and send it a command from a handler written in Rexx. The class inherits CommandHandler , and the objects answer to the same class methods as the handlers written in Rexx do. How a native environment runs a command , and what the environments of a host are , is specified in the environment chapter. The examples here use the environment SYSTEM and the commands echo and exit, which every host's shell has.

83.body: ANSI: 6.3.2, 8.3; rexxref: General Concepts > Clauses and Instructions An instruction is a clause that does something when the interpreter reaches it. A program is a sequence of clauses, and the interpreter runs them in the order written until an instruction moves control elsewhere or the program ends. This chapter specifies what each kind of instruction does. The lexical chapter already says where a clause ends and how its first tokens decide what kind it is, and the expressions chapter says how the expressions inside an instruction are evaluated, so this chapter takes both as given. The pages of this chapter are: Assignments : symbol = expression and the extended forms such as +=. Message instructions : a message term used as a clause, and the assignments term~name = expression and term[...] = expression. Commands : an expression sent to the current environment, and the return code that comes back. The keyword rule below lists the keyword instructions, with a link on each name whose page exists. The lexical chapter calls a keyword instruction simply an instruction, and this chapter says keyword instruction wherever the other three kinds are also in play. The directives, which start with two colons, are not instructions, and their own chapter specifies them.

831.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > [ ]; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > [ ]=; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > dropVar; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > environment; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > error; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > getVar; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > hasVar; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > input; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > isRedirected; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > isValid; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > output; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > raise; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > raiseError; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > raiseFailure; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > setVar; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandContext Class > variables Deviations: D109 When a command reaches a handler written in Rexx, the interpreter makes a CommandContext for that one command and passes it to the method command of the CommandHandler as the second argument. The context is the handler's view of the command's surroundings: the variables of the code that sent the command, the ADDRESS ... WITH redirections of its input, output and error, and the one condition that the command may raise when the handler is done. The streams that a context hands out are CommandInput and CommandOutput objects. The redirections themselves, ADDRESS ... WITH, are specified with the ADDRESS instruction . Which activity runs the handler, and how commands to the environments of a host work, is specified in the environment chapter ( how a native environment runs a command ); the examples here register environments of their own under names that no host has, so that nothing depends on the host.

[class.commandcontext.raise] raise(condition, rc, description, additional) makes the command raise a condition. The condition is raised in the code that sent the command, when the handler's method command returns, as if the command itself had raised it: a SIGNAL ON or CALL ON trap for it answers it as for any condition, though a CALL ON ANY trap does not see the conditions that only SIGNAL can trap ( the CALL ON rule ); the handler goes on running after the call. A condition that no trap answers is treated as the page of that condition says. The method answers rc. What command answers is not used when a condition was raised: RC holds rc as it is, whatever object it is, the number or the text, .nil too, so a handler may return the answer of the call or anything else. A HALT is delayed like any HALT ( the HALT rule ), so the clause after the command is run before a trap for it. condition is a string: ERROR, FAILURE, HALT, LOSTDIGITS, NOMETHOD, NOSTRING, NOTREADY, NOVALUE, or USER followed by a name of one word, in either case; SYNTAX is the other form, which the next rule states. The string is read as words separated by whitespace , so the blanks and tabs around and between the words play no part, and the name after USER may be any word; the condition is named in upper case (USER 1X). A command that raises ERROR or FAILURE has the status .RS of the status rule . description is what CONDITION('D') answers and the DESCRIPTION entry of the condition object holds; when it is omitted or .nil, it is the command, and the null string is a description like another. Another object is replaced by its string value as the conversion rule finds it: request with STRING is sent to it first, and its string method when that answers no string, so that a class with its own request decides the description. The condition holds that string; an instance of a subclass of String is a string here ( the deviation rule ). additional is the ADDITIONAL entry of the condition object, the object as it was given, and when it is omitted or .nil the condition object has no such entry. The condition object has RC, holding the rc object. condition and rc are required: SYNTAX 93.901 when they are fewer than two, SYNTAX 93.903 when an omitted place stands for one of them, and SYNTAX 93.902 for more than four arguments. A condition that is none of the forms above, ANY, NONE, PROPAGATE, USER with no name or with more than one, any other text, the null string and .nil among them, raises SYNTAX 93.900. A call that raises an error does not use up the command's one condition, which the second rule says. x = .commandhandler~register('spec_cc_raise', .raiser~new)

[class.commandcontext.copy] copy answers a new object that stands for the same command: it works with the same variables and the same redirections as the original, and is valid while the command runs, as the original is. A variable that one sets, the other reads. The same holds for the streams that input, output and error answer: a copy of a stream reads from the same source and writes to the same target, so that a line that one reads is not read by the other. A copy keeps its own record of the one condition. The record starts as the record of the object that was copied, as it is at that time, so that a copy made after the original asked for a condition refuses one with SYNTAX 93.900. 838.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandInput Class A CommandInput is the stream from which a handler written in Rexx reads the input of a command that was sent with ADDRESS ... WITH INPUT. The handler gets it from input of the CommandContext of the command. It reads the source of the redirection, a stem, a stream or the object of a USING ( the redirection rules ), as a list of lines, one after the other and once. It is a stream of the input kind: its class inherits the mixin class InputStream, whose other methods, arrayIn among them, are specified with the stream classes . This page states the four methods that the class defines for itself, the text that they read, and what they do at the end of the input. The input of a command is read by the handler, or by nobody; which commands of the host read their standard input from it is the business of the environment chapter.

[instr.index.kinds] A clause that is not a null clause, a label or a directive is an instruction of one of four kinds: an assignment, a message instruction, a keyword instruction or a command. The lexical rule decides from the first tokens of a clause which of the four it is, so a symbol followed by = is an assignment before any keyword is looked at. This chapter adds the naming and the pages. A message assignment, which the message page specifies, is a message instruction like the lone message term, and what the lexical chapter calls an instruction is the keyword instruction here. Because every clause that is none of the other three is a command, a clause that holds only a function call, a string, or a parenthesized expression is a command, and so is a message term that an operator or another term follows. address system

A clause that is not an assignment and whose first token is one of these names is that instruction, whatever the case of the name. A name that is not on the list starts no keyword instruction. A clause that begins with such a name is a command, so that the name is evaluated as an expression like any other symbol. The names of directives and of builtin functions are not keywords: endlocal as a clause is a command, and so are class and method without colons. The words THEN, ELSE, END, WHEN and OTHERWISE are the exception, and the next rule covers them. address nosuch

[class.commandinput.text] The input is a list of lines. A source that is a stem gives the lines stem.1 to stem.n that stem.0 counts, a stream gives its lines, and an object of a USING gives the lines that it supplies, an array's items for one. Each line is followed by a line end of one character, '0A'x: the characters that the stream reads are the characters of the lines, each followed by that line end, the last line too. A line that holds a line end is one line, and it is not split where the line end is. Reading goes from the first line to the last and never back: the first argument of charIn and lineIn, which would give a position, is refused with SYNTAX 93.963. 842.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > CommandOutput Class Deviations: D109 A CommandOutput is the stream to which a handler written in Rexx writes the output or the error output of a command that was sent with ADDRESS ... WITH OUTPUT or WITH ERROR. The handler gets it from output or error of the CommandContext of the command. What it is given goes to the target of the redirection, a stem, a stream or the object of a USING, as lines, in the way that the redirection rules say for any command. A command that is sent without a redirection has no such stream; a handler that is to write then uses SAY or a stream of its own. The class inherits the mixin class OutputStream, whose other methods, arrayOut among them, are specified with the stream classes . This page states the four methods that the class defines, how text becomes lines, and when a line that is not finished is written.

847.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > new (Inherited Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > create (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > delete (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > exists (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > open (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > delete; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > empty; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > get; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > init; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > lineIn; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > lineOut; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > makeArray; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > pull; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > push; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > queue; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > queued; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > say; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RexxQueue Class > set Deviations: D109, D135 A RexxQueue is an object that works with one of the external data queues, the lists of lines that are kept outside the program in a service and that the QUEUE and PUSH instructions fill and the PULL instruction empties. The object holds the name of a queue, adds lines to the queue and takes them out, and asks how many there are. Besides the instance methods the class has methods that make, open, delete and ask after a queue by its name. They are the same queues as those of the RXQUEUE function , and the rules that function states for the names of queues, for the queue SESSION and for a queue that does not exist hold here too. A program has a current queue that the instructions use; the object has a queue of its own, and the two are the same queue only when they have the same name. How programs and sessions share the queues is specified by the session rule and the child rule . Note. The examples create a queue under a name that no other example uses and delete it when they are done, so they leave nothing behind. An example never waits for a line that nothing will add, because a program that does that does not end.

93.902 [class.rexxqueue.init] init(name) connects the object to a queue and takes at most one argument (SYNTAX 93.902). It decides the name in one of three ways. With no argument the name is SESSION. With .nil it makes a queue whose name the service picks, as the class method create does with no argument, and uses that name; no program can know the name beforehand. With any other argument it sends the argument the message upper, and the answer is the name: a string in upper case, a number such as 12 or a MutableBuffer gives its upper-case string, and an object that does not understand upper, an Object or an Array for one, raises SYNTAX 97.1. For a name that was given, init then sends the class of the receiver the message open with the name, as the class method says: a queue of that name is kept as it is with its lines, or made when there is none. An init does not look at the answer of open, so a name that no queue can have raises no error here: the object is made, and the methods that need the queue fail later, as the missing queue rule says. 85.body: ADDRESS [name | VALUE expression | (expression)] [command] [WITH redirection] ANSI: 6.3.2.21, 8.3.1; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > ADDRESS Deviations: D52 ADDRESS chooses the environment that receives the commands of a program, and it can also send a single command to another environment, and redirect where a command reads its input and writes its output. This page specifies the forms of the instruction and the redirections. The environment that is current, the name that the ADDRESS function answers, the swap of the current and the previous environment and the scope of both across calls are specified with that function, and the page links them. What a command is, how it is evaluated and sent and what its return code is belong to the commands page . The environments that exist, other than the one that runs commands in the host's shell, belong to the names rule . The examples use the name system for that shell and, in a few, names of environments that do not exist, because the result of the instruction shows in the ADDRESS function.

An entry is an index and an item. The supplier method of every collection class answers a supplier that holds the entries of the collection; the page of each collection class says which entries those are and in what order. A program can also make a supplier of its own from two arrays, one for the items and one for the indexes. The loop DO WITH INDEX name ITEM name OVER collection walks the supplier of a collection ( the loop rule ). This page states the class: how a supplier is made, how it is read and advanced, what it answers at its end, and how copies and subclasses behave. 868.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RegularExpression Class; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RegularExpression Class > new (Class Method); Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RegularExpression Class > match; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RegularExpression Class > parse; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RegularExpression Class > pos; Builtin Classes > Utility Classes > RegularExpression Class > position Deviations: D87, D88, D89 A RegularExpression holds a pattern and tells whether a string matches it, and where in a string it is found. The pattern language is small: literal characters, a single-character wildcard, repetition, alternatives, groups and sets of characters. The class is not preloaded. A program makes it available with ::requires "rxregexp.cls", and the package that file names is part of every installation; every example on this page does so. A traceback that runs through that file shows interrexx's own lines of it, their numbers and their text, not ooRexx's, and an error the package raises may be reported from another clause of it or from the caller ( Deviation 89 ). The page first states the class and how a pattern is read, then the grammar and what it matches, and last the matching calls. Characters are bytes: the pattern and the string are compared byte by byte, and no case is folded. A '00'x ends a pattern, and what match and pos answer for a string that contains one is not specified ( the grammar rule gives the first).

The redirection is then one of NORMAL; STEM followed by a stem symbol, which ends in a period; or STREAM or USING followed by an expression in parentheses, a string, a constant symbol or an environment symbol, where STREAM names a stream. A plain variable symbol after STREAM or USING is not one of these. OUTPUT and ERROR may put APPEND or REPLACE before STEM, STREAM or USING, and replace is meant when neither is written. The keywords may be in any case. The word WITH directly after ADDRESS is the name of an environment and not the keyword, so ADDRESS WITH OUTPUT NORMAL sends the command OUTPUT NORMAL to the environment WITH. address first

[class.regularexpression.parse] parse(pattern, mode) replaces the pattern of the expression and, when mode is given, its mode; without it the mode stays what it was. It answers a code: 0 when the pattern was read, and otherwise one of 1 to 6 that the next rule lists. The pattern is required. The arguments are checked as the argument rule says, and a mode that is not MAXIMAL or MINIMAL, in any case, raises SYNTAX 93.0. position answers how many characters of the pattern were read. When the code is 0 that is the length of the pattern, unless the text after a complete pattern was left unread, as the grammar rule says. When the code is not 0 the old pattern is gone and the expression matches every string: a later match answers 1 and pos answers 1, both with position 0. re = .RegularExpression~new('ab', 'MINIMAL')
say re~match('abc') re~position
say re~parse('abc') re~position re~match('abc') re~position
say re~parse('abc', 'MAXIMAL') re~match('abcd') re~position
say re~parse('[') re~position
say re~match('zzz') re~position re~match('') re~position
say re~pos('zzz') re~position
call try 're~parse'
call try 're~parse("a", "MAXIMAL", 1)'
call try 're~parse(.nil)'
call try 're~parse("a", "bogus")'
exit

Code 1 is a symbol where none is allowed, or a pattern that ends where something has to follow: a pattern that is empty or starts with *, +, |, ), ], { or }, an empty group (), and an alternative with nothing in it, as in a|, a||b and (a|). Code 2 is a group that is not closed, as in (a. Code 3 is a set that is not valid or not closed: [, [a, [], [a- and [a-], a range that has no end, and a \ that ends the pattern inside a set, as in [a\. Code 4 is a pattern that ends after an escape outside a set, as in a\, or inside a count: a{ and a{3. Code 5 is a count that is not a number or is below 2, as in a{}, a{x} and a{1}, and a number too large for the pattern to be built. Code 6 is a symbolic name in a set that is not one of the defined names , or has no closing colon: [:foo:] and [:alpha]. position answers the number of characters before the one at fault, so 0 when the first character is at fault (*), 1 for () and 2 for a|*, and the length of the pattern when it ends where something has to follow ((a, a|, a\, [, [a, [a-c). Two kinds of error count differently. An error in a set other than a missing ], which is codes 3 and 6 and a \ that ends the pattern inside a set, counts the characters up to and including the [ ([] 1, xy[a-] 3, [a\ 1, xy[:foo:] 3), and so does a set that the pattern ends before its first member (q[^ 2). An error in a count, codes 4 and 5, counts those before its { (a{ 1, xyz{3 3, xyz{x} 3). The example shows it for a pattern of each kind. re = .RegularExpression~new

870.title: Reading a pattern

871.body:
[class.regularexpression.grammar] A pattern is one or more alternatives separated by |, and an alternative is one or more elements. An element is a character that stands for itself, the wildcard ?, a set in square brackets, or a group in parentheses, and it may be followed by one quantifier. Any character that is not special stands for itself, a blank, ., ^, $, -, : and , among them; case counts. ? stands for any one character. \ makes the character after it stand for itself, whatever it is; a \ that ends the pattern is error 4. An alternative may not be empty, and neither may a group. | separates whole alternatives: it ranks below joining elements, so ab|cd is ab or cd, and a group is how the choice is limited to part of a pattern. A * or + or {n} applies to the element before it. Reading stops, without an error, at a symbol that cannot continue a pattern that is complete: a ) with no group open, a second quantifier after a quantifier (a**, a+*, a{2}+), a ], or a } after an element; parse answers 0 and position says how many characters were read, so the rest is not part of the pattern and has no effect. Where an element is needed, such a symbol is error 1. A '00'x in the pattern ends it in the same way: what follows is not read, and position counts the characters before it. re = .RegularExpression~new

A ^ right after the opening bracket negates the set: it matches one character that is not a member; a ^ anywhere else is an ordinary member. A - between two characters makes a range. For a range the bytes count as numbers from -128 for '80'x up to 127 for '7f'x, so '80'x to 'ff'x come before '00'x. When the first character is not above the second, the range is all characters from the first to the second; when it is above, it is the characters above the second up to the first, so [d-a] is b, c and d. In a chain such as [a-c-e] the character that ends a range also starts the next one, so that set is a to e. A \ right after the - of a range is the end of the range and not an escape, and a - after a symbolic name starts a range at the closing colon of the name, which is left out when the end is above it: [:digit:-z] is the digits and the characters from ; to z. A [ inside a set is an ordinary member. A - that opens the set, or follows the ^ that opens it, is an ordinary member, and a - that ends the set is error 3. Inside a set the characters ?, *, +, |, (, ), {, } and . stand for themselves; \ makes the next character an ordinary member, which is how ], - and \ itself are members, and a : that is not preceded by \ begins a symbolic name. A set must have a member, and its closing bracket must be present: error 3. re = .RegularExpression~new

This page states what is the method's own: how an object is made, the argument errors and the answers of the methods, and the messages that a method sends to its receiver and to its arguments, where a subclass or an argument can override them. The answers are strings. A method with no counterpart among the functions, or whose messages another rule states, has a rule of its own. 1 [class.stream.args] The arguments of a message are checked in this order, and the first error is the one raised. First comes the form of the arguments that a method reads before it counts them: a start, a line number or a count of charIn, lineIn, charOut and lineOut that is no whole number in the range that the arguments give raises SYNTAX 88.907, and a string to write that has no makeString method raises SYNTAX 88.909 ( the strings rule ); the option of open, lines, seek and position is read through makeString too, and one without it raises SYNTAX 88.909 ( the objects rule ). Then comes the count of arguments, as the count rule says, and before the stream is opened: a message with more arguments than the method takes raises SYNTAX 88.922 for chars, charIn, charOut, close, description, flush, lineIn, lineOut, lines, open, position, qualify, seek, state and uninit, and SYNTAX 93.902 for arrayIn, arrayOut, command, init, makeArray, query, say, string and supplier; for these nothing is read before the count. Last come the values: a lineIn count above 1 raises SYNTAX 93.0, an option that is not allowed raises SYNTAX 93.0 or 93.915 as the rule of the method says, and, once the stream is open, a start or a line number below 1 raises SYNTAX 93.907. charIn, charOut, lineIn, lineOut and arrayOut take two arguments, lines, open, position, seek, arrayIn, makeArray, command, init, query and say one, and the others none. arrayOut, command, init and query need their argument, and a message without it raises SYNTAX 93.901; position and seek raise SYNTAX 88.901. No argument is required by say, lines, open, arrayIn or makeArray. In the example the state is still UNKNOWN after every message that raised. f = 'spec-stream-args-zq.tmp'

end
say '--'
do m over 'arrayOut command init query position seek'~makearray(' ') call try 's~' || m
end
say s~state
say '--'

877.title: What the stream functions do

878.body:
[class.stream.open] open opens the stream as OPEN does, with the options of the option rule in its one argument, a string that may be left out, and answers READY:, or ERROR: with the host's number and the NOTREADY condition when it cannot. An option that is not allowed, such as a word that no option starts with, raises SYNTAX 93.0, and the stream is not open after it, also when it was. The state is that of the state rule . Opening a stream that is open opens it afresh, as the function does . When open with BINARY and no RECLENGTH raises SYNTAX 93.0, the stream is UNKNOWN afterwards ( Deviation 145 ). f = 'spec-stream-open-zq.tmp'
call lineout f, 'abc'
call lineout f
s = .stream~new(f)
say s~open('read') s~state
say s~lineout('x') s~state
say s~open s~state '['s~charin(, 2)']'
say s~open('REP') s~query('size')
say s~close
say s~open s~state
signal on syntax name bad
say s~open('bogus')
bad: say condition('o')~code s~state
say s~open s~state
signal on syntax name bad2
say s~open('read write')
bad2: say condition('o')~code s~state
signal off syntax
n = .stream~new('spec-stream-open-nodir-zq/x')
call on notready name trap
say n~open~left(6) n~state
call sysfiledelete f
exit

What it forces out is in the file afterwards, so a stream that reads the file after the writing stream was flushed sees it. An instance may keep what it writes until it is flushed or closed, as the stream that a function names may: another stream on the same file, an instance or a function, may not see it before then, as the second example shows. f = 'spec-stream-flush-zq.tmp'

881.body: rexxref: Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class; Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > arrayIn; Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > charIn (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > charOut; Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > chars (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > close; Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > lineIn (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > lineOut; Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > lines (Abstract Method); Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > open; Builtin Classes > Stream Classes > InputStream Class > position InputStream is a mixin class that gives a class the methods of a stream that is read: the ones that read, and the ones that a stream of that kind does not have. A class that inherits it, or a subclass of it, writes the methods that read, charIn, chars, lineIn and lines; the rest the mixin answers in a way a program can rely on: an error for the methods that make no sense, a method that does nothing for open and close, and arrayIn, which reads with the lineIn of the class. The classes of the library that inherit it are CommandInput , InputOutputStream and, through that, Stream . What the standard input is, and what the .input of a program is bound to, is specified in the bindings rule . The examples define their own classes.

889.body: rexxref: Rexx Runtime Objects This chapter specifies what surrounds a program while it runs: the objects that every program can reach by an environment symbol without declaring them, and the places that a name such as .output is looked up in. The pages of this chapter are: Environment objects : the directories .environment and .local, every entry that the language puts in them, what the entries are bound to when a program starts, the order in which an environment symbol is looked up, and what a program may change in them and where the change is seen. Invocation : the rexx command, its words and options, how the arguments reach the program, the status it ends with, what a program sees at its start, what is sent to its objects when it ends, and the command rexxc and the images it writes. Search : how an external routine, a required file, a program called by name and a library are found: the places, the extensions, the case of a name, what is read again at every call, and what a program that is called by name leaves in its caller. Command environments : the environments that run a command on Linux and the program each runs, how the return code of a command comes out of its exit status or signal, what a command starts with, the commands cd, export, set and unset that the interpreter does itself, and the rxqueue filter that puts the lines of a command on a queue of the program. Security manager : the object that is asked before the code it governs calls an external routine, runs a command, loads a file, reads a name from .local or .environment, names a stream or sends a message to a protected method: what a manager belongs to, which code it governs, what each checkpoint sends and what the answer does. Debugging : interactive tracing: how it starts and ends, when the interpreter stops, what it reads at a stop and from where, what each kind of line does, where its own lines are written, and the RXTRACE variable. An example in this chapter changes the objects that its own program reads, as a program does. Each example restores what it changed when a later line of the example needs the original, and an object that an example adds to .local or .environment has a name that no other example uses.

The value of such a symbol is found by a lookup that this page specifies: first which objects exist and what they are, then the places the lookup goes through and their order, and last what a program may change. The lookup that reads the symbol is the environment rule of the lexical chapter; the order in which it consults the places is the rule of this page. A program adds its own objects to them as it adds entries to any other Directory. Note. Each interpreter instance has its own .environment ( Deviation 85 ). A program that rexx runs has one instance, and so has every example in this book.

898.body: rexxref: Rexx Runtime Objects > The SYSCARGS Array (.SYSCARGS); Rexx Runtime Objects > The Local Directory (.LOCAL); Useful Services > Distributing Programs without Source Deviations: D41, D96, D141, D153 A program is started by the command rexx, which reads the words after its name, finds the program, runs it, and ends with a status. This page specifies what the command does with its words, what a program sees of how it was started, and what happens when it ends. The words are the ones the host hands to the command: a program that is started from a shell sees them after the shell has quoted and split them, and a word may be empty. The command has three forms. rexx with a program name and any arguments runs a file. rexx -e with a string runs the string as a program. rexx -v prints a version banner. A second command, rexxc, translates a program into a file that holds no source , which rexx then runs. Note. The test harness starts each example's program without any words of its own, so an example cannot show the words of the command. The rules about them are tested by the recorded runs of the command in rust/crates/interrexx/tests/rexx_command/cases, which run interrexx and ooRexx on the same words and compare what they write and their status; each such rule is cited there. The examples of this page show what a program sees when it was started without words, and what happens when it ends.
898.title: Invocation

899.body: [env.invocation.forms] A command with no words, or whose words end before a program name or a string is found, runs nothing: it writes a usage text, a blank line and then three lines, to its standard error stream, and ends with the status 255. The text names the three forms. The words that lead up to the end are the option words of the next rule, so rexx -x, rexx -e, rexx -o and rexx -o with its string and nothing more all give the usage text. [env.invocation.words] The words from the first one are option words as long as they begin with a minus sign; the first word that does not is the program name, and every word after it is an argument, even one that begins with a minus sign. Only the letter after the minus sign of an option word says which option it is, in either case: e is the expression option , o is the options option , and v is the version option . Any later letter of the word is ignored, except the d that may follow o, so -ev is an expression option and -vo a version option. An option word whose letter is none of these, a minus sign alone, and a word of two minus signs are ignored, and do not end the option words, so that -x before a program name has no effect other than the place it takes in .syscargs . [env.invocation.version] An option word -v, in either case, makes the command print the version banner to its standard output stream and end with the status 0. It does so wherever it stands among the option words, including after the string that -o takes, and whatever the other words are: no program is looked for or run. What the banner says is stated below . A -v that stands after the program name, or is the word after -e, is not an option word: the first is an argument and the second is the text of the program, and neither prints the banner.
