900.body: [env.invocation.expression] An option word -e takes the next word as the text of a program, and runs that text as a program. The words after the text are its arguments, as they are for a file, and a second -e among them is an argument like any other. -e with no word after it is the usage text. An empty text is a program without clauses, which ends with the status 0. The program has no file: its PARSE SOURCE shows INSTORE where a file shows its name, and its error reports name INSTORE where a file's name its path. The array .syscargs does not exist for it, so .local holds one entry less than it does for a file, and the symbol .syscargs has the value of an environment symbol that nothing is stored under ( the lookup rule ). A -o option word before the -e is ignored; one after the text is an argument.
900.title: Running a string

901.body: [env.invocation.optstring] An option word -o takes the next word as a string of options for the program, and -o with no word after it is the usage text. The string is read as an ::OPTIONS directive that stands at the head of the program. If the byte after its first non-blank byte is a colon, the string is the text of that directive as it is given, and it is refused with SYNTAX 93.900 unless it begins, after its blanks, with two colons; otherwise the command puts ::OPTIONS and a blank before it. Only its first 511 bytes are read. An empty string followed by a word that begins with a colon is refused with SYNTAX 93.900; followed by any other word, it sets nothing. A directive other than ::OPTIONS is read too, but what it defines does not reach the program. A second -o replaces the first: its string, and whether the letter d follows the o. The options apply to the main program only, and -od, with the letter d after the o, makes them apply to every program that is translated during the run as well, one that a ::REQUIRES directive loads or one that is called by name. An ::OPTIONS directive of the program itself comes after them and replaces what it sets. A string that is refused ends the command before the program is looked for, with the status of an error for the error it raises, as an ::OPTIONS directive in the program would: 231 for bogus 9 (SYNTAX 25.924), 230 for digits x (SYNTAX 26.5), and 163 for a string that is no directive (SYNTAX 93.900).
901.title: The options string

902.body: [env.invocation.program] The program name is a file that the command finds as the program rule of the search page states. The name that the program reads from PARSE SOURCE ( the rule ), and the one that its error reports give, is the absolute path of the file that was found, with every . and .. of the path resolved, and with a link in the path left as it is. A word that is not valid text is a name all the same: names and arguments are the bytes that the host gave. [env.invocation.notfound] A program name that no file answers to, or that names a directory, runs nothing and writes the error 3.901 to the standard error stream; a file that is found and cannot be read gives the error 3.1, which names the file. Both end with the status 253.
902.title: The program

903.body: [env.invocation.arguments] The program starts with its arguments as one argument: the words after the program name, joined by one blank between each two. An empty word at the head of the words adds nothing, not even its blank, so that the arguments '', '' and x make the string x, and every later empty word is kept with the blank before it, so that a, '' and b make a b, and a and '' make a . A command with no words after the program name starts it with no argument, so that ARG() is 0 and ARG(1) the empty string; a command with one empty word starts it with one argument, the empty string. PARSE ARG , ARG and USE ARG read this one argument as they read any other. A program that -e runs gets its argument in the same way ( Deviation 141 ). [env.invocation.syscargs] The array .syscargs holds the words after the program name one by one, without the joining. A word is the entry whose index is its place among all the words after rexx, counted from 1, less one. When the program name is the first word, that is the index 1 for the first argument. Each word before the program name, the string of -o included, moves the arguments one index to the right and leaves the index below them without an entry: after -x before the program name, hasIndex(1) is false, items counts only the entries that exist, and size and last count the empty places too. A command with no arguments leaves .syscargs an array with no entry at all, and an empty word is an entry that is the empty string.
903.title: The arguments

904.body: [env.invocation.status] The command ends with the status of the program: the value of its EXIT or of the RETURN that ended it ( the exit code rule ), or, when an error ended it, 256 minus the major number of the error ( the error rule ). On Linux the command's status is the low eight bits of that integer, so that exit 300 gives 44 and exit 70000 gives 112. A program that -e runs hands on its value as a 16-bit integer: a whole number from -32768 to 32767 gives the same status as it does from a file, and any other gives 0, so that exit 33000 gives 0 under -e and 232 from a file. The errors that the command finds itself have a status of the same kind: 253 for a program that cannot be found or read, and that of its error for a refused string of -o. The usage text, which is no error, has the status 255.
904.title: The status

905.body:
[env.invocation.start] A program starts with the three standard streams READY, with SESSION as its current queue ( the RXQUEUE rule ), which holds nothing when the program is started from a shell, and, when the command gave it no words, with no argument and no entry in .syscargs. A program that a command of another Rexx program starts shares that program's SESSION queue, as the child rule states. The monitors that connect the streams to the program are the bindings of the environment objects. With /dev/null as standard input, what CHARS and LINES answer is Deviation 54 ( for CHARS , for LINES ). say stream('STDIN', 'S') stream('STDOUT', 'S') stream('STDERR', 'S')
say queued() rxqueue('Get')
say .syscargs~items arg() '['arg(1)']' READY READY READY
0 SESSION
0 0 []
905.title: The start

906.body:
[env.invocation.end] When the main program ends, by its last clause, by RETURN, by EXIT, or by an error that no trap handles, the status of the command is the program's own ( the status ), whatever the objects that the program holds do. Whether the interpreter sends UNINIT to those objects at that end, and in what order, is not specified ( the rule of UNINIT ), so a program that needs something done at its end does it itself. The first example ends the program by EXIT and the second by an error. say 'before exit'
call quit
say 'not reached'
quit: exit 5 before exit say 'before error'
say 1 / 0 before error [env.invocation.uninit] The interpreter sends the message UNINIT to an object that has a method of that name when it finds that the program cannot reach the object any more; what it frees by doing so is up to the method. This is best effort, and a program may rely on two things only: an object is sent UNINIT at most once by the interpreter (a program that sends UNINIT itself does not count), and it is never sent it while the running program can still reach the object, for example through a variable, an argument or the receiver of a method or routine that is running, an entry of .local, .environment or a package's local directory, or another object that it can reach. An object that is held when the main program ends is therefore not sent it before the end. It is not specified whether or when an object that the program has stopped referring to is sent UNINIT, whether the objects that are left when the main program ends are sent it, or in what order. The first example holds three objects of a class whose UNINIT counts the messages it gets: while they are held, the count is 0 however often storage is reclaimed ( GC ), and after one is dropped the count is at most 1. In the second, the UNINIT of the object stores it again, so that the program can reach it once more, and the object is still sent UNINIT at most once. .environment~count = 0
.local~one = .guard~new
.environment~two = .guard~new
keep = .guard~new
do 3 call gc 'force'
end
say 'held:' .environment~count
drop keep
do 5 call gc 'force'
end
say 'dropped:' (.environment~count <= 1)
::class guard
::method uninit .environment~count += 1 held: 0
dropped: 1 .environment~count = 0
.environment~back = .nil
x = .phoenix~new
drop x
do 20 until .environment~count > 0 call gc 'force'
end
.environment~back = .nil
do 20 call gc 'force'
end
say 'at most once:' (.environment~count <= 1)
::class phoenix
::method uninit .environment~count += 1 .environment~back = self at most once: 1 [env.invocation.end.uninit] An EXIT, or an error that no trap handles, in the UNINIT method of an object ends that method only, and an error there writes no report, whether the interpreter sent the message at the end of the main program or earlier. It does not change the status of the command. In the first example, the UNINIT of a dropped object exits with 9, and that of a second one divides by zero, each after the object is dropped and storage is reclaimed; in the second, an object that the program holds has an UNINIT that divides by zero when the program ends, if the interpreter sends it. The status stays that of the main program, with nothing written but what the program says. .error~destination(.stdout)
.environment~ran = 0
bad = .bad~new
drop bad
do 5 call gc 'force'
end
say 'after' (.environment~ran <= 1)
bad2 = .bad2~new
drop bad2
do 5 call gc 'force'
end
say 'after2'
return 3
::class bad
::method uninit .environment~ran += 1 exit 9
::class bad2
::method uninit say 1 / 0 after 1
after2 .error~destination(.stdout)
bad = .bad~new
say 'main'
return 3
::class bad
::method uninit say 1 / 0 main Note. What happens to an activity that is still running when the main program ends, and to the activities that an UNINIT method starts, is the business of the end rule , the started rule and the Deviation 21 rule of the concurrency chapter, and this page states nothing of it.
906.title: The end

907.body: Note. The command rexxc translates a program and writes the result to a file, the image, so that the program can be handed on without its source; rexx runs an image as it runs the program it came from ( the run rule ). The rules below state what rexxc takes and writes, what an image is to a reader, what a run of one shows, and what it is refused for. A program that the test harness starts cannot run rexxc, so the rules of this section have no examples. Each is tested by recorded runs of rexxc and of rexx on both interpreters, in rust/crates/interrexx/tests/rexxc/cases and rust/crates/interrexx/tests/compiled/cases, and by the tests of rexxc.rs and compiled.rs, which run both interpreters on copies of their images whose base64 text is laid out anew or holds a character that is not base64, and interrexx alone on images that are cut, extended or changed ( Deviation 153 ); each rule is cited there.
907.title: Programs without source

908.body: [env.invocation.rexxc.words] rexxc reads its words in order. The first is the name of the program, whatever it looks like, so that rexxc -x looks for a program called -x. A second word that does not begin with a minus sign is the name of the output file. Every word after those is a flag, and so is a second word that begins with a minus sign. A flag begins with a minus sign, and only the letter after it counts, in either case: s and e are the two flags that exist ( the banner rule and the image rule ), and a later letter of the word is ignored, so -S and -sx are the flag s. A flag may stand more than once and the flags may come in any order. A flag that is neither, a minus sign alone, and a word after the flags that does not begin with a minus sign are errors, and so is a name after the first flag, as in rexxc a.rex -s b.rxo. The command then writes a line that says its parameters are incorrect and the usage text, to its standard output stream, and ends with the status 255, before it looks for the program. With no words at all it writes the usage text alone, with the same status. [env.invocation.rexxc.check] Without an output name rexxc only translates the program and keeps nothing of the result: it ends with the status 0 when the program translates, and reports the error when it does not. The flag e changes nothing then, and the flag s only leaves out the banner . [env.invocation.rexxc.banner] Unless the flag s is given, rexxc writes the version banner of the -v option to its standard output stream once its words are accepted, and before anything else it writes, so that a command that ends with an error writes it too. A command that ends with the usage text writes no banner. The banner is as the version rule states. [env.invocation.rexxc.names] When the output name and the program name are the same string of bytes, the command ends with the status 254 and the line Output file name must be different from input file name. on its standard output stream, before it looks for the program, so that it ends so even when no such program exists. Words that are in error ( the words rule ) are reported before this check, so that rexxc a a -x ends with 255. The check compares the two words and not the files they name: for it a and a.rex, or a.rex and ./a.rex, differ, and the translation of a.rex is then written over the file a.rex. [env.invocation.rexxc.output] The program is found as rexx finds a program , and a name that no file answers to, a directory, and a file that cannot be read give the errors of that rule , with the same status. The output file is written after the program has translated, with the name as it was given and no ending added. An existing file of that name has its content replaced. A program that does not translate writes nothing and leaves an existing file as it was. An output file that cannot be written gives the error 3.902, with the status 253, and leaves an existing file as it was. [env.invocation.rexxc.translation] rexxc translates a program as it is translated before a run, and a run finds the same errors in it, with the same report: the line of the clause, the error numbers and the status of the error rule , so that say ( ends the command with 221 (SYNTAX 35.1). The EXTERNAL option of a ::ROUTINE, ::METHOD or ::ATTRIBUTE directive is bound then, so that a library that cannot be loaded (SYNTAX 98.903), a method entry of the REXX library that does not exist (SYNTAX 90.998) and a REGISTERED routine that cannot be found (SYNTAX 90.999) end the translation. Nothing else is looked up: a required file , a library that ::REQUIRES names with LIBRARY, and the superclass of a class are looked for when the image runs, so a program that requires a file or a library that does not exist, or whose class has a superclass that does not exist, translates. [env.invocation.rexxc.status] rexxc ends with the status 0 when the program translated and, with an output name, the file is written. Every other end has one of the statuses already given: 255 for the words , 254 for equal names , 253 for a program that cannot be found or read and a file that cannot be written ( the output rule ), and for an error of the program, 256 minus its major number as the status rule gives it.
908.title: What rexxc takes

909.body: [env.invocation.rexxc.image] An image is the program in its translated form. Only its opening is specified, and it is the same for both interpreters. The first line is #!/usr/bin/env rexx and a line feed. The nine characters /**/@REXX follow, and then either two bytes of 0, for the binary form that rexxc writes by default, or the character @ and a line feed, for the form that the flag e asks for. The binary form is not text: it goes on with a header and the translated program, which include the byte 0, and what they hold is not specified. In the encoded form what follows is lines of base64 text, each of 72 characters and each ended by a line feed, except the last, which may be shorter. Decoded, they give bytes that begin with /**/@REXX and the same two bytes of 0, as the binary form does after its first line.
909.breadcrumbs: Environment » Invocation » What an image is
909.title: What an image is

91.body: ANSI: 6.3.2.8, 8.3.3; rexxref: General Concepts > Clauses and Instructions > Assignments; General Concepts > Assignments and Symbols; General Concepts > Assignments and Symbols > Extended Assignments An assignment gives a variable a new value. Its form is a symbol, an equal sign and an expression, and the symbol decides which variable changes: a simple symbol names one variable, a stem symbol names a stem, and a compound symbol names the variable that its tail works out to. This page specifies what the assignment does with the value, the order in which its parts are evaluated, what it does to a stem, the extended forms that combine an operator with the assignment, and the errors it raises. How a clause is recognized as an assignment is the business of the lexical rules , and the variables themselves are specified in the expressions chapter .
91.title: Assignments

910.body: [env.invocation.rexxc.run] rexx runs an image as it runs the program that it was made from: the words are its arguments, a RETURN or EXIT gives its status , and a program it calls or requires is looked for as for any program, beside the image first ( the caller rule ). A file is an image when its bytes begin, after a first line that begins with #! or with no first line, with the characters /**/@REXX and the two tag bytes of the image rule . Nothing else about the file counts: its name has no part in it, and the first line may say anything after the #!. The ending .rxo is not among those that the search adds , so rexx name does not find a file name.rxo, while rexx name.rxo runs it, and rexx name runs an image that is called name. A file that begins like an image but has another letter in place of one of the four letters of REXX, or another byte in place of the byte that follows them (the first byte of 0, or the @), or, in the encoded form, another byte in place of the line feed after the @, is not an image: it is source, and its @ is the character that SYNTAX 13.1 reports. A file that is given to rexxc is always translated as source, an image too, so that it ends with the same error. [env.invocation.rexxc.source] A program that runs from an image has no source. SOURCELINE() answers 0, and a call with a whole number n of 1 or more raises SYNTAX 40.34, as the past-the-end rule says for a number above the count. .context~package~source has no lines and sourceSize is 0 ( the package rule ). The source of every routine and method that the image defines has no lines either, and the package's sourceLine answers the null string for every line, but the data of a ::RESOURCE directive and the values of ::ANNOTATE directives are kept. PARSE SOURCE gives the same three words as it does for a file ( the rule ), and the name is the path of the image. A line number is still the number of the clause's line in the program that was translated: an error that ends the run, and the traceback of a condition, show it, and show in place of the text of the clause a line that says no source is available. The text of an INTERPRET string is source and is shown as it is for any program. [env.invocation.rexxc.trace] TRACE in an image is accepted and changes the setting that TRACE() answers, but a clause of the image itself traces nothing: the clause lines and the results and values that go with them are not written, whatever the setting is. The >I> and <I< lines that the tags rule gives to the entry and the exit of a routine or method are shown, and the clauses that an INTERPRET string holds trace as they do in any program, with the line number of the INTERPRET clause. A pause of the interactive trace happens only before such a clause. [env.invocation.rexxc.options] An image takes no options from the -o option : it runs with what it was translated with, an ::OPTIONS directive that was in the program included, and the string is not spent on it. A string without the letter d goes to the first program of the run that is translated from source: for an image that requires two source files, the first of them, and for one that calls a source file by name and requires none, that file; a program translated after it takes none. With the letter d every program that is translated from source takes the string. [env.invocation.rexxc.routes] Besides the command, a call by name , ::REQUIRES and newFile of Routine and Method restore an image from a file. The lines of an encoded image, read as an array of lines, are restored by new of Routine, Method and Package and by loadPackage; one string that holds them is source, and so are the lines of a binary image, so that new of Routine with them stops at the first @ with SYNTAX 13.1. A routine or method restored from lines sees nothing of the program whose new or loadPackage restored it: a routine of that program that its code calls by name is not found (SYNTAX 43.1), where the same code given to new as source finds it. A routine that newFile or new restores is named by the path of the file that rexxc translated, and its package by the name that the call gave; a routine that a call by name restores is named by the name of the call, and its package by the path of the image.
910.title: Running an image

911.body: [env.invocation.rexxc.foreign] An image that the other interpreter wrote is refused when it is run, before any of its code runs, with the error 3.903 and the status 253, although its opening is that of any image. Which versions of an interpreter accept each other's images is not specified. [env.invocation.rexxc.damaged] In an encoded image a carriage return and a line feed are skipped between the groups of four base64 characters, so that the lines may have any length that is a multiple of four and may end with a carriage return as well. One that stands inside a group makes the image refused with the error 3.905 and the status 253, as does any other character that is not a base64 character, a blank or a tab included, before any of its code runs. The skipping holds for the base64 lines only: the line feed after the @ stands alone, so a copy in which that line too ends with a carriage return is source ( the run rule ) and stops at its @ with SYNTAX 13.1. An encoded image whose decoded bytes lack the binary tag is the case of Deviation 41 . Otherwise an image that ends too early, one that has a changed byte in its header or a changed second byte of 0 in the binary form, one that has a changed byte anywhere after its header, and one that has bytes after its end, an encoded one once its text is decoded, are refused with the error 3.903 and the status 253, before any of its code runs ( Deviation 153 ).
911.breadcrumbs: Environment » Invocation » Images that are refused
911.title: Images that are refused

912.body: [env.invocation.deviation.96] The version banner that -v prints names interrexx, its version, the ooRexx version it follows and its licence, and none of ooRexx's product, copyright or licence lines ( Deviation 96 ). Its other two lines, Build date: followed by the date of the build, and Addressing mode: followed by the width of an address in bits, are as ooRexx writes them. [env.invocation.deviation.141] The argument string of a program that rexx -e runs is made as the arguments rule makes it for a program in a file, so that the words ' ' and x after the text give the string of two blanks and x. ooRexx drops one leading blank of the string when it is longer than one character, and gives ' x' ( Deviation 141 ). [env.invocation.deviation.41] An encoded image whose decoded bytes lack the tag of an image, as the base64 of say 'decoded' does, is refused with the error 3.903 and the status 253, as the damaged-image rule refuses other damage. ooRexx translates the partly decoded bytes as source with unpredictable results ( Deviation 41 ). The rule of Method states the same for a program made by new. [env.invocation.deviation.153] An image that ends too early, one that has bytes after its end, and one that has a changed byte in its header, the second byte of 0 of the binary form included, are refused with the error 3.903 and the status 253, before any of its code runs. So is an image with any other byte changed: rexxc writes a SHA-256 digest of the image into it, and rexx refuses an image whose bytes do not give that digest. interrexx does not check the digest yet (issue #235), and no test covers that part. An encoded image whose base64 text does not decode whole, because characters follow the = that closes it, an = stands inside it, or it ends with a group of fewer than four characters, is refused with the error 3.905 and the status 253. ooRexx runs an image that has bytes after its end, ignores some changed header bytes and crashes on others, and crashes on an image that ends too early ( Deviation 153 ).
912.title: Deviations

913.body: rexxref: Functions > Search Order; Functions > Search Order > Locating External Rexx Files; Directives > ::REQUIRES A program names code that lives outside it in four ways: a call of a routine that the program does not define, a ::REQUIRES directive, a program name on the command line, and a library name. This page specifies how each is found: the places that are searched and their order, the extensions that are added to a name, how the case of a name matters, what a repeated search finds again, and what a program called by name leaves behind in the program that called it. The page states the behavior of a Linux host. The names of the places depend on the host: / separates the parts of a path, : separates the entries of REXX_PATH and PATH, and a file name is case sensitive. Note. The test harness runs each example from one working directory. interrexx runs it without a program file. ooRexx runs it as a file with the extension .rex in that directory. So no example depends on the directory or the extension of its own program: where one matters, the example writes a calling file of its own. An example that needs a directory builds one, and uses names that no host has. The examples set REXX_PATH and PATH with VALUE, change the current directory with DIRECTORY, and put them back. The rules about the rexx command are tested by the recorded runs of the command in rust/crates/interrexx/tests/rexx_command/cases, which run interrexx and ooRexx on the same words from a directory of known programs and compare what they write and their status; each such rule is cited there.
913.title: Search

914.body:
[env.search.kinds] These situations search for what a name stands for, and newFile takes a file without a search. A call of a routine that nothing in the program, no required package and no built-in function answers to searches for a file, a registered function and a macro, in the order of the order rule . A ::REQUIRES directive without LIBRARY, and the methods new and loadPackage of Package when they are given only a name, search for a file of Rexx code as the required-file rule says. findProgram of Package searches for a file in the way of a routine call ( its rule ). The command rexx searches for the program it is told to run, as the program rule says. newFile of Method and of Routine takes the file as it is named and searches for nothing ( its rule ). A library name is searched as the library rule says. A search that finds nothing is the error of the situation: SYNTAX 43.1 for a call (the name is shown in upper case when it was written as a symbol, as CALL says ), 43.901 for a ::REQUIRES and for new and loadPackage ( the file rule ), and 3.901 for the command ( its rule ). call try 'call a3zqkindsx'
call try 'r = a3zqkindsx()'
call try 'r = .package~new("a3zqkindsx")'
call try 'r = .package~new("a3zqk1", .array~of("::requires ""a3zqkindsx"""))'
call try 'r = .package~new("a3zqk2", "nop")~loadPackage("a3zqkindsx")'
call try 'r = .routine~newFile("a3zqkindsx")'
say .package~new('a3zqk3', 'nop')~findProgram('a3zqkindsx')~isNil
say .package~new('a3zqk4', 'nop')~loadLibrary('a3zqkindsx')
exit
try: signal on syntax name e interpret arg(1) say arg(1) '=> ok' return
e: say arg(1) '=>' condition('o')~code return call a3zqkindsx => 43.1
r = a3zqkindsx() => 43.1
r = .package~new("a3zqkindsx") => 43.901
r = .package~new("a3zqk1", .array~of("::requires ""a3zqkindsx""")) => 43.901
r = .package~new("a3zqk2", "nop")~loadPackage("a3zqkindsx") => 43.901
r = .routine~newFile("a3zqkindsx") => 3.1
1
0
914.breadcrumbs: Environment » Search » Which names are searched
914.title: Which names are searched

915.body:
[env.search.places] A name that is not a path, as the next rule says, is looked for in these places, in this order: the directory of the file that holds the code that makes the call; the current directory; each directory that the environment variable REXX_PATH lists, in its order; and each directory that PATH lists, in its order. The directory of a caller is skipped when the caller has no file: the code of a package made from source text and the string that rexx -e runs have none, and the command rexx has no caller at all. The code of a routine of a file has the directory of that file, wherever it is called from, so a routine that a required package supplies looks first beside the package's own file; the caller rule gives an example. REXX_PATH and PATH are read at the time of each search, and list their directories separated by colons; a directory that does not exist or has no such file adds nothing, a directory that is not absolute is read from the current directory, and a variable that is not set lists none. In the example, the files of the same name stand in the places one after another, and each call finds the first place that has a file; the last lines make the entries of REXX_PATH relative to the current directory. d = directory()
do n over .array~of('a3zqpl', 'a3zqpl/rp1', 'a3zqpl/rp2', 'a3zqpl/pp') call sysmkdir n
end
oldrp = value('REXX_PATH', d'/a3zqpl/nonesuch:'d'/a3zqpl/rp1:'d'/a3zqpl/rp2', - 'ENVIRONMENT')
oldp = value('PATH', , 'ENVIRONMENT')
call value 'PATH', d'/a3zqpl/pp:'oldp, 'ENVIRONMENT'
call show 'none'
call put 'a3zqpl/pp/a3zqwhere.rex', 'PATH'
call show 'PATH'

[env.search.extension] A name that has a period in its last part, the part after the last slash, names a file, and no extension is added to it. Any other name is tried with each of these endings in turn, and the first ending for which a file is found in some place ends the search: the endings come before the places, so that a file that has an earlier ending in a later place is found before a file that has a later one in an earlier place. The endings are, in order: .cls, only for the required-file search ; the extension of the file that holds the calling code, from the last period of the last part of the file's name, when that part has one; .REX; .rex; and no ending at all. A call, findProgram and the command rexx leave the .cls out, and the command has no calling file. In the example, a file a3zqxc.xyz calls a routine, and the files of that name are taken away one by one: the routine is found with the ending xyz, then REX, then rex, then with none. The file with the ending .cls stays to the end and is never found by the call. A second caller, a3zqxd, has no extension, and so has no ending of its own to add: it finds .REX first, and the file that has the extension xyz is not tried for it. [env.search.case] A file name is tried in two forms, the name as it was written and the whole name in lower case, directories included; the extension that is added is never changed. The two forms come after the extensions and before the places, so that for each ending the written form is tried in every place before the lower-case form is tried in the first. A call written as a symbol is written in upper case ( the call rule ), and so finds a file of the name in lower case. [env.search.required] A ::REQUIRES directive without LIBRARY, and new and loadPackage of Package given only a name, search for a file by the places , the names , the extensions and the case of the rules above, with these differences. The first ending is .cls, so that a file name.cls is found before every file name.REX, name.rex and name. The place that comes first is the directory of the file of the requiring package for a ::REQUIRES, and of the file of the receiver for loadPackage; new of Package has no caller, so it looks in the current directory and then in the other places, and findProgram, which has the directory of its receiver, has no .cls ending. A package that was made from source text has no file, so no directory. A name with a period has no ending, so that name.REX finds neither name.REX.cls nor name.REX.rex. The package that is found is installed as the file rule says, and is not read again when a file of that name was loaded before. In the example, the file a3zqrd/a3zqrreq.rex requires the file a3zqrsib that stands beside it and not in the current directory, where the file is a3zqrsib.cls and not the file a3zqrsib.rex. 921.body: [env.search.program] The program that the command rexx is told to run is looked for in the places with no directory of a caller: the current directory, then the directories of REXX_PATH, then those of PATH. The names of the names rule and the case of the case rule hold, and the endings are .REX, .rex and none, in that order and with no .cls: an ending is tried in every place before the next ending is tried, so that name.REX of REXX_PATH is run before name.rex of the current directory, and a file with no ending is run only when no file with an ending is found. A name that finds a directory only, or nothing, is the not-found error . The program is named as the program rule says. The cases in the test of the command show the order of the places and of the endings, the missing .cls and the not-found error, each with a file of one name in two places or with two endings; the string of rexx -e has no file and so no directory of a caller, and a program that the command runs searches the directory of its own file first for the routines that it calls.

927.body: rexxref: General Concepts > Commands to External Environments > Environment; Useful Services > The RXQUEUE Filter Deviations: D11, D93, D146, D147, D148, D149 A command that a program sends goes to an environment, which runs it and answers with a return code. The commands page specifies what is sent and how RC and .RS are set, the ADDRESS instruction chooses the environment and redirects its streams, and the conditions chapter specifies ERROR and FAILURE. This page specifies the environments that the interpreter has on Linux and what they do with a command: which program runs it and with what, the return codes they answer, what the command starts with, the commands that the interpreter does itself, and the rxqueue filter through which a command puts lines on the program's queue. CommandHandler and NativeCommandHandler are the classes of the environments, and a handler written in Rexx gets CommandContext , CommandInput and CommandOutput objects for a command that it runs. The examples start commands that every Linux host has: the shell's own commands, echo, printf, cat and cd. An example that changes the current directory, HOME, PATH or the queue puts it back.

The argument is the rest of the string after the blanks that follow cd; with no argument the directory is the value of the environment variable HOME, read as any other argument is: unlike DIRECTORY with ~ , a value that does not start with a slash is taken from the current directory. When the argument as written begins with ~, the tilde is read before anything else. A ~ alone, or followed by a slash or a blank, stands for the value of HOME, which is then read as the rest of the argument is, its double quotes and backslashes dropped, but not read again for a ~. After a slash the rest of the argument follows as usual; after a blank the rest is not read. A ~ followed by a name, which runs to the first slash or to the end of the argument, stands for the home directory of the user of that name in the host's user database. When there is no such user, the command is not done by the interpreter: the string goes to the shell, as any other string does. A ~ that is not the first character of the argument as written, and one that a quote or backslash comes before, is an ordinary character. In the rest of the argument every double quote is dropped, even one that nothing closes, and so is a backslash, the character after it being kept. Nothing else is read: a blank at the end is part of the name, as is a -, a single quote, a dollar sign or a star. A name that does not start with a slash is taken from the current directory. When HOME is the null string, cd with no argument fails as below, and a ~ that stands for HOME stands for nothing, so that cd ~ and cd ~/ make / current and cd ~/x makes /x current. When the directory cannot be made current, the command answers the number that the host gives the error, as Linux numbers them: 2 when there is no such directory, 20 when a part of the name is not a directory, 13 when permission is refused. [env.commands.rxqueue.filter] rxqueue is a program of the interpreter's installation that a command finds by its name, as it finds any program. It reads its standard input and puts the lines on a queue of the program that ran the command, which makes it the way for a command to hand lines to the program: a command whose output is piped into rxqueue leaves its lines in the queue when it ends. That queue is the program's SESSION queue, the one that PUSH, QUEUE, QUEUED and PULL work on until RXQUEUE sets another ( the get rule ), and the lines are put on it as the rules of its options say. A line of the input ends at a line feed, or at a carriage return followed by a line feed; a carriage return that no line feed follows also ends a line, and the character after it begins the next line and belongs to it whatever it is, so that a second carriage return directly after the first is text of the next line, not the end of an empty one; text after the last line end is a line, an empty line is a line, and input with no character puts none. The text is not changed, so that case, blanks, tabs and control characters stay as they are; only PULL changes the case, as its rule says. A line is cut after its first 65472 characters, and the rest of it up to its end is lost. The filter ends with the status 0 when it did its work, and the status of a pipeline that ends in it is its status, as for any pipeline of a shell. The other statuses are in the rules below. The text that it writes when it fails goes to its standard output, and this book does not specify it. address system

[e] [env.commands.rxqueue.options] rxqueue takes at most one option and at most one queue name, in either order. An option is / or - directly followed by FIFO, LIFO or CLEAR, in any letter case, and is the whole word; an abbreviation is not an option. The option /FIFO, which is the default, puts each line at the end of the queue, so that the lines come out in the order of the input after what the queue held. /LIFO puts each line at the front as it is read, so that the lines come out in the reverse order of the input and before what the queue held. /CLEAR removes every line of the queue, reads no input and puts nothing on the queue. A word that begins with / or - and is not one of these options, a second option, and a second name are errors in the call: rxqueue writes a usage text, puts nothing on the queue and answers the status 0. address system

935.body: rexxref: The Security Manager; The Security Manager > Calls to the Security Manager; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Routine Class > setSecurityManager; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Method Class > setSecurityManager; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Package Class > setSecurityManager A program can run code that it does not trust, and a security manager is the way to keep that code inside bounds. The manager is an object of the program's own. The interpreter asks it before the untrusted code does any of a short list of things: calls a routine that lives outside the code, runs a command, loads a file of Rexx code, reads a name from .local or .environment, names a stream, or sends a message to a protected method. The manager can let the action go on, can do it in its place, or can raise an error. The class pages own the methods that set a manager, and they own the rules of each checkpoint that are tied to a class: setSecurityManager of Routine , of Method and of Package , and the checkpoint rules that follow the first of them. This page ties those rules into one model: what a manager belongs to and which code it governs, when a change of manager takes effect, what each checkpoint sends and what its answer does, and what the code that is governed sees when a manager answers with something wrong. A rule here links the class rule it extends and states only the part that rule leaves out. The examples call the code that they govern through Routine objects and Package objects that they make from source text, so that the code is another package than the example. Where a command is run, it is exit with a number, which writes nothing and answers the number in rc.
935.title: Security manager

936.body:
[env.security.model] A security manager is any object. Each checkpoint is a message that the interpreter sends to it, named for the checkpoint: CALL, COMMAND, REQUIRES, LOCAL, ENVIRONMENT, STREAM and METHOD. The message has one argument, a Directory that the interpreter makes for that message and that holds the entries that the checkpoint names. The indexes of the entries are in upper case, and the interpreter reads only entries stored under those spellings: an entry stored under 'result' is not the entry RESULT ( the example of the call rule shows it). The entries are NAME and ARGUMENTS for CALL, and the manager may set RESULT; COMMAND and ADDRESS for COMMAND, and the manager may set RC, FAILURE and ERROR; NAME for REQUIRES, which the manager may replace, and it may set SECURITYMANAGER; NAME for LOCAL and for ENVIRONMENT, and the manager may set RESULT; NAME for STREAM, and the manager sets STREAM; OBJECT, NAME and ARGUMENTS for METHOD, and the manager may set RESULT. The manager answers 0, which lets the action go on as if there were no manager, or 1, which says that it dealt with the action and that the interpreter is to take what the action needs from the entries; any other answer is an error ( the answer rule ). A manager that has no method of the name of the checkpoint is sent UNKNOWN as every object is, with the name and an array of the one argument ( the checkpoint rule ). The clause of the governed code that reached the checkpoint goes on only when the manager has answered. In the example, a routine reaches every checkpoint once. The manager writes the name of each message it is sent and the indexes of the entries of its directory; it answers the first two itself and the others with 0. call sysfiledelete 'envsec_m1.tmp'
call sysfiledelete 'envsec_m2.tmp'

call lineout 'envsec_m1.tmp'

call sysfiledelete 'envsec_m2.tmp'
exit

[env.security.set] A manager belongs to a package. setSecurityManager of a Package sets the manager of that package. setSecurityManager of a Routine or a Method sets the manager of the package that holds its code, so a routine or method that new or newFile made, which has a package of its own, is governed alone, and several routines and methods that one package holds share one manager: setting it through one of them replaces what was set through another, and a call with no argument through any of them removes the manager from the code of all. In the example, the routine and the method of one package are governed by the manager of the package, then by the one the routine sets, then by the one the method sets, and the call with no argument through the method leaves the package with none, so that both run their commands. src = .array~of('::routine zqr public', ' address system "exit 1"', - ' return rc', '::class zqk public', '::method m', - ' address system "exit 2"', ' return rc')

r = p~findRoutine('ZQR')
m = p~findClass('ZQK')~method('M')
k = p~findClass('ZQK')~new

say 'package:' r~call k~m
r~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new('routine'))
say 'by the routine:' r~call k~m
m~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new('method'))
say 'by the method:' r~call k~m
m~setSecurityManager
say 'removed:' r~call k~m
exit

Code of another package is not governed, whoever calls it: a routine of the program that made the package, a routine of a package that it requires, an external program that it calls. These run under the manager of their own package, or under none. A package that the governed code makes with new or loadPackage has no manager unless the REQUIRES rule gives it one. A routine of a governed package that other code calls is governed as it runs: what is governed is the code, not its caller. In the example, the package has a routine with a label, a class whose method runs directly and as two started messages, and a required file. The manager answers each command with its number plus 100, so that the commands that reach it show as three-digit codes, and the command in the required file, which does not reach it, shows its own number. call sysfiledelete 'envsec_other.tmp'

A run is a call of a routine, a run of a method, or the main code of a program, and the labels that it calls and the text that it runs by INTERPRET are part of it. It takes the manager that its package has when it starts, and sends CALL, COMMAND, REQUIRES, STREAM and METHOD to that manager until it ends: a manager that the run removes or replaces keeps being asked, and a package that had no manager when the run started is not asked about them, whatever the run sets. LOCAL and ENVIRONMENT look at the manager that the package has when the name is read, so they follow a change at once. In the first example the routine replaces its manager old by new after its first command: its second command still goes to old and the name goes to new, and a second call of the routine, which starts with new, sends everything to new. In the second example the program governs itself. [env.security.call] The CALL checkpoint is sent as the class rule says, and also for the built-in functions BEEP, DIRECTORY and FILESPEC, which are offered like external routines. No other built-in function is offered, and the stream functions have their own checkpoint . A function of RexxUtil is offered like one of a library, and so is a program file that the search finds, at every call that finds it; the program that then runs is code of another package and is not governed. NAME is the name as the call rule reads it: in capitals for a symbol, as it is written for a string. ARGUMENTS is an array with one position for each argument up to the last one that was written: an argument that was left out in the middle is an absent position, and arguments left out at the end are not counted, so the call f(1, , "x") has size 3 and two items and f( , ) has size 0. A manager that answers 1 takes the call over, and the value of its RESULT entry is the value of the call, .nil included. With no entry a function call raises SYNTAX 44.1, and a CALL instruction leaves the variable RESULT dropped, as a call that returns no value does. A manager that answers 0 lets the search go on, and nothing it set in the directory counts: a name that the search does not find raises SYNTAX 43.1 although RESULT was set, and a changed NAME does not change the routine that is searched for. The first example shows the name and the arguments, and each way that a call ends. In the second, each built-in function of this book is called once and the manager notes the names it is sent; it takes those calls over, so that nothing runs. In the third, a program file is offered at each of two calls, and the command in it is not, and so is a function of RexxUtil. tests = .array~of('return envsecfun(1, , "x")', - 'call "EnvSecMix" 2; return result', - 'call envsecnone; return symbol("RESULT")', - 'return envsecnil() == .nil', 'return envsecnone()', - 'return envsecpoor()', 'return envsecpass()')

end

0 [env.security.command] The COMMAND checkpoint is sent as the class rule says, for the commands of the ADDRESS instruction and those of a clause that is an expression alone. ADDRESS is the name of the environment as the clause wrote it: in capitals for a symbol, as it is written for a string. COMMAND is the string after its expression is evaluated, and an empty or blank string is sent like any other. The directory holds just those two entries, also for a command with a redirection . A manager that answers 1 takes the redirection over with the command: nothing is read from an INPUT source or written to an OUTPUT or ERROR target (the third example). A clause that only names an environment sends nothing. A command that names no environment is sent with the name of the current one, which a program starts with as the initial environment rule says. What the manager sets counts only when it answers 1. RC is stored in the variable rc as it is, whatever it is. FAILURE and ERROR raise their condition whatever their value is (0 and .false included) and whatever RC is, so an ERROR entry with an RC of 0 raises ERROR with rc 0; when both are set, only FAILURE is raised. A manager that answers 0 leaves the command to run as it was written, whatever else it set: its RC is not used, and a changed COMMAND is not run. In the first example the commands of several clauses are shown to the manager. In the second, each line is a manager that answers one of the ways above, to a command that would end with rc 4 and has a handler for both conditions. tests = .array~of('address system "exit 1"', 'address "EnvSec" "exit 2"', - 'address envsec "exit" 1 + 2', - 'address system "exit 4" with output normal', 'address system ""', - 'address system " "', - 'o.0 = "untouched"; address system "echo hi" with output stem o.;' - 'say o.0', - 'address envsec')

That includes .environment and .local, which are entries of .environment ( the directories rule ), and the symbols that the interpreter answers itself, .context, .methods, .routines, .resources, .rs and .line, so a manager can provide .context to the code it governs. A name that .local already holds, such as .stdout, is asked of LOCAL only. A manager that answers 1 and sets RESULT provides the object that the symbol is, and the lookup stops there; .nil is an object, so a manager can provide it, and the symbol is then found and is .nil. A manager that answers 1 and sets no RESULT says that it found nothing, and the lookup goes on to the next place. A RESULT that a manager sets while it answers 0 is not used. Stream [env.security.stream] The STREAM checkpoint is sent when one of the stream functions CHARIN, CHAROUT, CHARS, LINEIN, LINEOUT, LINES and STREAM, with any arguments, names a stream whose absolute name is not in the program's table of streams, except for the standard streams, which the next rule takes out. NAME is the name that the function was given, made absolute as QUALIFY does . The table is one for the whole program and is keyed by the absolute name, so x and ./x are one entry. CHARIN, CHAROUT, CHARS, LINEIN, LINEOUT and LINES enter the name that they are given in the table, whether the code is governed or not and whether or not the stream can be opened. STREAM enters it only with an open command that succeeds; its other operations, such as D, S and a query command, are offered each time and leave the table as it is. The name is then not offered again, to any manager, until a close command of STREAM, or an open command of STREAM that fails, takes it out. A close sent to another Stream object of the same file does not. A stream that a manager chose is in the table under that name, so the code that no manager governs gets it as well. A manager that answers 1 and sets STREAM gives the function that object, which must understand the messages of a stream; one that answers 1 and sets no STREAM leaves the function to open the name as a file, as an answer of 0 does. In the example the program has the file open when the first manager is to be asked, so it is not asked. After the program closes the stream, the first manager is asked and provides a stream of another file; the second manager is not asked about that name while the stream is open, and the program gets the same stream. After the stream is closed once more the name is the real file again, and the second manager is asked. The second example shows the table for a file that does not exist: two query exists commands are offered and enter nothing, the first lines is offered and enters the name, the second and the one that spells the name with ./ are not, a failing open takes the name out, a close sent to a Stream object does not, and the close command does. f = 'envsec_real.tmp'

loaded 3 rc 4 [env.security.method] The METHOD checkpoint is sent as the class rule says. A method is protected when PROTECTED was declared or setProtected was sent, and the built-in methods that are protected are the ones that the second example prints. What is checked is the send, by governed code, to a protected method, in any form of a send: send, sendWith, the cascade ~~, the send of a Message and a send to self are all offered, and for an attribute the setter has the name with = after it. The messages that the interpreter and the built-in methods send while they carry out a clause of governed code are offered in the same way: the INIT that new sends, the MAKESTRING that a string value asks for (SAY, concatenation, request), the MAKEARRAY that DO OVER asks for, and a message that a built-in method sends to an argument, such as the COMPARE that sortWith sends. FORWARD, an operator, a message to the superclass (~name:super) and a protected class method are sends like the others, and for a class method OBJECT is the class. A message that the receiver has no method for, and that goes on to the receiver's UNKNOWN method, is not a checkpoint, even when UNKNOWN is protected: the message that the code sent names no protected method. A message that is started is not offered: the start of an object and of a Message run the method on another activity with no checkpoint. A protected method is run without a checkpoint when the sender is code with no manager, as the class rule says. The setSecurityManager methods are protected, so governed code that changes its manager is passed through the manager, which can stop the change by answering 1; the third example shows that the manager is still in place for the next run. In the first example, a package that has a manager sends messages to a protected method in the forms above, and the manager answers 1 with a result for those it is sent. 939.body:
[env.security.answer] Every checkpoint takes the same answers. The answer is 0 or 1 and nothing else: the strings 0 and 1 and the objects .false and .true are accepted, and any other value, such as 2, 01, 1, the empty string or an object, raises SYNTAX 34.903. A method that ends without an answer raises SYNTAX 91.999, whether it falls off its end or ends with a return or an exit that has no value. The error is raised by the clause that reached the checkpoint, in the code that the manager governs, so a handler of that code receives it as it does any error of the clause. In the example, one manager per checkpoint answers each of five ways, and the table shows what the governed code gets. The answers 0 and 1 are shown by the examples of the class rules. names = .array~of('CALL', 'COMMAND', 'LOCAL', 'ENVIRONMENT', 'REQUIRES', - 'STREAM', 'METHOD')
answers = .array~of('2', ' 1', '01', '', 'none')
n = 0
do cp over names line = left(cp, 12) do a over answers n = n + 1 src = 'signal on syntax;' act(cp, n) src = src || '; return "no error";' src = src 'syntax: return "error" condition("o")~code' r = .routine~new('agent', src) r~setSecurityManager(.mgr~new(cp, a)) line = line left(r~call, 12) end say line
end
exit

This holds for the other conditions too: RAISE ERROR, FAILURE, HALT, NOTREADY and USER in a manager method are handled by the matching SIGNAL ON of the governed code, with the description that the RAISE gave. An error of the manager's own code, such as a division by zero or a message that an object does not understand, is raised there in the same way. In the example the manager of each line raises one of these when it is asked about a command, and the handlers of the governed code write what they got. The errors of a wrong answer have the position of the governed clause. [instr.assignment.special] The names that the interpreter sets itself, RC, RESULT and SIGL, are ordinary variable symbols, and an assignment to one of them is an assignment like any other. So are TRUE and NIL, which differ from the environment symbols .TRUE and .NIL in the period. The interpreter assigns the three special variables again when the event that sets them happens, as a command sets RC. rc = 'mine'; result = 'mine'; sigl = 'mine'

In a program file the fault is found when the program is read, so that no clause runs, even one before the assignment, and the exit code is 225, which is 256 minus 31. exit

940.body: rexxref: Debugging Aids; Debugging Aids > Interactive Debugging of Programs; Debugging Aids > RXTRACE Variable Deviations: D150, D151, D152 Interactive tracing lets a person, or a program that stands in for one, step through another program: after each clause that is traced the interpreter stops, reads a line, and runs it or goes on. This page specifies how that state is entered and left, when the interpreter stops, what it reads and from where, what each kind of line does, and where its own lines are written. It leaves to other pages what they already own: the settings and the question mark prefix are those of the TRACE function , the format of the lines that show clauses is that of the TRACE instruction , and the objects .debuginput and .traceoutput are among the environment objects . Note. The examples feed the lines that a person would type from objects of their own, which a program installs as the debug input, and never from the terminal. The class in that most of them define answers its lines one at a time and then the empty line, and writes each line it answers in brackets, so that the output shows when the interpreter stops. The class show that most of them define receives the lines of the trace; it leaves out the line that holds the program's source string, which names the host's file. The line that the opening rule describes is checked in its own example.
940.title: Debugging

941.body:
[env.debugging.start] Interactive tracing starts when a TRACE instruction or a call of the TRACE function gives a setting that turns it on, and it starts with whatever letter that setting has. The clause that turns it on is traced under the old setting, as the effect rule says, so it is shown only when the old setting shows it. A TRACE instruction, and an assignment that calls the function, are followed by no stop: the first stop follows the next clause. Any other clause that calls the function and turns it on, a CALL, a SAY, an IF or a PARSE VALUE for instance, is followed by a stop at once, after the lines it caused; the notice comes before that stop and the source line before the next clause that is shown. How a package asks for it with ::OPTIONS TRACE is the business of the directive ; the environment variable RXTRACE is described below . In the first example the first clause that is shown is say 'one', the one after trace ?a, and the stop follows it, after what it wrote. In the second, the function turns it on from inside an assignment, and the stop follows the clause after that one. In the third, a CALL of the function turns it on, and the stop follows the CALL at once, so that say 'b' is shown only after it. In the fourth, the old setting is R, so the clause that turns interactive tracing on is shown. .debuginput~destination(.in~new(.array~of('', '')))

trace ?a
say 'one'

exit

[env.debugging.read] At a stop the interpreter sends the message LINEIN, with no argument, to the object that the entry DEBUGINPUT of .local holds, and takes the answer as the line that was typed. When the line is the empty string, the stop is over and the program goes on, so an input that has run dry and answers the empty string lets the program run on. The example installs an object of its own on .debuginput: it is sent LINEIN three times, with no argument each time, for the line it answers, the empty line that follows, and the stop after the second nop. .traceoutput~destination(.quiet~new)

The example makes .debuginput the way it was by taking the destination that it installed off, and then sets the destination of .input: the stops read from that object. .traceoutput~destination(.quiet~new)

Replacing the entry INPUT of .local by another object changes what .input finds and not the monitor that .debuginput is connected to, so the stops do not read from it; and an object that is in .environment under the name DEBUGINPUT is not read when the entry of .local is gone. When the entry is gone, a stop reads nothing and the program goes on; interactive tracing stays on. 944.title: What is read

945.body:
[env.debugging.input.clause] A line that is not empty and not = is run as the clauses it holds, in the way an INTERPRET clause would run it: it can hold several clauses, separated by semicolons, and a group such as a DO must be complete in it. Variables that it sets stay set. The clauses of the line are not traced, so they write no line, and no stop follows any of them. After the line has run the interpreter stops again: it reads another line, and goes on to the next clause of the program only when the line is empty or does one of the things that the rules below give. A line that holds only blanks, only a comment, only a semicolon or only nop does nothing and is followed by another read. A LEAVE or an ITERATE in a line does not reach the loops of the program: it raises error 28, which is reported as the next rule says. An INTERPRET in a line runs its string untraced too ( Deviation 150 ). In the example the interpreter reads eight lines after say 'prog' x, the last one the empty line. .debuginput~destination(.in~new(.array~of('x = 5; y = x * 2', 'say x y', 'do k = 1 to 2; say k; end', ' ', ';', 'nop', '/* just a comment */', '')))

946.body:
[env.debugging.end] Interactive tracing ends when a line typed at a stop turns it off, as the rule for TRACE lines says; when the program calls the TRACE function with a setting that turns it off, as the prefix rule says, where a TRACE instruction does nothing, as its rule says; when the code that turned it on returns, as the next rule says; and when the program ends. An input that has run dry does not end it, as the last row of the table of the rule for TRACE lines shows. In the example the first routine turns it on and returns after two stops, and the second turns it off by a call of the function, so that the clauses after the call have no stop; the count of reads shows it. .traceoutput~destination(.quiet~new)

In the example the internal routine inner stops, and so does the code after it; the routine outer is not traced and has no stop, and the caller reads ?A again after it. .debuginput~destination(.in~new(.array~of('', '', '', '', '', '', '', '')))

946.title: How it ends

947.body:
[env.debugging.rxtrace] When the interpreter starts, it reads the environment variable RXTRACE once. If its value is ON, in any combination of upper and lower case and with nothing else in it, the program starts as if its first clause were TRACE ?R, and so does each program that it calls by name and each routine object, whether a ::ROUTINE directive defines it or new or newFile of Routine makes it: trace() answers ?R in it and its first clause is shown. A method starts with N as without the variable, and an internal routine starts with its caller's setting, as the scope rule says. Any other value, among them one with a blank around ON, and the empty value, is ignored. A later change of the variable changes nothing. An example cannot start the interpreter with the variable set, so the rule is tested by the cases of the command-line tests, which set it and show the main program and a program called by name starting with ?R, a routine called by name, as a function and as a routine object starting with ?R, a method with N, and every other value ignored. The example shows the later change: a program called by name before and after the variable is set to ON starts with N both times. .traceoutput~destination(.quiet~new)
call lineout 'a6rrzqrx.rex', 'return trace()'
call lineout 'a6rrzqrx.rex'
say 'before' a6rrzqrx()
old = value('RXTRACE', 'ON', 'ENVIRONMENT')
say 'after' a6rrzqrx()
call value 'RXTRACE', old, 'ENVIRONMENT'
call sysfiledelete 'a6rrzqrx.rex'
exit

::method lineout return 0 before N

948.body:
[env.debugging.deviation.150] An INTERPRET in a line runs the clauses of its string as the rest of the line runs: they are not traced and no stop follows them, so that the line interpret 'say 7' writes 7 and the interpreter then reads the next line. ooRexx traces the clauses of the string: it writes the line of say 7 and then stops once more before it reads the next line, so that it reads one line more than interrexx does; a string of several clauses causes a stop after each. The example is not run against it. .debuginput~destination(.in~new(.array~of("interpret 'say 7'", '', '', '', '')))

say 'two'
say 'three'

949.body: rexxref: Concurrency This chapter specifies how a program does more than one thing at a time: the activities that run its code, how they are made, what they share and what they keep apart, and what one of them can and cannot know of the others. The pages of this chapter are: Activities : what an activity is, which code runs on which activity when a program uses start, REPLY, a message object, an alarm or a ticker, how the result or the error of a message that another activity ran reaches the program, and which things happen in an order that a program can count on and which do not. Locks : what a lock belongs to, which methods take one and when, what an activity that holds one may do, how often it is held, and what happens when activities wait for each other in a ring. Halt and program end : where a HALT asked for by another activity or by the host lands in an activity and what it does not end, what keeps a program alive after its main program has ended and what its status is then, and how the message UNINIT that the interpreter sends works with more than one activity. The methods of the classes Message , Alarm , Ticker , Monitor , EventSemaphore and MutexSemaphore , and the instructions REPLY and GUARD , are specified on their own pages; this chapter links them and specifies only what they have in common. Every example in this chapter that uses more than one activity forces the order of what it prints. It waits for the result of a message, parks an activity on a GUARD ... WHEN that the program opens when it is ready, or asks for results in a fixed order; it never relies on how long an activity takes, and the output of such an example is the same on every run.
949.title: Concurrency

950.body: rexxref: Concurrency; Concurrency > Early Reply; Concurrency > Message Objects Deviations: D18, D20 A program is run by an activity: a thread of control that runs the clauses of the program one after another, keeps the calls it has made, each with the variables that the rules of its call give it. A program starts with one activity. It gets more by asking for them: it starts a message, replies early from a method, or sets an alarm or a ticker. The activities that exist at one time run side by side. They share every object they can reach, and each keeps its own calls, its own variables and its own traps. This page specifies what an activity is, where each kind of new activity comes from and which code it runs, how the answer or the error of a message that another activity ran reaches the program, and what a program may count on about the order in which activities do things. The lock that an object has, the methods that are guarded or unguarded and the GUARD instruction are specified on the locks page of this chapter, and HALT and the end of a program that still has activities on the halt page ; this page uses GUARD ... WHEN only as the way a program makes one activity wait for another. The methods of Message, Alarm and Ticker and the instruction REPLY are specified on their own pages, which this page links: it states what they do to activities, and not what they check or answer. The examples force the order of everything they print. An activity that has to wait for the program does so on a GUARD ... WHEN that the program opens when it is ready, and a program that needs a result asks for it with result or wait. A method that another activity waits for, or that waits for the program, is UNGUARDED, so that the program can still use the object meanwhile ( the exclusion rule ).

[conc.activities.model] An activity runs one clause at a time, in the order the program gives. Two activities share the objects they can both reach: an object that one of them changes is changed for the other, and so are the entries of .local and .environment. They do not share the variables of a call. The variables of a method or routine call belong to the activity that made the call, so a method that another activity runs starts with its own variables, even when the same name is set in the code that started it. [conc.activities.creation] A program makes a new activity by each of the following, and by nothing else (the UNINIT methods of objects are run as the halt page says): start and startWith of Object, and start and startWith of a Message, which run the message on a new activity; reply and replyWith of a Message, which run a copy of the message on a new activity; the REPLY instruction, which runs the rest of a method on a new activity; an Alarm or a Ticker , which sends its target triggered on an activity of the library; and a message object that receives messageComplete or triggered, which runs itself on a new activity ( the rule ). The call that makes the activity does not wait for the code the activity runs: it returns, and that code runs next to the program. send and sendWith of a Message and an ordinary message to an object are not among the list. The method they run is run by the activity that sent the message, which goes on when the method has ended or has replied. log = .array~new

954.body:
[conc.activities.order] Two things done by different activities happen in a known order only when the second activity can learn that the first has done its part. The ways it learns are these, and nothing else orders two activities. One is the order of the clauses of one activity: what an activity did before it started a message, or made an alarm or a ticker, is done before the first clause of that message, or of the target's triggered, runs, and what a message did is done when result or wait returns for it, except the report of its error ( the unasked rule ), and before the targets of its notifications are sent. Another is a GUARD ... WHEN whose condition is false, which does not go on until another activity has made the condition true, and what that activity did before is done when the first goes on. The third is a wait on an EventSemaphore, which ends when another activity posts it, and a MutexSemaphore, which is acquired only after its owner has released it: what the other activity did before the post or the release is done. The fourth is the guard of an object: an activity that takes it, by calling a guarded method or by GUARD ON, does so only after the activity that held it has given it up, and what that activity did before is done ( the scope rule ; the exclusion rule ). Anything else is not ordered. A clause that does not wait (none of the waits of the waiting rule ) and that calls no method, routine or function of the program, and no library method that runs code of the program, is one step: no clause of another activity runs while it is half done. The library's own methods are part of the step however they are built. The clauses of activities that nothing orders may run in any interleaving that keeps the order of each activity's own clauses, and which one runs may differ between runs and between implementations ( Deviation 22 , and Deviation 7 for trace lines). That one message was started before another does not make it run first. log = .array~new

The second has two activities that nothing orders write three entries each: the log always has six entries, and the entries of each activity are in order. The third has the program store a value and then post a semaphore that a message waits for, store another and then release a mutex that another message acquires, and has two activities ask for the same result. [conc.activities.waiting] An activity that waits does not hold up another. The waits are: result and wait of a message, a GUARD ... WHEN whose condition is false, the lock of an object that another activity holds, an EventSemaphore's wait, a MutexSemaphore's acquire that has to wait, lineIn of a RexxQueue that holds no line, a command that runs without redirection, and the waits of the semaphore functions and SysSleep of the RexxUtil library; an activity in one of them goes on to its next clause only when what it waits for has happened (a GUARD ... WHEN evaluates its expression again meanwhile, as the rule on WHEN says), and every other activity that is not itself waiting makes progress meanwhile. How fast each progresses, and whether the activities that are not waiting share the time fairly, is not specified, and so is how soon an activity whose wait has ended runs again. When several activities wait for the same thing, which of them gets it first, such as a line of a queue or a mutex, is not specified. [conc.activities.deviation.18] Two activities that each busy-wait inside nested constructs, such as INTERPRET, for a variable that only the other sets, where the program must run the other for either to go on, never end. The program prints nothing of what they would return, and neither activity gets past its wait. ooRexx preempts both and they complete ( Deviation 18 ). [conc.activities.deviation.20] A wait that no other activity, alarm, ticker or call can end is refused, and the program ends with exit code 120. It is, for instance, the wait for the result of a message that has never been sent and that no activity can still send, or the original of a reply, whose copy ran; the same holds for wait. ooRexx waits for ever ( Deviation 20 ). 956.body: rexxref: Concurrency > Default Concurrency; Concurrency > Sending Messages within an Activity; Concurrency > Using Additional Concurrency Mechanisms; Concurrency > Using Additional Concurrency Mechanisms > SETUNGUARDED Method and UNGUARDED Option; Concurrency > Using Additional Concurrency Mechanisms > GUARD ON and GUARD OFF; Concurrency > Using Additional Concurrency Mechanisms > Guarded Methods Deviations: D14, D20, D160 Methods of one object can run on several activities at once, and a guarded method must not run at the same time as another guarded method that works on the same object variables. The interpreter keeps them apart with locks. This page specifies what a lock belongs to, which methods take one and when, what an activity that already holds a lock may do, how often a lock is held, and what happens when activities wait for each other in a ring. The GUARD instruction owns the instruction and its WHEN form, the ::METHOD directive owns the options, and the Method class owns the methods that change them; this page links those rules and says what they mean for the locks. The page says only what is guaranteed. Which of several activities that wait for the same lock gets it first is not specified, and neither is how long a wait lasts; the examples are arranged so that nothing in their output depends on either. An example that must show that a method can run while another holds a lock makes the program wait for it: if the method could not run, the example would not end. An example that must show that a method cannot run starts it, lets the holder end, and shows the order in which the two ended, which the rule forces. How activities are started and how they end is the matter of the activities page of this chapter; here every activity is one that the program starts with start.
956.title: Locks

957.body:
[conc.locks.scope] An object has one lock for each of its scopes, and the lock of a scope is held by at most one activity at a time. A guarded method holds the lock of its scope from its first clause until it ends or gives it up, and an activity that asks for a lock that another activity holds waits until the holder lets it go. The scope of a method is the class that gave the method to the object, as the scope rule says, and the object variables of that class are the ones its methods share ( the scope rule of EXPOSE ). So two guarded methods of the same class run one after the other when they work on one object, and run together when they work on two objects. Guarded methods of different scopes of one object run together as well, whether the scopes are a class and its subclass, a class and a mixin class that it inherits, or a class and one of its superclasses. In the example every trial has a holder, which stays inside a guarded method until the program lets it go, and a probe, which appends a word to a log. Where the probe can run at once the program waits for it before it lets the holder go, and the log shows the probe first. Where it cannot, the log shows the holder's end first. call trial 'sub holds, sub probes', 'subHold', 'subProbe', 'wait'

958.body:
[conc.locks.default] A method is guarded unless it is unguarded, and a guarded method takes the lock of its scope when it starts. A method that a ::METHOD directive declares is guarded unless the directive says UNGUARDED, class methods included. The two methods of an ::ATTRIBUTE directive take the option of the directive, so both are guarded or both unguarded. A ::CONSTANT directive makes an unguarded method. A method of the name UNKNOWN, a method that define gives to a class and a method that new makes are guarded unless they were made unguarded, whatever the code they run. The method options and isGuarded say the same of the options and of what a Method object answers; this rule says what it means for the locks. In the example a guarded holder keeps the lock of the class, and an unguarded relay method sends each probe to the object and appends a word to the log when the probe has answered, so the log shows whether the probe had to wait. The probes that wait for the holder are the guarded methods, the accessors of a guarded attribute, and the UNKNOWN method that answers a message the object has no method for; the others run at once. .k~define('made', .method~new('made', 'return 1'))
