959.body:
[conc.locks.nested] An activity that holds the lock of a scope of an object can send a message to a method of that scope of that object, and the method runs at once, as a call inside the activity: the activity holds the lock already and holds it once more for the length of the call. It does not matter who sends the message: the object to itself, a method of another object that the first called, or code outside any object that a method of the first called. A message to a method of another scope, or of another object, takes the lock of that scope or object, and waits for it if another activity holds it. A message that is started, as start does, is run by another activity, which holds nothing of the sender's, so it can wait for a lock that the sender holds. In the example an object sends a message to itself, and it sends a message to another object whose method sends a message back to the first. Both run on the one activity and both end. a = .node~new('a')

A GUARD ON in a method that holds the lock already, and a GUARD OFF in a method that does not, change nothing, so repeated ones do not count. The lock is free for the other activities when the activity holds it no more. A method that gives up its own hold with GUARD OFF therefore lets another activity in only when no method below it, on the same activity, still holds the lock. A method that replies keeps its hold on the new activity, or, when a guarded method below it on the old activity holds the lock as well, gives up its hold on the old activity and asks for the lock again on the new one, as the REPLY rule says. A line that TRACE writes in a method shows the count in the entries HASSCOPELOCK and SCOPELOCKCOUNT of its trace object . The first example prints them for the lines of three methods that call a method which does a GUARD OFF; where an outer method holds the lock, the inner one counts two holds and, after its GUARD OFF, one. The methods have no EXPOSE, whose effect on the entries is not specified. The second example starts a method that repeats GUARD ON or GUARD OFF and shows with a probe whether the lock was free while the method waited: repeated instructions leave the lock as the first one did. .traceoutput~destination(.sink~new)

96.body: CALL {name | (expression)} [argument] [, [argument]]... | CALL ON condition [NAME label] | CALL OFF condition ANSI: 6.3.2.37, 8.3.4; rexxref: Keyword Instructions > CALL CALL runs a routine as a subroutine and goes on with the clause after it when the routine returns. The routine is an internal one, which is a label of the same program, a built-in function, or an external routine, and the name of the CALL decides where the search for it looks. The routine may return a value, which the CALL leaves in the variable RESULT. The ON and OFF forms do not call anything: they switch the trap of a condition. This page specifies the arguments, the search order as far as it separates internal routines from built-in ones, RESULT and SIGL, and the errors. How a routine is found outside the program belongs to the order rule , and what a trap does when its condition occurs to the chapter on conditions .

960.body:
[conc.locks.when] GUARD ON WHEN and GUARD OFF WHEN give up the hold of their own method while the condition is false. GUARD ON WHEN takes the lock before each evaluation of the condition, so it evaluates it with the lock held and goes on holding it, as the WHEN rule says. GUARD OFF WHEN gives up its method's hold first and evaluates the condition without it each time, while another activity may hold the lock. The condition is evaluated again when another activity assigns a value to an object variable that the condition names as a simple symbol, even the value that it had, or drops one, whether or not the last evaluation reached that name; a variable that only a method that the condition calls reads is not one of them. A compound variable or a stem in the condition names the whole stem, which Deviation 160 describes. When the condition is evaluated at other times is not specified. The wait gives up only that one hold. When the method was called by a guarded method on the same activity, which holds the lock too ( the counting rule ), the other activities find the lock held while the condition waits, so that a guarded method of another activity cannot change the variable that the condition reads: only an unguarded method can. The example sends the change from an unguarded and from a guarded method, to a waiting method that a guarded or an unguarded method called. The three trials that end are the ones in which the method that changes the variable can run; the fourth, where a guarded method has to wait for the lock that its own caller's activity holds, is the case of Deviation 20 , and the example does not run it. The second example ends only if GUARD OFF WHEN evaluates its condition without the lock: a guarded method waits in it, a guarded method of another activity then takes the lock and keeps it until the waiting method has gone on, and an unguarded method makes the condition true. call trial 'guarded caller, unguarded setter', 'outerG', 'setU'

963.body:
[conc.locks.deadlock] An activity waits for another when it asks for a lock that the other holds, or when it waits, with result or wait , for a message that the other runs. A wait of either kind that would close a ring of such waits, with the waiting activity in it, could never end, and it is refused: it raises SYNTAX 98.905 in the activity that was about to wait, at the clause that asked for the lock or at the result or wait of the message. A guarded method asks for its lock when it starts, so a refused guarded method does not run: the sender sees the error, or the message keeps it when the message was started, and result raises it again. The lock that GUARD ON asks for is refused in the same way. When the waits of two activities close a ring at once, which of them is refused is not specified, and the other goes on when the refused one has ended and let go of its locks. In the first example a method holds the lock of its object and waits for the result of a message that it started to the same object, whose method needs the lock. Whichever of the two waits closes the ring is refused, the request for the lock or the result, and either way the error reaches the trap of the main program. The second is a ring of two objects, in which each of two activities holds the lock of its own object and then asks for the other's; one of them is refused, and the method that it asked for does not run. The third asks for the lock with GUARD ON in an unguarded method. The fourth has no lock in the ring: two started unguarded methods each wait for the result of the other's message; the one that closes the ring is refused, and the result of the other raises the same error again. o = .k~new

964.body:

In the first example the first message waits in an INTERPRET until a flag is set; the second sets the flag and then waits, in an INTERPRET, for the first one's result. In the second a method that run runs keeps the lock of the object and waits for a flag; the method that sets the flag then asks, in a method that run runs, for the same lock. say 'start'

965.body: rexxref: Concurrency; Builtin Classes > Fundamental Classes > Message Class > halt; Objects and Classes > Object Destruction and Uninitialization Deviations: D10, D21, D162 This page specifies three things that reach an activity from outside its own clauses: a HALT that another activity or the host asks for, the end of the main program while other activities still run, and the message UNINIT that the interpreter sends to an object that nothing can reach any more. The condition HALT itself, its traps and what an untrapped one does are on the HALT page ; the halt method of Message owns what the method checks and answers; the status of the command is the invocation rule , and when UNINIT is sent, and to what, is the rule of the invocation page . This page says where in a program with several activities each of these lands, and what the others do meanwhile. The examples force the order of what they print, as the chapter says. An example that has to show that a wait was not ended by a HALT cannot rely on a program having reached the wait before it sends the HALT: each such waiter tells the program that it is about to wait while it evaluates the clause that waits, by a call of a built-in method in the last clause of the method that marks it, so that no clause boundary is left between the mark and the wait, and a HALT is taken only at a clause boundary.

966.body:
[conc.halt.sent] halt of a message that another activity runs is the way a program raises HALT in an activity other than its own. The condition is raised in that activity, at a clause boundary, in the call that the activity is running then: the method that the message names, or any method or ::ROUTINE that method has called and that is still running. Only a trap of that call can answer it as HALT ( the scope rule ). A call that has no trap for it leaves it untrapped, and it becomes the SYNTAX error 4.1 there ( the rule ), which goes up to the callers as any SYNTAX error does ( the rule ): the HALT trap of a caller is not taken, a SYNTAX trap of a caller is, with no description, and an error that no call traps ends the message with 4.1 ( hasError ). A trap in the running call itself sees HALT with the description that halt was given. Which clause of the target is the first to see a HALT that is sent while the target runs is not specified ( Deviation 22 ). Deviation 17 names a case in which interrexx takes such a HALT only when a nested region that runs beneath the activity has ended; no example here shows it. g = .gate~new

On Linux, SIGINT and SIGTERM make this request, and a program can send one to itself with a command: kill of the shell's parent, which is the interpreter. 968.body:
[conc.halt.end.alive] When the main program has ended, the program goes on until every other activity has ended. It does not end while a started message has not ended, while the rest of a method that has replied is still running, while a call of the target of an alarm or a ticker is under way, while an alarm has neither gone off nor been cancelled, or while a ticker has been neither cancelled nor stopped. Each of them runs as it did before: the end of the main program is not a HALT for them, and they may wait for each other and use the objects of the program. An alarm that has gone off, an alarm or a ticker that was cancelled, and a ticker that an error in its target's triggered stopped ( the timers rule ) do not keep the program, so a cancelled alarm or ticker with a delay of a minute does not make the program last a minute. An activity that waits for something that nothing can bring about any more keeps the program for ever. interrexx refuses such a wait ( Deviation 20 ), but once the main program has ended it does not refuse it yet, and the program hangs (#249), which no example here tests. A main program that interrexx ends with a refusal does not wait for any of them ( the Deviation 21 rule ). The status of the command is the main program's ( the next rule ). g = .gate~new

[conc.halt.deviation.10] A HALT that a signal asks for ends the wait of an activity that waits for a GUARD ... WHEN condition, for the post of an EventSemaphore, for a MutexSemaphore, or in SysSleep. The clause that waited finishes, with wait and acquire answering 0, and the activity takes the HALT at once ( Deviation 10 ). It ends the wait for a command too, and RC is then -4. SIGINT and SIGTERM halt the program with 4.1 even when SIGHUP is ignored, as under nohup; ooRexx installs no handler then and the signal ends it, and no example tests that. A wait for the result or the end of a message, or for the lock of an object, is not ended. A halt of a message ends no wait ( the rule ). ooRexx ends none of these waits for a signal. The activity goes on waiting until its condition holds, the post or the release comes, or the time is up, and then takes the HALT, so that in the example, where nothing posts, releases or opens, it waits for ever. ooRexx's RC after a command that a signal interrupted is unpredictable. f = SysTempFileName('conc-halt-????.rex')

971.body: rexxref: Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil); Rexx Utilities (RexxUtil) > A Note on Error Codes Deviations: D34, D101 RexxUtil is the set of functions that a program calls to work with files, directories, stems, the macrospace, processes, time and the terminal. This chapter specifies the functions that exist on a Unix-like system, one page per function. This page holds what every function shares: how the functions are made available, how their arguments are read, what a name of a file is, and what the numbers they answer mean. The pages of this chapter are: SysFileDelete , SysFileExists , SysIsFile , SysIsFileDirectory and SysIsFileLink : removing a file and asking what a name is. SysMkDir and SysRmDir : making and removing a directory. SysFileCopy and SysFileMove : copying and moving a file. SysTempFileName and SysSearchPath : inventing a name that is not in use, and finding a file along a list of directories. SysStemCopy , SysStemDelete , SysStemInsert and SysStemSort : working on a stem array, and SysDumpVariables : writing the variables of the current scope. The macrospace and its functions SysAddRexxMacro , SysDropRexxMacro , SysQueryRexxMacro , SysReorderRexxMacro , SysClearRexxMacroSpace , SysSaveRexxMacroSpace and SysLoadRexxMacroSpace : the routines that the service keeps for every program, and how they are added, found, moved, saved and loaded. SysFileTree and SysFileSearch : finding files by a pattern and lines of a file by a string, and SysGetFileDateTime and SysSetFileDateTime : the times of a file. SysSleep , SysWait , SysFork , SysCreatePipe , SysQueryProcess and SysSetPriority : time and processes, and the event semaphore and the mutex semaphore functions. SysCls , SysGetKey , SysGetErrorText , SysGetMessage , SysGetMessageX , SysFormatMessage , SysLinVer , SysUtilVersion and SysVersion : the terminal, messages and versions; and the Windows-only functions . The rules state the behavior of a Unix-like system. The examples make their own files and directories, whose names start with c, a digit and zq, apart from one named after a function in the availability rule and the names that start with ~ before that prefix, and remove them again. What a function answers for a failure is what the answer rule gives: an error number of Linux for the functions that change files, and a fixed value for the functions that the rule names.

A function that reads a stem array reads the tail 0 first. It is n when it is a whole number, written as 4, 4, 04, 4.0, 4e0 or +4. A stem without that tail, a tail that is not a whole number after that rounding, such as 1.5 or a word, a value at or above that limit, and a stem that has only a default value (s. = 'x') raise SYNTAX 40.922: the default of a stem is never the value of a tail that has none. A position or a number of items that is outside the array raises SYNTAX 40.923. An item can be any object, and a function that moves an item moves the object itself, so that the item is still the same object. [util.index.codes] A function that works on the system answers what it did, and a failure of the system is an answer, never a SYNTAX condition. A missing file, a directory in place of a file, a refused permission and a name that is already taken leave the program running. What a function raises is limited to bad arguments, which the page of each function lists. SysFileDelete, SysMkDir, SysRmDir, SysFileCopy and SysFileMove answer 0 when they did it. Otherwise they answer the system's error number for the failure: 2 for a name that nothing has or a directory in it that does not exist, 13 for a permission that the system refuses, 17 for a name that is taken, 20 for a name that must be a directory and is not (a component before the last, or the target of a directory that is moved when that is an entry other than a directory or a regular file, such as a fifo, and not a symbolic link that leads to a regular file), 21 for a directory where a file is needed, 22 for a directory moved into itself, and 39 for a directory that is not empty. Other failures answer the system's other numbers, such as 36 for a name that is too long. The page of each of these five functions gives the number of every failure it lists, and says where the function departs from the system's number. The other functions answer fixed values, which their pages state. SysFileTree answers 0 whether or not it could read what it was asked for. SysFileSearch answers 0, or 3 for a file that it cannot read. SysSetFileDateTime answers 0, or -1 for every failure. SysGetFileDateTime answers a time, or -1. SysTempFileName and SysSearchPath answer a name, or the null string. A function that answers a state, such as SysFileExists, answers 0 or 1 and has no failure to report. say SysFileDelete('c1zqidxnone') SysMkDir('c1zqidxnone/sub') SysRmDir('c1zqidxnone')

[instr.call.search] A name written as a symbol is read in upper case and searched in this order: a label of the code that holds the CALL, then a built-in function, then an external routine. That code is the main program, or the body of the one routine or method that the CALL is in, so the labels of the other parts of the file are not searched. A label wins over a built-in function of the same name, so a program can replace a built-in one. A name written as a string is used as it is written and is not searched among the labels at all, so the search starts with the built-in functions, whose names are in capitals, and goes on to the external routines. A string that is not in capitals therefore never reaches a built-in function, and a label of the same text is not found by it either: with the labels 'myLab': and mylab:, the string 'myLab' finds neither. The labels of a method are the ones that a CALL in it finds, as the second example shows. How external routines are found is the subject of the order rule . A name that nothing answers to raises SYNTAX 43.1 when the CALL runs. call length 'abc'

[instr.call.result] When the routine returns a value, RESULT is set to it, and when the routine returns no value, RESULT is dropped and is unset afterwards. This holds for every kind of routine, so a built-in function that answers a value sets RESULT like any other, and a routine that returns nothing drops the value that an earlier call left. A function call in an expression does not set it. Where a message instruction sets the variable, the message rule says. call giver 2
say 'giver:' result
call quiet
say 'quiet:' symbol('result')
result = 'old'
call abs -4
say 'abs:' result
result = 'old'
call quiet
say 'quiet:' symbol('result') result
result = 'kept'
x = giver(1)
say 'function:' result
exit
giver: return arg(1) * 21
quiet: return giver: 42
quiet: LIT
abs: 4
quiet: LIT RESULT
function: kept [instr.call.restore] The settings of an internal routine are its own. When NUMERIC settings, the trace setting or the default environment of ADDRESS are changed inside the routine, the caller has the ones it had before the CALL when the routine returns, whether or not the routine starts with PROCEDURE. For NUMERIC, the scope rule says it, and for the trace setting the TRACE rule does. The same holds for the address environment, which the ADDRESS page specifies, and the traps of conditions that the conditions chapter specifies. The routine of the example traces, and that trace output goes to standard error, so the output block shows only the standard output. numeric digits 5
trace o
address foo
call s
say digits() 1/3 address()
exit
s: numeric digits 3; trace r; address bar return 5 0.33333 FOO [instr.call.sigl] A CALL of an internal routine sets SIGL, in the variable scope of the caller, to the line number of the CALL clause, which is the line where the clause starts when it runs over several lines. A routine that starts with PROCEDURE has its own scope and sees SIGL only if it exposes it. A CALL of a built-in function or of an external routine does not set it, and an external routine has a scope of its own that holds no SIGL. The SIGNAL rule says what SIGNAL sets. say 'start' sigl
call abs 1
say 'builtin' sigl
call ext
say 'external' sigl
call sub
say 'sub' sigl
call psub
call esub
call sub 1, 2
say 'two lines' sigl
exit
sub: say 'in sub' sigl; return
psub: procedure say 'in psub' symbol('sigl') return
esub: procedure expose sigl say 'in esub' sigl return
